Why settle for decorations that only last a few weeks? Create beautiful seasonal containers that can brighten your entrance well into winter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Holiday porch pots are a cheerful way to decorate your home's entrance for the festive season. These outdoor winter arrangements look beautiful and welcoming when placed near front doors, steps, or entryways to greet guests during the holidays.

As October ends, the holiday season approaches. Families make Thanksgiving plans, starting a season that lasts right through the new year. This is the ideal time to start putting together natural holiday decorations that bring bright colors and greenery to your home's entrance.

If you are ready to jump into a creative gardening project for winter, we’ve got the ideas to get you started. The basic idea is to combine beautiful plants and greenery to make spectacular seasonal containers. But you should plan to have some fun while you are doing it.

The best plants for DIY holiday porch pots combine appealing structure with festive cut boughs. They should be hardy enough to survive cold weather and add winter curb appeal.

Why not start with an evergreen that nobody else on your block is likely to display? This silver Korean fir cultivar is one of a kind: a curious, fascinating dwarf evergreen with twisted, curled silvery needles. The twisted needles of ‘Ice Breaker’ Korean fir (Abies koreana), available at Nature Hills, have frosted undersides, making it look as if it is perpetually snow-covered. These little beauties grow very slowly, getting to 2 feet tall after 10 years. They are hardy down to -20°F.

It’s easy to find evergreen foliage plants without red berries, but harder to find red berries without evergreen foliage. That’s exactly why winterberry holly (Ilex verticillata) in holiday porch pots is totally intriguing. You can order a best-selling Berry Poppins winterberry holly from Plant Addicts.

These native hollies – growing in eastern Canada through the southern United States – are pretty plants all year long, but they become stunningly beautiful at the dreariest time of the year. They lose their leaves in autumn, leaving only the amazing crop of bright berries to light up your winter pots. They are hardy down to USDA zone 3.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Ornamental cabbages and kales (Brassica oleracea) are cold-hardy foliage plants that provide exceptionally vivid white, pink, red, and purple winter colors for holiday pots. They are technically edible but are not grown for eating. Rather, they are cultivated for their bright, rose-like center rosettes.

Ornamental cabbage and kale plants maintain their bright structure and color well into freezing winter months. For a festive container, they can be combined with winter-hardy pansies, berried twigs, chrysanthemums, or ornamental grasses.

Pick up a four-pack of Song Bird Red Ornamental Kale Plants from Burpee.

You may know these stunning plants as hellebores (Helleborus niger), or as Christmas roses. Whatever you call them, they make fantastic additions to holiday porch pots, with their shining white flowers and strong, dark green leaves. The only issue with hellebores is that they usually don’t bloom until January – past the heart of the holiday porch pot season. But some cultivars bloom just in time for the holidays, such as ‘Christmas Carol Early’, 'Jacob', and 'Snowbells', available at Plant Delights Nursery. The Christmas rose is usually hardy to USDA zone 3.

This dense, naturally round shrub is a perfect little ball of soft green needles. Its small size and low-maintenance nature make Little Gem Norway spruce (Picea abies 'Little Gem') a popular addition to your holiday porch pot. You can order a plant from Magic Valley Gardens at Walmart.

Norway spruce grows slowly, adding only about an inch or two in size every year and topping out at about 3 feet tall and wide. Don’t worry about winter weather – ‘Little Gem’ is hardy down to -40°F. The new growth emerges soft and bright lime, but by Christmas it will be a handsome forest green.

The flowers that give Heuchera its common name of coral bells only appear in spring and summer. By the time the holiday season rolls around, you’ll appreciate this plant's incredible foliage. Coral bells offer a wide range of leaf colors beyond green, including apricot, bronze, pewter, burgundy, and deep purple. The foliage often adds even more enchantment with scalloped, wavy, or veined edges. Select ‘Caramel’ or ‘Peachberry Ice’ cultivars, both available at Plant Addicts, for foliage with rich tones and holiday warmth.

Many trailing “spiller” plants work well in holiday plant pots, but few are better than the classic evergreen trailing English ivy (Hedera helix), available in an ivy variety pack from Plant Addicts. This hardy vine softens the edges of holiday planters and offers all-weather resilience. It stays vibrant throughout the season and works well with flowers or small evergreen shrubs to create a festive feel. The cascading leaves create a rich, full look, balancing upright or mounding holiday plants.

If you’re ready to create gorgeous holiday plant pots of your own, a few practical tips will help. Let’s get down to the basics of how to put it all together.

The base of it all is the pots or containers you select. Choose pots in materials that can handle winter temperatures, like metal, wood, or even plastic. Avoid materials that will crack when the temperatures drop. Get pots that are big enough, but not too big. Generally, front door holiday plant pots should be between 12 and 30 inches in diameter and between 12 and 18 inches deep.

You’ll want to use potting soil in the containers. Leftover summer potting soil works just fine, but it’s best to buy fresh, like Miracle-Gro Organic Outdoor Potting Mix, from Amazon.

Next, you’ll want to put in the plants, and I suggest using a classic thriller, filler, spiller design. Start with the thrillers. These are the tall, eye-catching focal plants that make guests admire the pots. You can use one of the taller plants you have selected – like winterberry holly or ‘Ice Breaker’ fir – or you can use cut boughs after trimming the stems.

Get ready to layer in the fillers. This is the place for medium-height evergreens or foliage plants. Coral bells or ornamental cabbage work well in this role. Alternate textures and shades.

Last, add the spillers, plants with draping or trailing foliage. These go around the bottom edge of the container so that they cascade gracefully over the edges of the container.

Creating your plant pots is fun, but you’ll also have to put in a little effort to keep them going strong through the season.

This starts with care immediately after you set out the pots. Give each of them a deep watering, enough to saturate the entire soil. Excess water should run out of the drainage holes in the bottom of the pot. Make sure that’s the case, or your plants will die of root rot. It helps to add pot feet to elevate the containers off freezing patios.

Don’t worry too much about freezing weather. It is normal for the moisture in the patio pots to freeze. Keep checking the soil and add more water if the top inches are dry. Mist the evergreen branches during dry winter days to rehydrate the foliage. As the weather cools, cluster the containers close to the house wall to shield them from winter winds and create a microclimate.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

#7987. ‘Fireworks’ Goldenrod: A Pollinator Favorite with Bold Yellow Blooms

When you garden with ecology in mind, choosing plants becomes less about you and more about the local birds, mammals, and invertebrates that could benefit from your latest addition. Learn more about ‘Fireworks’ wrinkle-leaved goldenrod, one of Melissa Starkey’s favorite underappreciated native plants.

Watch: Super Cool Plants Podcast | Underappreciated Native Plants

We’re moving into fall for this next pick. Goldenrods are amazing plants in general, even though they get a bad rap. People sometimes associate them with allergies, but they are confusing goldenrod with ragweed (Ambrosia spp.). Not all goldenrods are too aggressive. They are host plants for over 120 different moth and butterfly caterpillars, and the seeds feed birds and other animals.

If I had to pick just one to highlight, ‘Fireworks’ wrinkle-leaved goldenrod would be my gateway plant to goldenrods. Anyone can use it in their garden, including in formal settings and in containers. ‘Fireworks’ is an appropriate name for this cultivar, as spires of bright yellow flowers explode in early to mid-autumn. It has a compact, clumping habit. This goldenrod can spread a little bit in moist soil, but it is not difficult to control, and it will stay put if you site it in a drier area. It likes full sun, but I have it in partial shade and it still looks lovely.

Learn more from Melissa about this plant on Fine Gardening’s podcast, Super Cool Plants, or watch the episode on our YouTube channel!

Melissa Starkey is the marketing and communications manager and an instructor at Mt. Cuba Center, a botanical garden in Hockessin, Delaware.

#7986. 5 Easy Fall Wins to Help Your Backyard Birds Survive Winter – How to Beat the Big Chill and Ensure More Visits

Squirrels Don’t Like These 3 Types of Bird Seed – Fill Your Feeders and Watch Songbirds Flock In

Huddled in hedgerows and shedding trees this fall, your backyard birdies need your help. Here are the simple things you can do now to keep them healthy and happy through winter

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Fall can be deceptive: for a while, the lingering sunlight might be warm, and there might still be pops of color as late-season annuals stand in defiance. But all it takes is one big cold snap or a nibble of frost for the whole yard to change, literally overnight. The transition from late fall color to the reality of several months of winter can be a shock – and not just for us. As we huddle over morning hot drinks and contemplate the gaps in the yard, imagine how it feels for our feathered chums.

From plump northern cardinals to energetic black-capped chickadees, these shifting conditions present a challenge for bird feeding, shelter, and survival. Tree cover is starting to bleed away as fall leaves spiral to the ground, exposing branches to biting winds, cold rain, and sharp frosts. The juicy bugs of July are history, dogwood berries are being stripped, and crisping soils mean foraging birds have to work twice as hard for every meal. For birdies that only weigh a couple of nickels, getting through the night means burning nearly an entire day’s energy just to stay warm.

So for our pint-sized backyard companions, the big chill isn’t just an inconvenience; it’s a fearsome calorie crunch. This narrow window in late fall is your best opportunity to step in with kind, targeted care. These little backyard wins won’t punish your wallet and they don’t demand much time. Just a little thoughtful prep today will keep your feathered neighbors safe, spunky, and singing outside your window all winter.

Preparing your backyard for happy wintering birds is all about timing. Whatever you do, don’t be tempted to put these little fall tasks off too long. I get it: in the whirl of leaf raking, perennial cutting, and hose winterizing, it’s easy to get distracted. But waiting until the first blizzard strikes and the ground freezes is a classic birdcare blunder, and one that tends to result in a yard devoid of birdsong.

Early winter is when resident birds establish foraging routes. By taking action now with these simple steps, you set up your yard as the place to stop mid-route – before the mercury plunges. Your USDA hardiness zone and regional climate have a part to play. In colder northern areas (zones 3-5), the risk of sudden hard freezes requires an earlier focus on high-density fats and ice-free water sources. Warmer zones 7-10 may host nomadic cedar waxwings and lingering eastern bluebirds as well as year-round residents. Yet they tend to share the same priorities: fast fuel, reliable drinks, and a cozy place to ride out a gale.

Before diving into these quick fall tasks, survey your yard. Observe how morning light strikes your patio, identify sheltered spots safe from north winds, and check that feeding and water stations are 10 feet (3m) from protective shrubs and safe staging or waiting branches for timid finches to peek out. Speaking of peeking, if you can’t afford a smart feeder, keep some compact binoculars or a monocular scope on hand to monitor visiting species and track which treats disappear first. The Pankoo 16x52 High Powered Monocular Telescope, available from Amazon, is a great way to enjoy shy songbirds on a budget.

Helping your birds thrive during winter starts now. These timely acts of care require minimal effort, and the payoff for getting your yard dialed in for the season is huge. By setting up your stations for winter, you’ll be rewarded with fluttery visitors even when the snow starts to fall. Here’s how easy it is to create a sanctuary for birds to fly in the face of the big chill…

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

As late fall chills settle in, backyard birds undergo a dietary pivot. During summer, they could thrive on lean insects and grains. But once night temperatures flirt with freezing, survival tilts towards fats. Burning fuel just to stay warm until breakfast is serious business. Now’s the time for you to swap out cheap summer filler seeds like red milo for lipid-rich options that deliver maximum energy per beakful.

This is the time to load your feeders with black-oil sunflower seeds. Their thin, papery shells are easily cracked by finches and chickadees, and their plump hearts are packed with plant oils. For ground-foraging juncos and sparrows, sprinkle hulled sunflower chips on low platforms so they don’t have to waste energy on dehulling. And hang some rendered suet cakes laced with berries or raw peanuts to nourish blue jays, red-bellied woodpeckers, downy woodpeckers, and nuthatches. C&S Peanut Suet Treat Cakes, available from Amazon, come in great-value packs.

Toss a handful of crunchy, dried mealworms onto a shallow tray to entice visiting eastern bluebirds and hermit thrushes to the party. Just make sure your feeder is able to support these extra nibbles, as well as allowing fall rains to drain freely. An open platform feeder, like the Kingsyard Hanging Platform Bird Feeder Tray from Amazon, can house a healthy fall feast in comfort while reducing the risk of mold.

Some of the simplest (and yet oddly, easily overlooked) fall birdcare measures involve your bird bath. Yes, topping up the seed hoppers and platform feeders is critical, but what’s worse is when the trusty bath is just left to freeze over. For birds, crunching on cold snow isn’t a fun winter pastime but an energy disaster. It drains their internal body heat precisely when they need every drop of warmth to survive.

It’s frustrating, because this is such an easy problem to avoid. At this time of year a heated bird bath, such as the Allied Precision Heated Bird Bath with Mounted Bracket, from Amazon, can pay for itself in terms of bird visits. Alternatively, you can keep water in motion (and so reduce freezing) by adding a rubber duck or ping pong ball to your bird bath. Ensure that the water depth in the bird bath remains shallow, never exceeding a couple of inches (5cm), so that small visitors like American goldfinches and purple finches can drink safely.

Drop in a flat, textured stone so little feet have a non-slip surface. Finally, keep water supplies fresher for longer by adding a copper disc to your bird bath. The Mellbree Bird Bath Copper Cleaning Disc from Amazon is a brilliant way to prevent algae build-up between cleans. Easy!

Sitting on a bare branch in a sharp November breeze is an everyday winter reality for your garden birds, but it is one you can help them with. Backyards are losing their natural windbreaks as deciduous trees drop their leaves, exposing birdies to the elements and also nocturnal prowlers. But you can bolster the availability of natural cover and create layered roosting pockets before deep winter sets in.

Late fall is an ideal time for planting certain key containerized native shrubs, such as Autumn Brilliance Serviceberry, available from Nature Hills, which establishes quickly in late fall, providing dense roosting cover and juicy berries for over 40 bird species. American beautyberry is another excellent bird-friendly native that you can also plant now, as long as you can tuck them in a few weeks before the ground freezes. You can pick up containers of Green Promise Farms’ American Beautyberry Live Plants from Amazon which will establish relatively fast. Remember to mulch with a 3-inch (8cm) ring of shredded bark.

Leaving dense conifers and arborvitae unclipped provides dense inner chambers where northern cardinals, dark-eyed juncos, and mourning doves can huddle. It’s also helpful to stack any thick trimmings you might have accumulated from fall pruning in a quiet border. A loose brush pile is perfect for winter wrens and ground-dwelling sparrows. Finally, you can convert unused wooden nest boxes into roosting cabins by sealing ventilation holes, flipping the front panel so the entrance hole sits at the bottom to trap rising heat, and layering the base with pine shavings.

At this time of year, it only takes a couple of heavy showers or sharp gusts to knock our bird-feeding routines into disarray. Even with the best intentions, we might put off bird feeder or bird bath cleaning, promising we’ll do it at the weekend, only to wind up catching up on box sets in our pyjamas (no judgments). But leaving a greasy ring of wet kernels or hulls stuck to the bottom of a feeder is a recipe for disaster, creating a breeding ground for killers such as Salmonellosis and Aspergillosis. Left unchecked, these can spread through the feathered community in a matter of days.

Establishing a rigorous weekly cleaning rhythm is your best line of disease defense. This can be as simple as a quick Sunday scrub routine (these can be surprisingly therapeutic!). It helps to have feeders that are easy to dismantle and clean in the first place. A good bird feeder option for weekly cleaning is the Woodlink Seed Tube Bird Feeder from Home Depot, with removable base ports that detach in seconds.

Once you have disassembled your seed tubes, hopper troughs, and platform trays, discard damp or caked seed remnants. Scrub tight nooks with an extra-long bottle brush, like the Songbird Essentials Extra Long Bottle Brush, available from Amazon. Then soak the parts for 10-15 minutes. Using a ratio of nine parts to one, dip in warm water laced with distilled white vinegar. Rinse thoroughly and ensure every component is dry before refilling. Sweep away soggy fallen hulls while you’re at it, to help out ground-foragers like juncos and mourning doves.

In the fall yard, pristine neatness can often be the enemy of wildlife survival. Many of the forager’s final treasures of the season may be tucked beneath curling leaf fall or wedged in that forlorn dangling seed head. Stripping away key perennial skeletons and scooping up fallen foliage deprive backyard birds of vital natural gifts. Such backyard litter costs you nothing to leave, and they keep your birds stocked up in other sleeping nibbles, such as dormant spiders and protein-packed pupae.

So leave perennial seed heads standing, kick a mound of leaves under your hedges, and let nature do the catering. Place a low, wire-mesh ground tray nearby, filled with a sprinkling of sunflower chips and crunchy protein-rich mealworms such as Kaytee Dried Mealworms from Walmart to reward their hard work. If you need a good ground tray feeder, the Mizxxidea Mesh Ground Bird Feeder from Amazon has an ultra-fine mesh base allowing fall rains to drain through cleanly. Blending handy extra feeding stations alongside natural foraging options creates the ideal birdie hangout.

These quick fall tasks are a lovely way of supporting your local birdlife as temperatures plummet, transforming your yard into a safe, high-energy refuge. While some of these fall extras are inexpensive, it’s worth investing in a few key features to help stay one step ahead of biting winds and winter chills. These curated staples will help you protect and nurture your resident songbirds from fall through winter.

Made of solid wood with a steep-pitched roof, this charming shelter offers visitors essential insulation against freezing drafts and rain. The side door makes cleaning simple, creating an ideal roosting cabin for chickadees, titmice, and wrens looking to huddle away from the worst of the winter weather.

This pretty jewel-toned basin is made from durable embossed glass and the textured presentation is kinder on birdie feet. It looks like high-end art, but is durable and rock-steady, although it's more likely to be filled with songbirds than hummers. Very easy to keep clean, and a real talking point for friends.

Crafted with vibrant stained-glass mosaic tiling, this fly-through feeder is great for shielding birds against winds and protecting seeds from drizzle. This pretty feeder's tunnel design also provides 360-degree visibility for skittish finches, chickadees, and nuthatches.

This timely fall intervention is all about making subtle, thoughtful shifts in our birdcare. By swapping in dense, high-calorie foods, maintaining easy-access water, supporting roosting options, cleaning feeders weekly, and leaving some fallen leaves around, you provide vital comfort and protection for vulnerable birds just when they need it most. It’s worth it to watch a puffed-up cardinal chewing on a mealworm, or a towhee poking out of some crunchy leaf litter, knowing that you’re doing your bit to keep nature’s sweetest living colors fluttering in and out of your yard.

#7985. Susan’s Minnesota Garden, Part 2: Spring and Summer

Hi GPODers! We’re back in St. Paul, Minnesota (Zone 5a), for Part 2 of Susan Warde’s garden tour! Earlier this week, Susan shared a look at her garden from late July through October. Today we’re heading back to spring to see what was growing earlier in the season. Let’s take a look!

Here are some photos from late May through July.

The back garden. Wild cranesbill (Geranium maculatum, Zones 3–8) in the upper left corner is the only plant in flower at this time (late May), but the foliage is pretty, I think. The dominant hosta is ‘Blue Ivory’ (Hosta ‘Blue Ivory’, Zones 3–9).

Front garden (late May). I think the azalea is ‘Rosy Lights’ (Rhododendron ‘Rosy Lights’, Zones 3–7) from the Northern Lights azalea series.

Tall bearded iris (Iris ‘Cherished’, Zones 3–9), late May.

Tall bearded iris ‘Sultry Mood’, late May.

A Siberian iris (Iris sibirica cvs., Zones 3–9); I don’t know the cultivar name (late May).

My earliest clematis (Clematis ‘Acropolis’, Zones 4–9), with ‘Kansas’ peony (Paeonia lactiflora ‘Kansas’, Zones 3–8) in the background (early June).

This Asiatic lily (Lilium ‘Stracciatella Event’, Zones 3–8) was labeled ‘Stracciatella Event’, but it doesn’t look like the photos of that cultivar. Within a couple of days of this photo, taken July 6, the lily was demolished by scarlet lily beetles, which ultimately made mincemeat of all my lilies. The foliage looked so terrible that I had to cut them all down.

‘Lavender Moonchild’ daylily (Hemerocallis ‘Lavender Moonchild’, Zones 3–9), mid-July. Deer are a very rare occurrence in the city. I hadn’t seen one for years, but this summer two young bucks roamed the neighborhood, and every night they snacked on daylily buds and blossoms. They were not deterred by either of the sprays I tried.

This daylily is ‘Marquee Moon’. Set farther back in the garden, it was spared by the deer (mid-July).

A view of the side yard (July 25). Daylilies, garden phlox (Phlox paniculata cvs., Zones 4–8), coneflowers (Echinacea cvs., Zones 3–9), black-eyed Susans (Rudbeckia cvs., Zones 3–9), and blazing stars (Liatris cvs., Zones 3–9) are all in bloom.

Thank you for sharing another look at your garden, Susan! I especially enjoyed seeing your collection of irises and daylilies, although I’m sorry the deer and lily beetles caused so much trouble this year.

#7984. Israeli Jews Vote by Economic Status, Even Though Elections Turn on Other Issues

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

A fascinating chart from Yedioth Aharanot newspaper shows the voting breakdown of the Jewish electorate in the Israeli election.

People the pollsters deem to be in the bottom 10% in socio-economic status voted 96.7% for Netanyahu's Likud and parties aligned with it. Those in the top 10% voted 80.9% for opposition parties.

What makes this particularly interesting is that the election turned almost entirely on issues that are not economic in the ordinary sense, such as conscripting Haredi Jews, which factions would best resist outside pressure for a Palestinian state, who is best-positioned to finish the wars in Gaza, Lebanon, and Iran, and who is to blame for 10/7. Many voters expressed concern to pollsters about the cost of living, but none of the major parties talked much about it.

So to a large and often unappreciated (at least outside Israel) extent, Israeli politics is culture-war politics. Netanyahu and his allies represent voters who are more religiously traditional, less-educated, live on "the periphery," poorer, and, importantly, of recent North African or Middle Eastern descent--Israelis who were treated as outsiders by the Ashkenazi socialists who ran the country until Menahem Begin broke their stranglehold on elections in 1977. Netanyahu's opponents rely on voters who are disproportionately Ashkenazi, better-educated, wealthier, live in Tel Aviv or Haifa, and more secular-minded.

Another interesting aspect of this is that while the religious/secular divide comes up in politicking all the time, Israeli politics mostly avoid explicit ethnic or wealth-based appeals. The de facto leader of the opposition, Gadi Eisenkot, is the son of Moroccan immigrants. Moroccans are a huge part of Netanyahu's base, but Eisenkot's potential to be the first Moroccan (and first non-Ashkenazi) prime minister barely played a role in the campaign, and he did not try to give it one.

I will leave it to those more expert than I on Israeli politics to analyze this further, but it sure seems like a big factor in the election was a visceral fear among groups that feel historically marginalized in Israel that victory by the anti-Netanyahu faction would amount to a loss in status.

#7983. The Law and Democrats Allegedly Recruiting Second "Dan Sullivan" to Run in Alaska Senate Race

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Election law expert and UCLA Prof. Rick Hasen (Election Law Blog) has a post about this; an excerpt:

Today's New York Times story, if true, strikes me as a political bombshell: despite public denials of a connection, people associated with Democratic U.S. Senate candidate in Alaska Mary Peltola and Democratic Party officials recruited the second "Dan Sullivan" to run against the incumbent Republican U.S. Senator from Alaska, Dan S. Sullivan. The hope would be to siphon votes away from Sullivan. (As a political play, I'm skeptical that this would work, given Alaska's ranked choice voting approach would allow ranking both Dan Sullivans as 1 and 2, thereby not helping Peltola.)

But what, if any, are the legal implications of the story (if true)?

To begin with, I don't think it has any bearing at all on the current litigation in which the U.S. Department of Justice seeks to delay certification of the race if Dan S. Sullivan narrowly loses on grounds of purported voter confusion. The lawsuit is not going anywhere for any number of reasons, but even assuming DOJ's theory that it can sue to block certification, it is irrelevant as to why voters might face confusion over the two Dan Sullivans. (This has not stopped DOJ from now supporting DSCC intervention so that it can get discovery over a potential "conspiracy"). [Disclosure: I will soon be filing a motion to file an amicus brief on my own behalf supporting the State of Alaska in this case.]

Second, if there is any evidence that anyone lied under oath about the cooperation between Democrats and Dan J. Sullivan, that could be grounds for a perjury prosecution. So far I'm not aware of any such allegation in the case.

Third, this leaves the question whether this could be prosecuted as some kind of conspiracy against voters.

To begin with, it is regular practice for people to support candidates for bad motives: Republicans boosting Greens and Democrats boosting Libertarians. It turns out that Elon Musk alone may have bankrolled left-leaning Cornel West's quest to get on the 2024 presidential eiection ballot. The effort in Alaska is just an extreme version of that. From the Times's story: "Ballot-stacking tactics are common in politics and generally considered legal — and have been employed by both parties in Alaska. But this operation, which has not been reported before, reveals the lengths to which Democrats went to seek advantage in a Senate race that could determine control of the chamber." …

This is a case about someone running for office with impure motives who is lucky enough to have a name that could confuse some voters. The solution to this problem is counterspeech (as in: "Don't vote for J.! Vote for the real Senator Daniel S. Sullivan".)

I don't see how the government could criminalize his running for office for having impure motives. And if it could do so, then it could be a crime every time that the Republican Party backs a Green Party candidate, or Democrats support a MAGA candidate in a primary in the hopes that the candidate would be weaker against a Democrat in the general election. This stuff happens all the time….

#7982. Even "Trumpy Judges" and "Woke Judges" Might Know More Law Than You Do

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

I appreciate that many people are skeptical about judges. Indeed, it's good that people take with a grain of salt the statements of government officials, including judges. Judges are human, and humans make mistakes and have prejudices and blind spots.

At the same time, judges are generally quite well-trained lawyers, and know a good deal about what they're writing about. Conventional wisdom holds that federal judges generally are particularly well-qualified (of course, with exceptions, as is true for all institutions). Federal judges also generally employ quite well-qualified law clerks, who do much of the  research and initial opinion drafting.

This means that, for all the risk of error and ideological bias, judges generally (though not always) know what they're talking about in their legal analysis. They tend to particularly know more than non-lawyers, but also often more than lawyers who aren't specialists in the particular field. You might assume that some judge is "woke" or "Trumpy" or what have you, but there's a pretty good chance that the judge's legal analysis is still correct.

This post was prompted by a comment I saw on the Eric Coomer (of Dominion Voting) Loses Libel Lawsuit over The Deep Rig post, though this is just one example of a broader trend. The comment quotes an excerpt from the post's excerpt of the judge's opinion:

In short, if the law did not require "clear and convincing evidence" that the defendant subjectively doubted or disbelieved the published statements, it is likely that Byrne's motion for summary judgment would have been denied, and a jury would have had the opportunity to weigh in on this matter. However, under the law as it currently stands, Coomer's evidence is insufficient to meet these standards and summary judgment for Byrne is therefore required….

The comment then says, "Trumpy judge who apparently didn't bother to read Sullivan, which states" (emphasis added by commenter),

The constitutional guarantees require, we think, a federal rule that prohibits a public official from recovering damages for a defamatory falsehood relating to his official conduct unless he proves that the statement was made with "actual malice" — that is, with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard of whether it was false or not.

And the comment continues, "Seems like this is ripe for appeal. This Trumpy judge seems to think the current precedent requires that the defendant 'subjectively doubted or disbelieved the published statements,' when Sullivan has a looser standard."

The trouble with the commenter's analysis is that Sullivan was of course not the last word on the subject—as the judge knew. Indeed, if one searches for "subjective" in the judge's opinion, one sees a longish passage citing authority supporting the judge's analysis:

Actual malice requires proof that the defendant published the challenged statement with knowledge of its falsity or with reckless disregard for whether it was false. See id. [Coomer v. Donald J. Trump for President, Inc., 552 P.3d 562, 581 (Colo. App. 2024)]; New York Times Co. v. Sullivan, 376 U.S. 254, 279-80 (1964); St. Amant v. Thompson, 390 U.S. 727, 731 (1968). The test for actual malice is a subjective one. Thus, the issue is not whether "a reasonably prudent [person] would have published, or would have investigated before publishing," but rather whether the defendant "in fact entertained serious doubts as to the truth of [the] publication, or was highly aware of its probable falsity[.]" Coomer, 552 P.3d at 591; Diversified Mgmt., Inc. v. The Denver Post, Inc., 653 P.2d 1103. 1105-10 (Colo. 1982) (en banc); Michel v. NYP Holdings, Inc., 816 F.3d 686, 703 (11th Cir. 2016) ("[W]e ask whether the defendant, instead of acting in good faith, actually entertained serious doubts as to the veracity of the published account, or was highly aware that the account was probably false."); Dershowitz v. Cable News Network, Inc., 153 F.4th 1189, 1193 (11th Cir. 2025) ("[A]ll that matters are the speakers' subjective beliefs about the truth of their own statements.").

St. Amant, cited by the court, indeed states,

[The precedents] are clear that reckless conduct is not measured by whether a reasonably prudent man would have published, or would have investigated before publishing. There must be sufficient evidence to permit the conclusion that the defendant in fact entertained serious doubts as to the truth of his publication. Publishing with such doubts shows reckless disregard for truth or falsity and demonstrates actual malice.

Gertz v. Robert Welch, Inc. (1974) expressly quotes this passage as the Court having "equated reckless disregard of the truth with subjective awareness of probable falsity." The judge in the Coomer / Deep Rig case, whether you view him as "Trumpy" or not, knew the law here, and the commenter (who had elsewhere said he wasn't a lawyer) didn't seem to.

So, again, definitely view judges' work skeptically, and feel free to criticize it. But don't assume that just because you know one precedent in the field you know the law better than the judge. Don't assume that just because you think the judge has some ideological bias, that ideological bias has led the judge into legal error. And if you have some skepticism about the judge's analysis, check the sources that the judge cites in the full opinion; my posts usually just excerpt the opinion, and often don't include citations, but they generally link to the full opinion so readers can consult it directly.

#7981. Halloween in the Garden: 3 Spooky and Creative Displays

Happy Friday, GPOD! Halloween is tomorrow, so for our last post of the week, I couldn’t resist digging through past GPODs for a little spooky-season garden inspiration. Over the years, contributors have shown us that Halloween decor doesn’t have to stop at the front door. A foggy morning can turn a familiar garden wonderfully eerie, homegrown pumpkins can become an entire cast of characters, and flowers and foliage from the garden can transform simple gourds into works of art. Today we’re revisiting three very different Halloween displays that all have their own charm and appeal.

We’ll start in Hebron, Kentucky, with Keri Shinault’s perfectly spooky garden. Keri and her husband, Brandon, began hosting an annual Halloween masquerade after their October 2005 wedding, eventually decorating their home and garden with creepy critters, ghouls, headstones, and plenty of other spooky surprises.

A beautiful sitting area surrounded by lush plants becomes instantly more mysterious when fog blurs the garden beyond.

Sometimes Mother Nature provides the best Halloween special effects.

Sit a while! Take a load off those tired bones.

Stepping stones set into lush ground covers guide you around massive oakleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea quercifolia, Zones 5–9) shrubs.

Next up are Tom and Jeannie Tremont’s delightfully ridiculous pumpkin people. Rather than simply lining the porch with gourds, Tom and Jeannie turned their pumpkins into an entire cast of characters with their own poses, props, and personalities.

Why settle for a jack-o’-lantern when your pumpkins can go for a bike ride? Tom and Jeannie turned their fall harvest into a whole cast of characters, complete with wheels.

Tom and Jeannie Tremont clearly weren’t interested in ordinary jack-o’-lanterns. This pumpkin person looks like they got caught with their pants down while a family bikes by in the background. It’s ridiculous in the best possible way.

The mama-and-baby pumpkin pair might be the sweetest of the bunch. Even commenters on the original GPOD singled this little duo out as a favorite.

We’ll end with something completely different from Cherry Ong in Richmond, British Columbia. For her dazzling pumpkin display, Cherry repurposed the pallet-wood auricula theaters she and her husband had built for spring into a stage for decorated pumpkins and squash.

Auricula theaters traditionally protect auriculas (Primula auricula, Zones 3–8) from harsh rain and wind, but Cherry discovered they make a pretty spectacular fall display too.

Cherry and her husband built these pallet-wood auricula theaters a couple of years earlier—he constructed and hung the boxes, while Cherry designed and stained them. In fall, the shelves get a totally new look when pumpkins and gourds take the place of spring flowers.

Cherry had a little fun displaying the smaller pumpkins before giving them away, using old mini terra-cotta pots to add height and variation. Some pumpkins were decorated with seasonal flowers and foliage from the garden, turning the whole theater into one big botanical arrangement.

A small white pumpkin topped with clusters of Chinese tea rosebuds shows just how detailed Cherry gets with these creations. Elsewhere in the display, she also incorporated dried dahlias and other flowers and foliage from the garden.

I love how each of these gardeners found a unique way to bring Halloween into their outdoor spaces. That might be my favorite thing about Halloween in the garden: there really aren’t many rules. You can go creepy, silly, beautiful, botanical—or somehow all four at once. I hope everyone has a happy Halloween tomorrow! If you’re decorating your garden, porch, containers, or homegrown pumpkins this weekend, I’d love to see what you come up with.

If you’re planting bulbs in your garden this fall, try this simple but super-effective hack to stop squirrels digging up tasty tulips and ruining the spring show.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Freshly planted spring-flowering bulbs provide an easy feast for hungry garden critters as temperatures drop, and are often eaten before they even get a chance to grow roots. Tulip bulbs are always the first to be sniffed out as they taste sweet and provide the perfect high-calorie meal for chipmunks as well as squirrels. Crocus bulbs, too, are carb-rich favorites on the garden menu in fall.

If you’ve experienced squirrels digging up tulip bulbs, you’ll know what determined diggers they are. Gardeners are just as dogged, however, and popular tricks to protect spring-flowering bulbs include laying steel mesh or chicken wire over the top, disguising the appealing scent of tulip and crocus bulbs by planting unappetising allium bulbs alongside, and using bulb baskets. But there’s a far easier, cheaper and more effective way to stop squirrels eating bulbs, and it helps the bulbs grow well, too.

What’s more, this robust solution protects bulbs from rodents and other underground burrowers like voles, who also love to seek out this nutrient-dense food source in fall.

When you're planting bulbs in fall, the magic ingredient to keep these energy balls safe from squirrels is poultry grit made from crushed oyster shells. The sharp, jagged edges of crushed oyster shells means it's painful for paws to dig through, so it provides an effective barrier that stops critters eating tulip bulbs and even tempting crocus.

What's more, as well as keeping bulbs safe from sharp teeth this natural material improves soil drainage, making bulbs less likely to rot through wet winter weather. Crushed oyster shells also break down very slowly to provide plants with a steady supply of calcium, which supports strong root and stem growth.

Not all chicken grit is created equal when it comes to protecting fall-planted bulbs, however. Make sure you buy chicken grit like Pacific Pearl Oyster Shell Calcium Supplement for Chickens, available from Walmart, that's made purely from oyster shells as many products are cut with cheaper materials like limestone. Choose crushed shells (sometimes sold as chick grit) over flaked shells as this is both sharper on paws and easier for plant roots and shoots to grow through.

When planting bulbs in pots, simply add an inch-thick layer of chicken grit to the soil surface to deter squirrels from digging, where it will also act as a mulch.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Opt for a double layer of poultry grit when planting bulbs in the ground. Add an inch-thick layer of crushed oyster shells to the bottom of the planting hole, and sit the bulbs right on top. This helps to protects bulbs from burrowing pests who typically attack from below, when a landslide of sharp oyster shells will send them scurrying away in search of more easily accessible food. If voles, field mice and pocket gophers are a particular problem in your garden, you can also pack a shallow layer of grit all around the bulb to fully encase it.

Fill the planting trench with soil as normal but add a second inch-thick layer of oyster shell grit an inch or two below the surface. When squirrels or other critters hit this sharp, gravelly layer, they’ll give up digging. This top layer can also help deter raccoons and skunks who don’t eat bulbs but are attracted to freshly-dug soil to look for insects and grubs.

Crushed oyster shells will naturally improve soil drainage and create beneficial pockets of air, loosening up heavy soil. The shells also release calcium as they break down, which plants need to build cell walls.

Adding a heap of oyster shells to your soil can affect its pH levels long-term but this hard material breaks down so slowly, that’s not a problem unless you have soil that’s already very alkaline. While some bulbs like camassia (wild hyacinths) prefer acidic soil, more palatable tulip and crocus bulbs both tolerate mildly alkaline soil just fine. Testing your soil with simple pH test strips like these from Amazon will instantly give you an answer if you suspect your soil is highly alkaline.

There are so many striking spring-flowering bulbs to plant in November, and using this clever trick will keep them safe from hungry animals in fall. Whether you view squirrels as garden pests or like to welcome wildlife into your garden, crushed oyster shells are a natural solution to prevent them digging up freshly planted bulbs in fall. Poultry grit is as economical as it is effective, too, so you get to enjoy those beautiful blooms come spring without spending a fortune.

Little leaves on an orchid's old flower spike may signal trouble – but a keiki doesn’t always mean the plant is struggling. Here's how to tell the difference.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It usually gets spotted by accident, halfway through watering. The flower spike that finished months ago has a few green leaves sticking out partway up, and maybe a stubby root or two hanging under them. That's an orchid keiki. For a minute, finding one feels like getting a second orchid for nothing.

Then the doubt sets in. Read up on what a keiki is, and you'll soon come across the idea that orchids are more likely to sprout them when they're stressed or failing. Anyone whose plant has also dropped a leaf or two lately will find that hard to shake.

Stress can play a part, though it's far from the only thing. Heat, fertilizer, and genetics all factor in, and plenty of keikis grow on plants with nothing wrong at all. A few minutes at the sink with the parent plant will tell you more than the keiki does itself.

The name is Hawaiian – keiki (KAY-kee) means baby. Look closely at a moth orchid (Phalaenopsis) spike, and you'll see small bumps along it, each wrapped in a papery sheath. Those are nodes, each holding a dormant bud, and once in a while one of those buds grows leaves. What grows is a miniature copy of the parent.

Keikis aren't an orchid disease or a parasite, and they can't spread to your other plants. They're simply one way orchids reproduce without seed. Where it grows matters more. A spike keiki sits up on the flower stem. A basal keiki comes up at the bottom, squeezed in next to the lower leaves, and on a moth orchid, that second kind can point to trouble at the crown.

A stem keiki growing on a Phalaenopsis orchid stem

Sometimes a keiki does show up because the parent is in trouble. Moth orchids grow from one point only, right in the middle of the leaves. Lose that tip to rot, or a break, and no new leaves can form up there. With energy in reserve, the plant may instead push out a basal keiki below the damaged tissue. Dendrobium canes that lose their roots, or their link to the rest of the plant through rot or injury, sometimes sprout keikis as well.

Plenty of keikis turn up on orchids with nothing wrong, though. On moth orchids, they come naturally from the middle and upper nodes of the spike, and certain species and hybrids are just more prone to it. Hormones are what flip a dormant bud into a keiki. Dab cytokinin, one of those growth hormones, on a node and it can pull a keiki out of a perfectly healthy plant. Crazy Keiki Cloning Paste, available on Amazon, is a well-rated product that contains cytokinin.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Long spells of heat as a spike finishes, heavy nitrogen feeding late in the season, and too little light or humidity have also been tied to keikis.

Some longtime growers take a keiki as a sign orchid care could use adjusting – a dim corner or heavy feeding is a good place to start. On a plant with firm, flat leaves and plump roots, a spike keiki usually isn't hiding anything. A basal keiki pushing up beside a soft, dark center is the one to worry about.

A basal orchid keiki growing on plant with some shriveled old roots

Start by checking for orchid leaf problems. Healthy moth orchid leaves are thick and firm, almost leathery. An occasional yellow bottom leaf is normal – the oldest leaves dry up as the plant ages. Several leaves yellowing at once is another matter, and so are newer leaves that have gone limp and wrinkled. Leaves that shrivel like that usually aren't getting enough water. And in fall, don't be fooled by a cold windowsill – nights below 60°F (16°C) can yellow lower leaves on their own.

Next, slide the pot off and check the orchid roots. Good ones feel firm and plump. They look green right after watering and silvery once they dry. Rotted ones are brown and mushy, and if you pinch one, the outer layer may slip off, leaving nothing but a thin string.

Now peer into the middle where new leaves come from. That's the crown. It should be firm and green. If it has gone soft, black, or wet-looking, crown rot has likely set in, often from water molds such as Pythium ultimum and Phytophthora cactorum, and rot that spreads through the crown can kill the whole plant.

One yellow leaf proves very little. Slow decline is different. If the leaves feel a little softer each time you check and nothing about the care has changed, look underground – usually at the roots, or at old bark mix that's broken down into soggy muck. Good news shows up in the same places. New leaves unfolding from the crown, or fresh green root tips near the base, mean the plant is still growing.

A basal orchid keiki has been left to grow into an established offshoot on this neglected plant

Did everything look fine? Then leave the plant alone, keiki and all. If the check turned something up, fix that and only that. Cut rotted roots back to firm tissue with something small and sharp, and wipe the blades with rubbing alcohol between plants. Fiskars' micro-tip pruning snips are narrow enough to get in between roots.

For repotting, use a specialist orchid potting mix, like Better-Gro Phalaenopsis mix, available at Home Depot, which is a fir bark blend. Use a clear slotted orchid pot, like these Holanhing pots, so you can keep an eye on the roots.

After that, water orchids sparingly until new roots reach the fresh bark, and water in the morning so the leaves dry before dark. Tip out any water that pools in the crown. Moth orchids do well in bright, indirect light, just not pressed up against cold glass or sitting above a heating vent.

The keiki itself can stay put. Without roots of its own, a spike keiki draws water and nutrients through the parent's flower stem, and snipping it off does nothing for rotting roots or a damaged crown. Many growers leave a moth orchid keiki alone until it carries a couple of leaves and roots about 1–1.5 inches (2.5–4 cm) long. Smaller ones often struggle on their own. Once it reaches that size, separating and potting the keiki is a quick way to propagate your orchid.

It depends on the damage. A moth orchid that still has some plump roots and a firm crown can come back once its care is fixed, though you may wait a while for the first new leaf. Rot through the crown is a much tougher case. So is a pot where you find almost nothing but mush. Even then, a plant with enough energy stored up can sometimes send up a new plantlet from its base.

This is where a keiki helps. It grew from the parent's own tissue, so it carries the same genetics and can keep that orchid going if the parent doesn't make it. Leave it attached while the parent holds up.

What if a declining plant has a green flower spike but no keiki? Try using keiki cloning paste, mentioned above, to coax one out, though results vary.

So it’s not time to write that orchid off, just yet, because of one odd growth. Check the plant it's growing from. If the leaves are firm and the roots and crown look good, the keiki is no warning at all, just a free second orchid hitching a ride on the first. With a little TLC, you can get that orchid blooming beautifully in no time.

Anyone else been ogling Catherine's Thanksgiving decor on Instagram?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Anyone else already thinking about their holiday tablescapes? Because Catherine Zeta-Jones has just given us all the Thanksgiving inspiration we could ever need.

The actor recently shared a glimpse of her and Michael Douglas's Thanksgiving decor, and it's the kind of rustic autumnal display that makes you want to invite everyone over for dinner; think warm orange foliage, miniature pumpkins, natural branches and a gorgeous leafy garland.

It's the same sort of wonderfully unfussy vibe as Michelle Obama's twig tree, and you don't need a celebrity-sized decorating budget to recreate the look. In fact, I'd argue that some of the prettiest ingredients might already be growing in your backyard.

Catherine Zeta-Jones is one of those stars attached to countless big projects, from Wednesday to Chicago to America's Sweethearts. Still, though, she remains wonderfully down-to-earth... and even takes the time to make her own fall decor, too!

'A little DIY in anticipation of Thanksgiving,' she captioned a photo of her table on Instagram. 'I love this up coming holiday, my kids are home from college and I can’t wait!!!'

A post shared by Catherine Zeta-Jones (@catherinezetajones)

Keen to give it a go for yourself? Well, it's easy enough; all you really need to focus on is bringing the beauty of your autumnal garden indoors.

First things first, head outside and gather a selection of autumn leaves in warm shades of orange, red, bronze and gold. Maple and oak leaves are particularly lovely, but don't overlook interesting branches and seasonal greenery, either.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Make like Catherine Zeta-Jones and try using a mixture of different leaf shapes and sizes because it gives the arrangement a more natural, gathered-from-the-garden feel. Then, you can lay the foliage directly along the middle of the table, creating a loose runner that you can build the rest of your decorations around.

Something like the Oasis Forage Floral Create Kit on Amazon could help with this.

This clever little foraging kit has everything you need to get started on crafting your own fall decorations.

Whatever you do, just make sure anything you collect is clean and free from pests. And if you're gathering from outside your garden, always check that you're allowed to collect it.

You can't have a Thanksgiving centerpiece without pumpkins, can you? And Catherine Zeta-Jones's rustic look is a lovely reminder that you don't need enormous pumpkins to make an impact.

I'd choose a mixture of orange, cream and green varieties, placing them at intervals along the foliage. Try grouping a few together rather than spacing everything out too evenly. That slightly imperfect arrangement is what makes the whole thing feel so charming.

If you've grown your own ornamental gourds, even better! They're a wonderful way to give your Thanksgiving decorations a personal touch.

Now for my favorite part: the finishing touches! Honestly, a few interesting branches, seedheads or pinecones will add height and texture to the arrangement, and I particularly love the idea of incorporating dried ornamental grasses, which bring movement and a lovely natural softness to the display.

Then, make like Catherine Zeta-Jones and add small votive candles or LED tealights between the pumpkins and foliage. The warm glow will make the whole table feel wonderfully inviting once the evening draws in.

What I love about Catherine Zeta Jones's rustic decorations is that they remind us how much beauty there is to be found in the changing seasons!

You don't need elaborate floral arrangements or expensive accessories to make a Thanksgiving table feel specia; all it takes is a handful of colorful leaves, a few little pumpkins and some carefully chosen garden finds . Now if you'll excuse me, I think I'll be heading out to the backyard with a basket before all those beautiful fall leaves disappear!

#7976. Creating Voter Confusion About Candidates' Names is Bad - But Exploiting Voter Ignorance About Policy Issues is a Much Bigger Problem

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Democrats' apparent effort to confuse Alaska voters about candidates' names is reprehensible. But politicians' routine lying and exploitation of ignorance about policy issues is much worse.

A recent New York Times article presents evidence that Alaska Democrats sought to confuse voters in that state's 2026 Senate election by introducing a second candidate with a name very similar to that of the Republican incumbent, thereby potentially siphoning off some of the latter's voters. The incumbent senator is named Dan S. Sullivan, while the other candidate is Dan J. Sullivan. As the Times reports, some of the facts here are disputable, and it is not entirely clear whether Democratic candidate Mary Peltola knew about this effort or approved of it. But it seems likely that at least some of her staffers and other Democratic operatives were involved.

Before going further, I should emphasize that this effort is worthy of condemnation. Trying to confuse voters into voting for the "wrong" candidate in this way is not how democratic political participation should work. And the fact that other politicians (including Republicans) engage in various electoral "dirty tricks" doesn't justify this one.

Elsewhere, I have explained why these kinds of actions are not illegal, and why the Trump administration's lawsuit seeking to block certification of the Alaska Senate result deserves to fail. I stand by that conclusion. Legal scholar Rick Hasen (a leading election law expert) has a helpful recent post explaining why the New York Times revelations do not change anything from a legal point of view. But the fact that this scheme is legal doesn't make it right.

That said, it is important to keep this issue in proper perspective, and especially to recognize that many other types of lies and efforts to exploit voter ignorance are much worse. Confusion caused by candidates with similar names is relatively rare, and it is difficult to find examples where it affected more than a small fraction of voters. I am not aware of even one case where it was decisive to the outcome of an election. But I welcome correction on that latter point.

The Alaska case is unlikely to be an exception to the above generalization. In the first round of the ranked-choice voting election (which narrows down the candidates to the top 4), only 2.5% of voters picked Dan J. Sullivan. Peltola led the incumbent senator by a much larger margin than that (8.1 points). Even if every single person who voted for Dan J. did so because of confusion (which is improbable), that's unlikely to change the result.

Moreover, the Alaska ranked-choice voting system reduces the risk of error. Some of those who vote for the "wrong" Dan Sullivan might rank the "right" one second. After the former gets eliminated, those votes get transferred to the latter. On top of that, as Michael Dorf points out, the Alaska ballot explicit indicates that Dan S. Sullivan is the "incumbent." That further reduces any potential confusion. The widespread publicity this issue has gotten over the last few weeks further reduces the risk of error. Many voters have probably now heard about the two Dan Sullivans and will be on guard against the problem.

It is still theoretically possible that confusion between the two Sullivans will end up having a decisive impact on the election. Some people who voted for Dan J. might not rank the other Sullivan second, or might misunderstand how the RCV system works. And some voters might (understandably) not be very careful about how they mark their ballots, thereby making a mistake despite the various safeguards against it. Still, it seems highly unlikely that such errors will have a decisive impact on the outcome.

Overall, this kind of a thing is relative molehill of a problem. Elections where it makes a decisive difference are likely to be extremely rare, at worst. By contrast, candidate lying about policy issues and exploitation of voter ignorance about them is a veritable mountain. I summarized some of the relevant evidence in an earlier post about the Alaska controversy:

Donald Trump is a particularly egregious example, going all the way back to his first campaign in 2016, and more recently with his lies about the 2020 election and other issues. But more conventional politicians also often resort to lies and deception, even if not to the same degree.  President Obama, for example, famously  lied when he claimed that, under the Affordable Care Act, "if you like your health care plan, you can keep it." That deception won the 2013 Politifact Lie of the Year award. But it still helped Obama get reelected in 2012. I am not sure exploiting voter confusion about names is any worse than exploiting their ignorance about policy issues like crime, immigration, and health care….

Ultimately, both exploitation of voter confusion about names and other deceptions used in campaigns seek to exploit widespread voter ignorance. Because of the combination of "rational ignorance" (lack of incentive to seek out political information) and "rational irrationality" (lack of incentive to engage in unbiased evaluation),  most voters know little about government and public policy, and often do a poor job of evaluating the information they do know. This makes them vulnerable to deception and manipulation, and incentivizes politicians to lie and otherwise distort the truth.

I would add that lies and deceptions about policy issues affect vastly more voters and have vastly bigger impacts on electoral outcomes than confusion about candidates' names. To take just a few recent examples, Trump in 2016 and 2024 and Obama in 2012 probably could not have won without the former. If, in 2024, key swing voters had realized that Trump's policy agenda of tariffs and mass deportations was likely to raise prices (as it predictably went on to do) rather than lower them (as he promised to do), he likely would have lost. Polls showed that prices were the biggest issue in the election for key swing voters. Trump also might well have lost if GOP base voters realized he was lying about the 2020 election, among other issues. In 2012, Obama might have lost if swing voters realized that he was lying when said that, under his signature policy initiative (the Affordable Care Act), "if you like your health care plan, you can keep it."

Effective lies and deceptions about policy issues (often exploiting preexisting voter ignorance and bias, but also deliberately seeking to create more of it) are ubiquitous. And they very often affect electoral outcomes. Even when they don't change the outcome between the candidates who run, they often have an impact on the policies those candidates adopt in the first place. As described more fully in my book Democracy and Political Ignorance, political parties and their strategists know most voters are ignorant, and often deliberately select policy agendas based on the likelihood of successfully exploiting that ignorance. The result is that even the lesser of the evils on offer in a given election (or the less egregious liars) are often still very bad.

From a moral point of view, I don't see any reason to believe lying about policy issues and exploiting voter ignorance about them is any worse than trying to trick voters into selecting the "wrong" candidate out of confusion. In practical terms, the former happens much more often than the latter, and has a far bigger effect).

Cornell law Prof. Michael Dorf recognizes that lies about policy issues are bad, but suggests that efforts to create confusion about candidate names are worse, because the latter are harder to combat with "counter-speech." I think the truth is the exact opposite. People can and do use counter-speech to oppose lies and deceptions about policy issues. But "rationally ignorant" voters will often ignore the counter-speech (not wanting to take the time and effort to study it) or reject evidence that goes against their preexisting biases. Many policy issues require considerable time and effort to understand well.

By contrast, it's much easier to find out there are two candidates with similar names in the election, and to take precautions against accidentally voting for the "wrong" one. Counter-speech to that effect need not be very complicated at all, or take a long time to understand.  In the Alaska case, for example, you just need to remember to vote for Dan S. rather than Dan J. or just know to vote for the one marked "incumbent." And figuring this out does not require going against any partisan or ideological biases.

As I have emphasized in previous writings about voter ignorance, I do not believe we can or should fight it by trying to punish politicians for their lies, or by censoring "misinformation." There is, in fact, no easy solution to the problem. But I assess a range of  options in my 2023 article on "Top-Down and Bottom-Up Solutions to the Problem of Political Ignorance, and in Democracy and Political Ignorance. I believe the best approach is to make fewer decisions at the ballot box and more by "voting with your feet," where incentives to seek out information and evaluate it wisely are much better.  In the works linked above, I also argue that we should give consideration to simply paying voters to increase their knowledge levels (e.g. by establishing a "Voter Achievement Test" and offering rewards to high scorers). But I  recognize that any effective approach will take time, and there may be no one fix that is sufficient by itself.

The beginning of wisdom here is to recognize we have a wide-ranging problem of voter ignorance, and to prioritize the most significant types of ignorance and exploitation thereof. On that scale, ignorance about policy issues should rank high, while voter confusion about candidates' names is a very minor problem, by comparison.

#7975. Law Banning Employer Requirements That Employees Listen to Employer's Religious or Political Speech Likely Violates Employer's First Amendment Rights

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Calif. Chamber of Commerce v. Bonta, decided today by Judge Richard Tallman, joined by Judges Richard Paez and Mark Bennett:

California Senate Bill (SB) 399 prohibits an employer from subjecting, or threatening to subject, an employee to adverse action if the employee chooses not to attend an employer-sponsored meeting or receive communications from the employer, "the purpose of which is to communicate the employer's opinion about religious or political matters."

The court concluded that the law restricts speech and not just employers' disciplining employees:

It is true that SB 399 facially forbids only the act of "subject[ing], or threaten[ing] to subject, an employee" to discipline for declining to attend certain meetings. But the law only applies to employers who engage in expressive activity at those meetings: namely, "communicat[ing their] opinion. It does not, for example, prohibit taking adverse action against employees who decline to attend a meeting, the sole purpose of which was for employees to fill out their annual tax paperwork. It prohibits adverse action only when the meeting's purpose was for the employer to engage in expressive activity. Thus, the First Amendment applies.

Our conclusion accords with the Eleventh Circuit's recent decision in Honeyfund.com, Inc. v. Governor (11th Cir. 2024). In Honeyfund.com, employers challenged Florida's Individual Freedom Act [part of the Florida Stop W.O.K.E. Act -EV], which forbade subjecting "any individual, as a condition of employment," to "training, instruction, or any other required activity" endorsing certain ideas [related to race, sex, or national origin -EV]. As California does here, Florida defended the law as "a ban on conduct because only the meetings are being restricted," not the underlying speech.

Our sister circuit rejected Florida's conduct-not-speech defense because the only way to know if the law had been violated was to examine the message conveyed at the meeting. Because "the conduct regulated depend[ed] on—and [could not] be separated from—the ideas communicated," Florida's law was "functionally a regulation of speech" implicating the First Amendment.

So too here. If an employer disciplines an employee for failing to attend an employer-sponsored meeting, the only way to know if SB 399 was violated is to "examine the content of the message that is conveyed" at the meeting. We must ask: did the employer express an opinion on political or religious matters?

So "the disfavored 'conduct'"—subjecting absentee employees to disciplinary action—"cannot be identified apart from the disfavored speech"—the employer's opinion on political or religious matters. Further, that California's law (unlike Florida's law) is viewpoint-neutral does not make it content-neutral. Because employers are forbidden from taking adverse action only if they communicate certain messages at the underlying meeting, the law inevitably singles out employers based on their expressive activity….

The court then concluded the law was content-based ("because it applies only when the employer has discussed certain topics: politics and religion") and speaker-based (limited to speech by employers), and was therefore unconstitutional unless it was narrowly to a compelling interest. And it held that the law likely couldn't be justified by an interest in protecting a "captive audience":

California's argument goes too far. Both the Supreme Court and our Court have referred to "captive audiences" only when the government acts as a proprietor or in the context of content-neutral time, place, and manner restrictions. Neither court has relied on a "captive audience" theory to identify a compelling interest sufficient to uphold content-based restrictions on nongovernmental speech in a nongovernmental setting. Nor, as far as we can tell, have any of our sister circuits, with the Eleventh Circuit directly rejecting such a theory. Honeyfund.com. A brief review of the key cases on which California relies demonstrates the point.

The first is Lehman v. City of Shaker Heights (1974), in which the City of Shaker Heights sold advertising space on its public transit vehicles but refused to accept paid political advertising…. A four-Justice plurality … conclud[ed] that the city, operating "in a proprietary capacity," had decided to limit the kinds of advertisements displayed based on several prudential factors. One of those factors was "the risk of imposing upon a captive audience"—commuters. To the plurality, the commuters' "captivity" was merely a prudential consideration in the city's decision to not allow certain advertising on its property.

The Supreme Court has since characterized Lehman as recognizing the government's ability to "bar from its facilities certain speech that would disrupt the legitimate governmental purpose for which the property has been dedicated." Our precedents consider an audience's "captivity" in the same manner as Lehman: as a prudential factor for a government, acting as proprietor, to consider when deciding what speech to allow in a nonpublic forum.

The Supreme Court has also considered an audience's degree of captivity when deciding if content-neutral time, place, and manner restrictions on speech in traditionally public forums are reasonable. The two examples California cites involved such restrictions imposed on public ways near healthcare facilities, in which patients are "held 'captive' by medical circumstance."

In short, these cases reveal that an audience's degree of "captivity" is relevant when the government, acting as a proprietor, excludes certain kinds of speech from nonpublic forums or when evaluating the reasonableness of content-neutral time, place, and manner restrictions imposed by the government acting as a regulator. No federal appellate court, including the Supreme Court, has relied on a "captive audience" theory to identify a compelling interest sufficient to support a content-based restriction on nongovernmental speech in a nongovernmental forum.

Considering the dearth of support for California's position and that the "captive audience" theory has been applied to support content-based speech restrictions only in nonpublic government forums, we conclude that the industry groups are likely to succeed on the merits of their First Amendment claim.

The plain, if at times disquieting, truth is that in our pluralistic society, … we are inescapably captive audiences for many purposes. Much that we encounter offends our esthetic, if not our political and moral, sensibilities. Nevertheless, the Constitution does not permit government to decide which types of otherwise protected speech are sufficiently offensive to require protection for the unwilling listener or viewer.

The logic of the decision would also apply to similar laws in Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, and the Virgin Islands, many of which were enacted within the last several years. (Of course, the Ninth Circuit decision binding precedent is only binding in, of these states, Oregon and Washington; in others it is only potentially persuasive precedent.)

I expect the decision to be quite controversial, and there will probably be an en banc rehearing petition. Note, though, that the panel consisted of two Clinton-appointed Senior Judges and a Trump-appointed judge; this makes it hard to predict how the en banc court (currently split 16-13 between Democrat and Republican appointees) would vote.

Lonnie D. Giamela (Fisher & Phillips LLP) and Todd A. Lyon (Fisher & Phillips LLP) represent plaintiffs.

UPDATE 10/30/2026, 11:18 am: Note that I signed on to an academics' amicus brief in the case, written by Jennifer Safstrom and Ryan Riedmueller (of Vanderbilt Law School's Stanton Foundation First Amendment Clinic), which focused solely on the standing issues (not the First Amendment merits argument).

#7974. Kathy’s Fall Garden

Happy Monday, GPOD! Halloween may be behind us, but fall still has plenty to offer in Kathy’s Zone 6a garden. I love how she keeps the seasonal decorating simple and lets what’s already happening in the landscape do most of the work. A few pumpkins, a refreshed container, and plants still hanging onto their color are enough to make the whole front garden feel ready for November.

Keeping it sweet and simple this fall! It has been a beautiful fall in Michigan so far. Although I’ve been gardening for more than 40 years, this is my eighth year gardening at our current home in Macomb.

I love these Japanese forest grasses (Hakonechloa macra cvs., Zones 5–9).

I replaced this summer container display earlier than usual, and these plants have been hanging tough since the first week of September.

Just sweet! There has been a multitude of fancy pumpkins for sale this year, more than usual, and I think they are so pretty!

Boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9), Fire Chief arborvitae (Thuja occidentalis ‘Congabe’, Zones 5–8), ‘Orange Rocket’ Japanese barberry (Berberis thunbergii ‘Orange Rocket’, Zones 4–9), and Little Lime® panicle hydrangea (Hydrangea paniculata ‘Jane’, Zones 3–8) grow in front of our home.

Already, I’m looking forward to spring when I can plant this new garden arch! I’m thinking clematis (Clematis cvs., Zones 3–9).

Here is Belleza Dark Pink gaura (Oenothera lindheimeri ‘KLEAU04263’, Zones 6–9) and yellow ‘Lady Stratheden’ avens (Geum ‘Lady Stratheden’, Zones 5–9). They are hanging tough so far!

Thanks for sharing your fall garden with us, Kathy! I really like the little bed by the driveway. The purple tones of the ajuga carpeting the ground against that bright orange mum and the pumpkins make for such an effortlessly beautiful fall display. And I’m with you on already thinking about spring—I’d love to see what you decide to grow over that new arch!
