#7973. Supreme Court Clerks Who Become Law Professors (2012-2026)

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Yesterday, I wrote about the lateral hiring market. Here, I want to focus on the entry-level hiring market. Since 2012, the number of entry-level hires has dipped to the low 60s and spiked to the mid 140s. Professor Sarah Lawsky has carefully tracked these numbers over the years through a series of detailed hiring spreadsheets: 2012, 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, and 2026.

Lawsky tracks how many entry-level hires completed Supreme Court clerkships. (This category does not record already hired law professors who are subsequently hired for Supreme Court clerkships.) I thought it might be worthwhile to dig into the numbers a bit more. Moreover, to continue my prior post on laterals, I wanted to track how often former SCOTUS clerks moved to other institutions. You can see the details in this spreadsheet, which tracks hires of SCOTUS clerks between 2012 and 2026. Please let me know if I am missing any names or made any errors.

How many academics has each Justice "fed"? Counting is actually a bit tricky, so I had to make some judgment calls. If a senior associate Justice hired a clerk, who was then assigned to an active member of the Court, I counted the hiring Justice. (Still, I found at least one law school bio that listed the active justice before the senior justice, a faux pas in my mind.) Likewise, for the clerks hired during the final terms of Justice Scalia or Ginsburg's tenure, and who were then reassigned, I counted them as Scalia and Ginsburg clerks. What about the clerks who were hired by Scalia or Ginsburg for a future term after their passing? In that case, I chose the active Justice that made the decision to re-hire them. With all those caveats out of the way, here is the list.

First, during this time period, I suppose it makes sense that Justices Ginsburg and Breyer, both academics, hired so many law clerks who went onto become academics. But I was struck that Justice Kagan only hired three future academics. Perhaps her focus is not on the curious type that wants to write articles? Then again, as I've noted before, Professor Kagan didn't publish very much. She was a skilled administrator. To paraphrase John Kerry, "I was for originalism before I was against it." Who would have predicted that Justice Sotomayor would have twice as many academic clerks as Justice Kagan? Likewise, Justice Scalia, a former academic, only had three clerks hired into academia--only one of whom is conservative. Then again, I suspect ideological bias blocked many potential Scalia clerks from even considering the academy during this period. Justice Thomas has jumped ahead in the standings, but as I'll explain below, most of those placements are over the past three years.

Second, there are relatively few law professors who clerked on the Supreme Court. The percentage of entry-level hires with Supreme Court clerkships fluctuates. In 2012, there were seven clerks hired out of 140 reported hires: about 5%. In 2018, there were eight clerks hired out of 77 reported hires: nearly 10%. In 2026, there were four clerks hired out of 146 reported hires: about 3%. The hiring market has been fairly variable in recent years. Still, the persistent myth that you have to clerk on the Supreme Court to teach constitutional law should be retired. Very few ConLaw professors have actually clerked on the Supreme Court.

Third, the total number of hired clerks fluctuates each year, though it averages to about 5. I would wager that 100% of the clerks who apply for the entry-level market find a job somewhere. The Supreme Court pumps out about 36 clerks each year. Let's assume that around 13% of those clerks become law professors. Presumably, about 87% of Supreme Court law clerks do not go into academia, and find employment in the public or private sectors. Despite what one may think, the clerks who work to develop the law are not particularly interested in teaching it.

Fourth, the ideological imbalance of these clerks is stark, although it has corrected somewhat in recent years. Between 2012 and 2015, out of 25 entry-level hires, I count only four professors who were right-of-center: Chris Walker (Ohio State), James Stern (William and Mary), Will Baude (Chicago), and Justin Walker (Louisville). Between 2016 and 2019, there were also four right-of-center hires out of twenty total hires: Aditya Bamzai (Virginia), Steven Menashi (George Mason), Jennifer Mascott (George Mason), Robert Leider (George Mason). The rate has increased substantially from 2020 to the present with nine right-of-center hires out of twenty total hires: J. Joel Alicea (Catholic), Sherif Girgis (Notre Dame), Haley Proctor (Notre Dame), Garrett West (Yale), Steven Lindsay (Catholic), Lael Weinberger (George Mason), Brian Lipshutz (Florida), Micah Quigley (Notre Dame), and Brittney Lane Kubisch (Pepperdine).

Fifth, even as the rate of hiring has increased, left-of-center professors are still being recruited by higher-ranked institutions. Starting in 2012, there have been entry level hires of SCOTUS clerks at Harvard (5), Columbia (3), Virginia (3), Chicago (4), and more. Curiously, Yale has had zero progressive SCOTUS clerk hires, but it did hire Garrett West after he finished clerking for Justice Alito. By contrast, the bulk of the conservative hires have been at right-of-center law schools. George Mason, my alma matter, hired four SCOTUS clerks (two of whom are now federal circuit court judges). Notre Dame has hired four conservative SCOTUS clerks. Catholic has hired two.

Sixth, several schools recruited SCOTUS clerks as laterals. Jean Galbraith spent two years at Rutgers-Camden before moving to Penn in 2014. Michigan recruited Chris Walker from Ohio State, Harvard recruited Richard Re from UVA (previously at UCLA), and Harvard recruited Sherif Girgis from Notre Dame. The professor who moved around the most in the shortest span is Katherine Mims Crocker who started at William & Mary in 2019, moved to Texas A&M in 2024, and then to Cornell in 2026.

Seventh, this post only considered law professors hired on the entry-level market between 2012 and 2026. I did not consider several professors who started clerkships after their first appointment. Justice Gorsuch has hired several of these academics: Stephanie Barclay (BYU, then Notre Dame, then Georgetown); Mark Storslee (Penn State, then Emory, then UNC); Christian Burset, (Notre Dame then Penn); and Tyler Lindley (BYU). Rev. Patrick Reidy began a clerkship with Justice Kavanaugh after he was appointed at Notre Dame. Professor Kerrel Murray at Columbia later clerked for Justice Jackson.

It might be useful to expand this post further back from 2012 to see earlier trends. Another time.

NEXT: Law Banning Employer Requirements That Employees Listen to Employer's Religious or Political Speech Likely Violates Employer's First Amendment Rights

Josh Blackman is a constitutional law professor at the South Texas College of Law Houston and the President of the Harlan Institute. Follow him @JoshMBlackman.

#7969. A November Garden Walk in Downtown Milwaukee

November is definitely settling in here in downtown Milwaukee, Wisconsin (Zone 6a). Most of the summer flowers are gone, leaves are piling up, and plenty of perennials are heading into dormancy. But there’s still so much to appreciate. Today we’re staying close to home for a walk around my neighborhood. I walk these streets with my dog all the time, and there are a handful of gardens I always slow down to admire.

Starting off strong with this one! This prairie-inspired garden is always buzzing with pollinators in summer, and it’s one of my favorites to walk by. In fall, the large sweeps of switchgrass (Panicum virgatum, Zones 4–9) and little bluestem (Schizachyrium scoparium, Zones 3–9) really come forward. And wow, those fluffy switchgrass plumes make a statement when planted en masse.

From the other side, the pinkish-copper tones of little bluestem become much more prominent. The planting even carries across the sidewalk into the curb strip, making this small garden pretty hard to miss.

A few houses down is another garden that inspires me. The whole yard is planted so elegantly, with interest no matter the season. Bare spaces are usually filled with annuals. But even in November, we still get to see roses in bloom and hydrangeas giving it their all to remain relevant. The urn in the background with the pumpkin is a lovely seasonal touch.

This garden might look messy to some, but this is the kind of fall mess I truly enjoy. The hostas (Hosta cvs., Zones 3–9) spilling over the stairs, surrounded and covered by fallen red maple leaves… I love it!

This deep burgundy shrub covered in bright red berries certainly caught my eye. Unfortunately, it’s Japanese barberry (Berberis thunbergii, Zones 4–8), an invasive shrub here in Wisconsin. If you like the look, consider one of these native alternatives to Japanese barberry, including chokeberry, fothergilla, Virginia sweetspire, summersweet, and inkberry.

This Siberian crab apple (Malus baccata, Zones 2–7) is absolutely covered in clusters of warm orange fruit. Once so many summer flowers have disappeared, fruiting trees like this become some of the strongest color in the landscape.

It’s nice to see another garden extend beyond the front yard and into the curb strip. These often-overlooked spaces have so much potential. They can become a small garden, pollinator planting, or even a bee lawn.

And, of course, who can resist a strip of marigolds (Tagetes cvs., annual)? Especially when they’re still looking this good!

And one final reminder to leave the leaves this fall! Fallen leaves provide important overwintering habitat for pollinators and other beneficial insects, so leaving some in garden beds gives them a place to shelter until spring.

Thanks for coming along on my afternoon walk! While I wish this were a fall update from my little concrete jungle of a backyard, it’s all packed up now… because I’m moving to Georgia in just a few short weeks! I’ll definitely miss these neighborhood gardens, but I’m excited to see what new gardens and plants catch my eye down South.

#7962. ISIS-Inspired Terrorist Sentenced for Attacking Guards While Serving Sentence for Separate NYC Terror Plot

An official website of the United States government

Abdulrahman El Bahnasawy, 28, of Ontario, Canada, was sentenced today to 50 years in prison for offenses related to a 2020 attack on correctional officers at U.S. Penitentiary Allenwood. This sentence will run consecutive to the 40-year sentence he is currently serving for his role in plotting a mass-casualty terrorist attack in New York City on behalf of ISIS.

“Bahnasawy, who is already serving a 40-year sentence in federal prison for plotting mass casualty attacks in New York City on behalf of ISIS, savagely attacked corrections officers once again on behalf of ISIS,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “Today’s sentence will further ensure that Bahnasawy remains in prison, where he can do much less harm, for a very long time.”

“We will prosecute those who aid, attempt to aid, or commit violence on behalf of the pernicious ISIS ideology wherever they may be found,” said U.S. Attorney Brian D. Miller for the Middle District of Pennsylvania. “Today’s sentence reflects our unwavering commitment to fight those who perpetrate violence in the name of ISIS even behind prison walls.”

“Although he was behind bars, this convicted terrorist committed a horrific attack on two corrections officers in the name of ISIS, which they fortunately survived,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “Today’s sentencing shows that violent attacks by those who support the evil ideology of ISIS or other foreign terrorist organizations cannot be tolerated by our society. Fighting terrorism is a central part of the FBI’s mission to protect the American people, and the FBI is committed to working with our law enforcement partners to hold these vicious criminals accountable.”

Bahnasawy was an inmate at USP Allenwood who, on Dec. 7, 2020, attacked two corrections officers using a weapon made from part of a steel desk in his cell. Bahnasawy stabbed one officer in the head and face, and, when a second responded to assist, Bahnasawy stabbed her in the hand.

The first officer eventually lost his right eye as a result of the attack. When Bahnasawy was restrained, a note was found in his sock that read, “This is a terrorist attack for the Islamic State.” A pledge of allegiance to the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS) was also found taped to the inside of a locker door in Bahnasawy’s prison cell. Bahnasawy pleaded guilty in November 2025 to multiple counts of assault, assault with intent to commit murder, and possession of contraband inside a prison as well as providing material support to ISIS, a designated foreign terrorist organization.

At the time of the attacks at USP Allenwood, Bahnasawy was serving a 40-year sentence for his role in plotting a mass-casualty terrorist attack in New York City on behalf of ISIS. Bahnasawy, a then-20-year-old Canadian citizen and resident, plotted with Talha Haroon and Russell Salic to conduct bombings and shootings in heavily populated areas of New York City during the Islamic holy month of Ramadhan in 2016, all in the name of ISIS.

An undercover FBI agent (UC) infiltrated the co-conspirators’ terrorist plot, posing as an ISIS supporter prepared to join in the attacks. The FBI arrested Bahnasawy in May 2016 after he traveled from Canada to the New York City area in preparation for the attacks, and he has been in custody since that time.

This case was investigated by the FBI’s Philadelphia Field Office.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Geoffrey MacArthur for the Middle District of Pennsylvania and Deputy Chief Larry Schneider of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section prosecuted the case.

#7958. 10-Year "Harassment"/"Stalking" Sentence for Repeatedly Criticizing Police Detective Violated First Amendment, Amicus Brief Argues

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

I was delighted to sign on to this brief in State v. McMenamy (Mo. Ct. App.) just filed by the ACLU of Missouri Foundation and the Wash. U (St. Louis) First Amendment Clinic, on behalf the ACLU of Missouri and Profs. Jane Bambauer and Lyrissa Lidsky and me. The Introduction:

The First Amendment and article I, § 8 of the Missouri Constitution broadly protect the right to speak to the public about other people. This is true even when the speech "is intended to trouble or annoy, or to make another timid or fearful." United States v. Sryniawski, 48 F.4th 583, 587 (8th Cir. 2022). And it is true even when speech uses "social pressure and the 'threat' of social ostracism … to embarrass others or coerce them into action." NAACP v. Claiborne Hardware Co., 458 U.S. 886, 910 (1982). While individuals who are the subjects of unwanted speech may be able to limit some speech directed to them, they cannot limit offensive speech about them directed to others. Organization for a Better Austin v. Keefe, 402 U.S. 415, 419 (1971).

Contrary to this established law, Matthew McMenamy was convicted and sentenced to 10 years in prison for openly and vigorously criticizing a local police detective he believed had engaged in misconduct. Mr. McMenamy used his public social media accounts and publicly distributed flyers to attempt to draw the community's attention to the detective's actions. He expressed his hope that his revelations would result in the officer's removal.

While Mr. McMenamy's speech was certainly concerning to the detective, the circuit court did not make any finding that either the flyers or any one of the dozens of social media posts submitted as evidence fell within any category of unprotected speech, such as true threats. Nor could the circuit court have done so, as none of Mr. McMenamy's speech was outside the bounds of the First Amendment's protection. His convictions for harassment and stalking violate the First Amendment and should be reversed.

The opening paragraph of the section on the facts (for the full discussion of the facts, read the brief):

In August 2023, Matthew McMenamy began posting on social media about what he viewed as misconduct and racism by a local police detective, who years before had been involved in Mr. McMenamy's involuntary commitment. See State's Exs. 60A–M. Mr. McMenamy sought to publicize one of the detective's public Facebook posts, where the detective wrote: "If black lives matter then why are they shooting and killing each other at an alarming rate." State's Ex. 60B ("Let's make this racist post go viral … #BLM #RacistCop ….); State's Ex. 60A ("The people want answers. Is [detective] a racist? Does he feel that people of color do not matter because of an idea that they murder each other at an alarming rate?"). Many of Mr. McMenamy's posts were aimed at sharing with the public his concerns about the detective's fitness for his position. For example, Mr. McMenamy posted he was "in talks with a billboard company to put [detective's] racist quotes up next to a picture of him in uniform" because "[s]omeone like that shouldn't be a detective, an election [sic] official, or let alone anything near public service." Tr. 736:10–21, State's Ex. 60K. Mr. McMenamy's posts also described his feelings about his prior involuntary commitment and thoughts about hurting his parents before getting help. See State's Ex. 60E (Mr. McMenamy's post that he "had a bad day last Sunday … I still need time to heal but … I am going to counseling and I will be looking for support groups").

And the opening material in the legal argument (again, read the brief for much more):

All of Mr. McMenamy's social media posts and his distribution of flyers were protected by the First Amendment. Harassment and stalking laws may, in some circumstances, be constitutionally applied to protect unwilling listeners from unwanted, one-to-one speech directed to that listener. The government's power to protect an unwilling listener from speech about them directed to the public, on the other hand, is sharply limited, even when that speech is annoying, offensive, or alarming. Unless such speech falls within one of the narrow, historically recognized categories of speech that the U.S. Supreme Court has held may be regulated without violating the First Amendment, such as "true threats," it is presumptively protected.

Here, Mr. McMenamy spoke to the public, and his speech did not fall within any unprotected category. This Court should reverse Mr. McMenamy's convictions. Even if this Court does not find that all Mr. McMenamy's speech is protected from criminal prosecution by the First Amendment, he is at least entitled to a new trial. The circuit court allowed the State to present evidence of more than four months' worth of social media posts to the jury and then instructed the jury it could find Mr. McMenamy guilty based on unidentified "alarming content" in these posts. This means a juror could have convicted Mr. McMenamy based on speech protected by the First Amendment.

[I.] The State's prosecution of Mr. McMenamy for harassment and stalking based on unwanted speech about individuals directed to the public violates the First Amendment.

Speech directed to the public at large is presumptively protected unless it falls into one of the narrow, historic exceptions to the First Amendment. This is because even if some listeners are likely to be offended, others may be willing listeners who find the speech valuable. For this reason, while harassment and stalking statutes may, in some instances, be constitutionally applied to repeated unwanted communications to an individual, they cannot be constitutionally applied to communications to the public about an individual.

[A.] Stalking and harassment statutes were originally intended to limit unwanted communications directed to a specific person.

For decades, laws have "restricted certain kinds of unwanted speech said to a particular person." For example, state and federal criminal harassment statutes were enacted to prohibit unwanted telephone calls to a particular person. Similarly, the federal government and some states have banned certain unwanted mailings into the home. These laws reflect an intention to protect individuals from repeated, unwanted communications to them, particularly in the home.

More recently, states enacted stalking laws to proscribe behaviors such as physically following, surveilling, or engaging in repeated unwanted personal contacts with a particular person. Courts have relied on stalking laws or restraining order laws to ban repeated or annoying letters, phone calls, or personal contact from a particular person. While some of these laws have been struck down in some states, "they have generally been upheld by lower courts; and the U.S. Supreme Court has upheld the federal ban on repeated unwanted mailings."

These laws share something in common: In the vast majority of their applications, they restrict unwanted speech to a person, not unwanted speech about a person. It is in this context—where the laws are being applied to "one-to-one speech"—that they "have generally been upheld against First Amendment challenge." Id.

As the internet has made it easier for communications to reach the public, maintaining this distinction between constitutionally permissible punishment of certain one-to-one speech and constitutionally impermissible punishment of one-to-many speech is critical. Social media is "the modern public square." However, the increased exposure for "upsetting" or "frightening" online speech can bring with it an increased risk of overcriminalization. Online communication "lack[s] many normal contextual clues," including tone of voice and expression. "The ubiquity of this speech raises the possibility of highly discretionary enforcement." Thus, in the context of online speech, courts must exercise particular caution to ensure the state's application of harassment and stalking laws does not exceed the laws' original intention or permissible constitutional boundaries.

[B.] The First Amendment grants broad protection to speech directed to the public at large, even when the subjects of that speech may be alarmed or offended.

The U.S. Supreme Court has consistently recognized a distinction between speech directed to the public at large and interpersonal speech for First Amendment purposes. Even when the content of the speech is subjectively offensive or alarming, the U.S. Supreme Court has typically protected public statements about a person—absent a showing of a narrow and well-established First Amendment exception, such as true threats, fighting words, or defamation.

As now-Justice Alito stated: "There is no categorical 'harassment exception' to the First Amendment's free speech clause." Saxe v. State Coll. Area Sch. Dist. (3d Cir. 2001); [citing other cases]. Many courts have endorsed this very point, quoting Saxe, in the context of criminal harassment laws and the closely related harassment restraining order laws. [Citing still more cases].

Unlike prohibitions on speech said to a particular unwilling listener, restrictions on speech to the public deprive a speaker of the opportunity to communicate with willing listeners. Denying access to potentially interested audiences undermines the use of speech to influence opinion and conduct and, as a result, hinders the robustness of public debate—particularly when the restricted speech concerns a matter of political, social, or other concern to the community. One's interest in being free from public criticism is insufficient to overcome protection for speech….

Accordingly, public statements about a person that coerce, annoy, alarm, offend, or embarrass are generally protected by the First Amendment. {The State may have some power to restrict narrowly defined categories of speech that reveals private information about a person that is "almost never relevant to any discussion on either public or private topics" (e.g., nude photos, Social Security numbers). No such speech is at issue here.} In Organization for a Better Austin v. Keefe (1971), a local civil rights organization believed a local real estate broker's practices were improper. After the broker refused to sign an agreement not to solicit property in the organization's community, the organization distributed leaflets critical of the broker's supposedly racist real estate practices at a local shopping center, on the doors of his neighbors, and to people going to and from his church. Some leaflets accused him of being a "panic peddler" that employed tactics to scare white homeowners into selling their properties; others encouraged recipients to call his home phone number to express their disapproval. The U.S. Supreme Court concluded that the organization's "inten[t] to exercise a coercive impact … does not remove [speech] from the reach of the First Amendment. Petitioners plainly intended to influence respondent's conduct by their activities; this is not fundamentally different from the function of a newspaper." The U.S. Supreme Court explained, "so long as the means are peaceful, the communication need not meet standards of acceptability," particularly where the target of the speech "is not attempting to stop the flow of information into his own household, but to the public."

While speech that is intended to solicit violence against particular people may be punishable, speech to the public that harshly criticizes its target or that attempts to persuade through social pressure does not lose its protection even if some listeners may react with threats or violence. In NAACP v. Claiborne Hardware Co. (1982), organizers of a boycott of stores owned by white merchants read aloud and published the names of Black residents who weren't following the boycott to place pressure on them. As in Keefe, the U.S. Supreme Court held the disclosures constitutionally protected, noting the First Amendment extended beyond abstract discussions to protect "offensive" and "coercive" speech intended to influence action. This was true even though some of the people who chose not to comply with the boycott were beaten, had their property damaged, or had shots fired into their homes. The U.S. Supreme Court explained that speech designed to persuade "through social pressure and the 'threat' of social ostracism … does not lose its protected character … simply because it may embarrass others or coerce them into action." …

For a couple of articles of mine on the subject, see One-to-One Speech, One-to-Many Speech, Criminal Harassment Laws, and "Cyberstalking" and Overbroad Injunctions Against Speech (Especially in Libel and Harassment Cases.

The brief was signed by Kristin M. Mulvey, Jonathan D. Schmid, Gillian R. Wilcox, Jason A. Orr (ACLU Missouri) and Lisa S. Hoppenjans, Benjamin J. Wilson, and students Lindsey Bennett. Megan McConnell (Wash. U. First Amendment Clinic).

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Since a home studio has different needs than other rooms, those outfitting this space may want a professional product rather than residential curtains. Designed to dampen sound, minimize unwanted noise, and block light on movie sets, stages, and recording studios, the Filmcraft studio soundproof blanket is a relatively affordable pick that’s as versatile as it is effective. Measuring 80 inches long by 72 inches wide with grommets on all sides for easier hanging, this sound-minimizing curtain also doubles as a protective blanket to cover set pieces and instruments in transit.

We tested this blanket in a bedroom by using clamps to attach it to a curtain rod. It reduced noise by 10 decibels, matching the top score achieved by just two other picks. Though it isn’t as attractive as either of those options, it would work well in a studio or as a packing blanket. For those playing shows or working on sets. Because it’s designed for professional use, it comes only in black, in a single size, and its price rivals some of the soundproof curtains we tested.

Get the Filmcraft soundproof blanket at Amazon or B&H.

We tested the following options, and while they offered some soundproofing, they didn’t perform as well as our top picks.

To test soundproof curtains for possible inclusion on our list, we hung each set in a room with a single window for 3 to 7 days. We used a decibel meter to measure the level of ambient room noise, then had someone play a trumpet outside the window and measured the decibels again.  If the curtains had thermal properties, we evaluated the temperature difference in the morning, afternoon, and evening while the curtains were hanging versus when they were not. If they had blackout features, we observed how much light filtered in throughout the course of the day and whether we could see in the window from outside. When possible, we also washed and dried the curtains according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

We then scored the curtains according to an established rubric that considered appearance, soundproof quality, light blocking, and thermal abilities. We factored in the quality of the fabric and the durability of construction, eliminating products that didn’t meet our standards and assigning awards to ones that did.

Good noise-reducing curtains help absorb sound waves and reduce noise pollution, so they’re ideal for a bedroom, living room, home office, or home theater. Many can even double as blackout curtains or thermal curtains to help reduce natural light pollution and heating or cooling costs.

Shopping for soundproof curtains starts with choosing one of three types: insulation curtains, audio insulation sheets, and industrial blankets.

Insulation curtains look similar to regular window curtains found in most homes and can come in a range of designs as well, from neutral colors to bold patterns. The main difference is that insulation curtains are made with heavier materials that block some noise. Insulation curtains also often function as blackout curtains since the thicker material that insulates the room from sound also works to block sunlight.

Thermal insulation curtains also help lower energy bills. The same thick material that works to absorb sounds can contain thermal energy, adding a layer of insulation that prevents air from entering or escaping through windows.

While audio insulation sheets aren’t technically curtains, they can be hung to function like curtains. Audio insulation sheets are typically designed with grommets to allow them to hang from a curtain rod, making them easier to install than acoustic panels.

Audio insulation sheets can block more sound than insulation curtains and industrial blankets because they are constructed with multiple layers of heavy fabric, which makes them a nearly soundproof fabric. They also function as blackout curtains due to these multiple layers. However, the amount of fabric required to craft audio insulation sheets makes them a more expensive option.

Industrial blankets are primarily intended to protect furniture and other fragile items during the moving process. Because of this, they are made with thick and padded material, which allows them to serve as sound-eliminating curtains. Though you probably don’t want to use them to soundproof an office or other professional space long term, they can serve as excellent temporary soundproof divider curtains.

Some industrial blankets are designed with grommets, which makes them easier to hang. Otherwise, you’ll have to find a way to drape them over windows or rig up a hanging mechanism so that they can help absorb outside sounds. Industrial blankets are one of the most budget-friendly options for soundproofing walls or creating a soundproof doorway curtain to reduce outdoor sounds in your indoor space.

Before purchasing soundproof curtains, check to confirm that the product is available in the appropriate size. Measure the length and width of the window, and look for a curtain that is wide and long enough to sufficiently cover it. Ideally, soundproof curtains should cover a portion of the wall, in addition to the window, especially in small spaces like apartments, to be most effective.

If possible, choose a curtain that is up to three times as wide as the window and 10 or more inches longer. Floor-to-ceiling soundproof curtains can be even more effective at noise reduction. Heavier soundproofing curtains are more effective at absorbing sounds and keeping your space quiet than lighter ones. This is especially true for lower-frequency sounds. If deciding between two soundproof curtains, the heavier option may be the better choice.

The materials used to make soundproof curtains will affect not only the way they look but also how well they block and absorb sounds. More fibrous options, such as velvet curtains, can be more effective at noise reduction. Suede and polyester are also quality options to consider.

Many soundproof curtains on the market are crafted with triple-weave fabric, making them denser and more effective. Thermal soundproof curtains also offer additional insulation as well. Thermal insulation can both help to reduce energy costs and also make the curtains more effective at absorbing sounds. A general rule of thumb to keep in mind when looking for soundproof curtains is that more material usually equals better soundproofing capabilities.

Before hanging a new set of soundproof curtains, consider the curtain rods currently installed to see if they’ll work. Since soundproof curtains are heavier than traditional curtains, make sure the curtain rod can support the weight of heavier curtains, or consider installing new curtain rods.

Depending on their dimensions, soundproof curtains could weigh 8 pounds or more, compared to about 2 pounds for traditional light-filtering curtains. In addition to rod strength, shoppers may also wish to consider buying a wraparound curtain rod. This style of curtain rod is more effective at blocking sounds since it attaches to the wall at a curve and allows the curtain to provide a more complete sound barrier.

The color of the sound-blocking curtains won’t affect their noise reduction, but it will certainly visually affect a living space. Based on personal preferences and needs, consider acoustic curtains that match the aesthetic of the room—such as modern, vintage, or farmhouse, for example—and coordinate with the decor as well.

Finally, consider how easy it will be to install and maintain the soundproof curtains. One of the easiest ways to help soundproof a space is with insulation curtains that have grommets along the top for simple installation from a curtain rod.

Depending on their design, audio insulation sheets and industrial blankets may be more challenging to install. If possible, try to preview the manufacturer’s installation directions before making a purchase. Also, take note of the manufacturer’s care and cleaning instructions for each potential purchase. Machine-washable options are easier to maintain.

Hopefully, you now know more about soundproof curtains and how to choose the best product to reduce noise in your home. If you still have questions like where to buy curtains or how to take care of them, check out the following section for more information.

To increase the noise reduction of your existing curtains, add more layers of fabric. For best results, choose heavy and tightly woven fabrics, as they are more effective at reducing the amount of noise that enters your space. Ideally, the curtains should cover the full length of the wall—both above and below the window—since this will allow them to create a seal to block more sound.

Yes, traditional drapes will block some sound. However, the amount of sound absorption will vary significantly based on their thickness and the quality of the seal they create over a window. For example, heavy velvet curtains soundproof​ better than lightweight cotton ones.

You can soundproof a room in several ways without spending too much money. One idea is to use an industrial blanket, or even just thick regular blankets, to help soundproof windows and the surrounding wall space. The thick material can help to block a lot of noise from entering your space.In addition to purchasing soundproof curtains for door and window openings, there are many other DIY soundproofing tricks you can use to minimize noise. For example, you can place weatherstripping tape around your windows and door frames as well as seal gaps between doors and their thresholds with a rubber doorstop to further soundproof a room.

Yes, as evidenced by our tests, even low-quality soundproofing curtains work. All the soundproofing curtains we recommend reduced noise levels by 5 to 10 decibels, and those that didn’t make our list still brought them down by 2 to 3 decibels.

For soundproof curtains, look for dense, heavyweight fabrics like velvet or polyester. Multi-layered acoustic fabrics with thermal linings also make excellent soundproof curtains.

Yes, soundproof curtains can reduce your energy bill by providing thermal insulation and improving temperature control in your space.

Yes, if external noise is disrupting people’s sleep, soundproof curtains can help them sleep better by creating quieter spaces that allow for deeper, uninterrupted sleep.

Few things can bring a building project or repair effort to a grinding halt like a stripped screw or bolt, which is why keeping a screw extractor at the ready is key. These handy tools consist of a drill bit that grinds a hole into the head of a screw and a threaded extractor that bites into this hole, gripping the screw so you can remove it with a drill or ratchet.

There are many types and brands of screw extractors on the market, but few have the mettle to do the job properly. We put five screw extractor kits to the test by using them to remove various sizes of bolts and screws. With its effective design and affordable price, the Alden Grabit Pro Bolt and Screw Extractor Kit proved to be the best of the bunch. Read on to learn more about our test results for the Alden and other screw extractors, and find out what factors to keep in mind when shopping for the best screw extractor for your workshop.

Bottom line: Choosing the right screw extractor depends on your needs, with the Alden Grabit Pro Kit standing out for its effectiveness and value.

The products below represent some of the top screw extractors on the market. This includes small sets designed for occasional use and large sets for pros and avid DIYers who regularly deal with damaged screws and bolts.

Our Ratings: Performance 4/5; Durability 5/5; Value 5/5

Not only is this kit from Alden one of the cheapest of the bunch, it also happens to be the easiest to use and most effective at removing stripped screws. The kit’s design eliminates the guesswork of trying to match drill bits with extractors sizes—each of the four bit sizes is conveniently double-sided with the drill bit on one side and the threaded extractor on the other.

During testing, each extractor gripped nicely to the insides of the stripped-out holds, allowing us to remove screws easily. In fact, the Alden removed screws that two other screw extractor sets we tested failed to remove. Of all the kits we tested, this one most consistently gripped and removed screws.

Since this screw extractor set only comes with four bit sizes, it is somewhat limited. Still, those bit sizes are the most common you’ll find. The kit includes a small carrying case that keeps these bits organized, so they’re easy to find when needed. We also like the fact that this kit is small. This makes it easier to throw in a tool box or tool belt pocket so it’s at your side when you encounter a dreaded stripped screw.

Get the Alden Grabit Pro screw extractor at Amazon or Walmart.

Our Ratings: Performance 4.3/5; Durability 4/5; Value 4/5

This compact screw remover and extractor set includes five extractors and drill bit sizes. Each extractor and bit is conveniently paired in a storage box, so there’s no confusion as to which bit goes with which extractor.

While we liked the paired design of this set, we experienced mixed results during testing. The larger sizes worked well for removing bolts. The bits drilled nicely into the screw and bolts heads, and the spiral shape of the removers bit well into the drilled holes.

Unfortunately, we didn’t have very good results with the smaller drill bits and extractors. We couldn’t get the extractors to bite in the drilled head on stripped-out 3-inch decking screws despite several attempts using various sizes of drill bit and matching extractor. While we were ultimately able to back the screws out, we had to do so using very slow speeds so the extractor wouldn’t slip and strip out the pilot hole.

Although we would certainly recommend this set for removing bolts and larger screws, we’d consider other options for smaller stripped-out screws.

Get the Irwin 10-piece screw extractor at Amazon or Acme Tools.

Our Ratings: Performance 3.7/5; Durability 4/5; Value 4.5/5

We’ve typically found Bosch’s power tools and accessories to be of good quality while remaining somewhat more affordable than other power tool brands. This screw extractor kit from Bosch was, for the most part, no exception. It performed fairly well with bolts and smaller screws with a better-than-average success rate when compared with other sets.

Durability was also good but not great. All of the extractors feel as if they would last a long time. Our only concern was with the two smaller drill bit sizes, which feel as if they could potentially snap. While we didn’t experience any broken bits, this was a common complaint with online reviewers.

We like the handy carrying case, which is compact and holds each bit securely. We only wish it was easier to read the sizes on the case. Overall, though, this is a good screw extractor set that’s affordably priced and compact enough to fit in a tool bag or belt.

Get the Bosch screw extractor at The Home Depot.

Our Ratings: Performance 4.3/5; Durability 5/5; Value 4/5

With some 35 pieces, Topec’s screw extractor kit gives you plenty of options for removing all types of fasteners, ranging from small screws to large bolts.

In terms of performance, Topec’s effectiveness tilts to large fasteners. The bits and extractors perform best on larger screw heads and bolts. While we found some success removing bits with its spiral screw extractors, these multispline extractors, when used with a drill and bit driver, garnered the best results. The tighter threading of the splines just seemed to bite better into drilled-out holes than the spiral extractors.

While we liked the broad range of bits this kit offers, we didn’t like the fact that Topec doesn’t group the bits with the extractors. This leaves you to make those matches on your own, which can be a challenge, especially if you use the kit only occasionally.

This design makes the kit a tougher pick for those who don’t have a lot of experience using this type of tool. Given that and this kit’s size, the Topec extractor set is best suited for home mechanics who find themselves facing off against stripped-out screw heads and sheared-off bolt heads of varying sizes on a fairly regular basis.

Our Ratings: Performance 4/5; Durability 5/5; Value 4/5

This is no ordinary set of combination pliers. A closer look at its jaws reveals that it’s designed with one purpose in mind: to remove stripped screws. The aptly named Vampliers have fanglike serrated teeth and a concave opening in the jaws that fit around the contours of a screw head, making it an excellent tool for stripped screws.

The serrated teeth bit nicely into screw heads during testing, allowing us to turn the screws without having to put a death grip on the handle. The rubberized grip makes the handles fairly comfortable to hold. We also liked the fact that we could grip screw heads either by holding the teeth perpendicular to the screw for maximum grip or vertically over the top of the screw for heads just barely poking above the wood surface. Of course, the Vampliers are only useful if there’s something to bite into; they won’t work for embedded screw heads.

The Vampliers is an expensive stripped screw removal tool, especially for anyone who already has a pair of vice-grip pliers in their tool arsenal. Still, they’re worth the investment if you find yourself dealing with stripped-out or sheared-off screw heads on a regular basis.

Get the Vampliers screw extractor at Amazon.

While we didn’t test the products below, they still make the grade based on their impressive specs and extensive positive customer reviews.

This five-piece bolt extraction set from Irwin is a simple yet effective bolt removal tool. Each size extractor has a reverse spiral design that bites into the bolt head, making it easier to remove bolts that have been painted over, rounded-off bolts heads, and frozen bolts. The extraction kit for bolts comes with five sizes to suit bolts ranging in size from ⅜ inch and 10 millimeter (mm) to ⅝ inch and 16mm. And if that’s not enough, Irwin also makes a five-piece expansion set with additional sizes. The bolt extractor bits work with 1/2-inch ratchets, impact wrenches, flat wrenches, and locking pliers, and all five pieces fit into a hard plastic case that’s small enough to fit into a tool box or bucket.

Extracting large stripped-out bolts and screws can be a tough job. With its large extractors, this set is up to the challenge. It boasts 25 extractors that run in 1/32-inch increments from ⅛ inch all the way up to a hefty ⅞-inch extractor. Each extractor features microplaned reverse threads designed to thread into drilled-out holes to remove stripped screws or bolts with rounded-off or sheared-off heads.

Its hexagonal head fits into standard sockets for optimal torque. Socket sizes are etched into the metal, making identifying each extractor easy. The extractors consist of chrome molybdenum steel that is hard enough to extract these larger bolts, and all 25 pieces fit into a molded carrying case.

Get the Neiko screw and bolt extractor at Amazon or Walmart.

Removing tiny damaged screws from electronics such as laptop computers isn’t doable with a standard screw extraction kit. The bits are simply too large. With its ability to remove machine screws as small as a 1 rating, which is just 0.0781 inches in diameter, this small screw extractor kit is an excellent solution for extracting smaller stripped machine screws.

In addition to the 0.0781-inch size, it also includes 2, 3, and 4 machine screw sizes. Each bit is double-sided with a drill bit on one end and a threaded adapter on the other. They consist of durable high-speed steel that is heat tempered twice for maximum hardness. A plastic carrying case conveniently keeps all four bits organized so they’re easy to find when needed.

Get the Alden Grabit Micro bolt extractor at Amazon.

We assembled our list of the top screw extractors through a mix of research and hands-on testing. After comparing the specs and scouring reviews for some two dozen different screw extractors, we narrowed down the list to eight models, and then proceeded to test the top five sets.

We tested each on a variety of fasteners, including small and large screws and bolts, keeping in mind that screw extracting is challenging. No screw extracting kit will have a 100 percent success rate. Keeping that in mind, we assigned points to each kit based on how effective it was at removing fasteners and how easy it was to use. We also considered the range of extractor sizes, awarding points for those capable of handling a broader range of screw and bolt sizes. We considered the durability of each kit. Finally, we factored in performance and durability along with price to determine the value of each kit.

Screw extractors come in different types to suit the different sizes of damaged fasteners you can’t remove with a screwdriver. Read on to learn more about each type and crucial factors, including gripping power and the material one will want to consider when choosing the best screw extractor.

Screw heads come in a wide variety of sizes, so it’s important to pay attention to what sizes the screw extractor can accommodate. Most sets include sizes ranging from 0.125 inch up to 0.625 inch. Larger sets have extractors as large as 0.875 inch and are capable of removing large bolts on vehicles and industrial machines. Other sets can remove tiny machine screws found in electronics, such as laptop computers, with extractors as small as 0.0781 inch. While a small kit with four or five extractor sizes is adequate for most, it makes sense for pros or DIYers to invest in a set that can cover a broad range of sizes.

Different types of screw extractors use different strategies for gripping a stripped or rusted screw or bolt head. Some drill into the head and use reverse threads to bite into and grip the head, while others grab the head by fitting over it. Although the latter generally creates more gripping power, this style of extractor is limited to instances where the bolt or screw head is jutting out of the material enough to allow the tool to grip it.

The material type also affects gripping power. Drill bits and extractors made of high-quality steel alloys do a better job of boring into and gripping fasteners and last longer than those that use cheaper materials.

Since screw extractors must burrow into metal screws in order to work, they need to consist of hard metal. Most screw extractors are made of high-speed steel, the same steel alloy used in many drill bits and saw blades. This type of steel is harder than other alloys and is capable of enduring high temperatures without softening, a key characteristic for drilling into the heads of metal fasteners.

If it’s in the budget, extractors made of cobalt steel are even better, but they’re also pricier. Cobalt steel is harder than high-speed steel and holds up better to the high temperatures created by metal cutting into metal. Cobalt steel also has a higher tensile strength, which makes it a better choice for extractors with a narrower flute of 0.125 inch or less. Stay away from extractors that consist of softer alloys, as they will not be hard enough to do the job.

Screw extractors have features that make them easier to use and ensure that the right drill bit is used with the right extractor. Those that work in conjunction with a drill bit must match the bit size to be effective. This type of extractor should have the compatible drill bit size etched onto its side to avoid confusion.

Double-sided extractors are some of the most convenient models as they feature the drill bit and extractor on a single reversible shank, eliminating the need to hunt for a compatible drill bit. Simply drill the hole with one side, then flip the shank to apply the extractor.

Some kits use magnetic extension bit holders that can hold either the drill or extractor bit. This allows the user to quickly swap between them, speeding the screw-removal process along.

Since screw and bolt extractor kits can include 30 pieces or more, most come with handy carrying cases that keep all the pieces organized so they can be found when needed.

Most screw extractor tools are easy to use, even for beginners. Here are a few valuable tips for using a screw extractor.

If you have additional questions about how to use a screw extractor, read on for answers to some common queries about these handy tools.

The drill bit is a crucial part of the extractor that is used to bore a hole in the head of the damaged bolt or screw, creating a place for the extractor to penetrate and grip the screw head so you can remove it.

There really is no standard length for a screw extractor. In fact, short and long extractors work equally well at removing damaged screws and bolts. It’s more important to choose the correct- diameter drill bit and extractor to suit the damaged fastener.

To determine the proper extractor size, begin by choosing the proper drill bit size. The drill bit should be about half the diameter of the screw head. For example, to remove a 0.375-inch screw, begin by drilling a hole in the head with a 3/16-inch drill bit. Once the hole is drilled, use an extractor that’s slightly smaller than the drill bit—most kits conveniently match the bits on the kit to the extractor. The slightly smaller extractor should fit inside the hole but still be tight enough that its threads can lock into the hole’s contours.

Screw extractors are reverse threaded. This means that you’ll need to set your drill/driver or impact driver in reverse to remove the fastener. Keep in mind that the drill bits in screw extractor sets are also usually (though not always) reverse threaded, meaning you’ll need to set your drill in reverse when drilling the pilot hole.

A straight flute extractor is a smooth tapered bar. After drilling a pilot hole in the screw head, you have to hammer the straight extractor into the screw head, then use a pair of pliers to twist the extractor counterclockwise to remove the screw. A spiral screw extractor doesn’t require any hammering. It has threads that bite into the pilot hole, allowing you to remove the damaged screw with a wrench or drill.

#7954. Discovery Sanctions Recommended in "Are You a Jew? … Are You a Zionist?" Case

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The factual allegations, from a Sept. 2025 decision in the case by Judge Susan Illston (N.D. Cal.) (the case is Radice v. Jerusalem Boxing Club, LLC consolidated with the federal government's U.S. v. Harara):

The Jerusalem Coffee House [which Harara owns] is a business establishment open to the general public. The coffee house is located on the premises of the East Bay Community Space, "which regularly hosts events that are open to the general public for exhibition or entertainment …."

According to the complaint, on June 10, 2024, Michael Radice—who is Jewish—went to the East Bay Community Space "for the purpose of viewing the establishment for a fundraising event for his organization." Radice was wearing a dark blue baseball cap with a light blue Star of David and white Hebrew lettering. As he approached the community space from the side where the coffee house is located, a man sitting at a table in front of the coffee house asked, "Are you a Jew?" Radice answered in the affirmative. The man then asked, "Are you a Zionist?" Radice declined to respond.

The complaint alleges that "[t]he man then began shouting numerous accusations at Mr. Radice, including that he was complicit in Israel's military actions in the Gaza Strip following the October 7, 2023 Hamas attacks and guilty of 'killing children.'" As Radice began to walk away, the man stood up and asked, "Where are you going?" The complaint alleges, "Mr. Radice saw another man, whom he later learned was Harara, walk out of the coffee house and speak to the man, and the two went inside." …

And now from Judge Thomas Hixson's Report and Recommendation yesterday:

There is no dispute that Defendant Abdulrahim Harara violated at least six discovery orders. Motion at 4-7 ("Harara has flouted at least six discovery orders," and enumerating the violations); Opp. at 7 ("But the question on this motion is not whether any order was violated; it is whether the record as a whole shows the kind of deliberate, deceptive obstruction that makes a fair trial impossible and justifies ending the case without one.")….

The real issue is what remedy the Court should impose for the serial violations of its discovery orders. The impact of Harara's conduct basically falls into three buckets: documents were produced late that should have been produced earlier; some document productions are incomplete; and there has been a wholesale failure to produce email. But having reviewed the voluminous evidence submitted in support of Radice's motion for sanctions, the Court thinks truth is available to the parties, and they should go ahead and have a trial on the existing record.

Harara's biggest failure in discovery is the nonproduction of email, and he does not have a good excuse. In many cases the total failure to produce email would justify terminating sanctions or at least adverse inference instructions.

But the Court is skeptical that this is such a case. The relevant events are alleged in-person refusals to serve Radice and another individual because they are Jewish. In other words, the relevant events did not occur by email. Before email existed, public accommodation discrimination claims like this were tried the old fashioned way: The participants in the alleged events testified, and the trier of fact decided who to believe. That option is still available here.

Email is still relevant, of course, because it could contain statements about what happened, or have evidence of the defendant's allegedly prejudicial intent. But here a lot of that type of evidence was produced in the form of Harara's text messages and social media feeds and other electronic records. These include a statement that seems to be by Harara that seems to say he throws pennies on the ground when Jews walk by; the coffee shop menu and outdoor signage with inverted red triangles, which Radice alleges is a symbol used by Hamas to mark Israeli targets in propaganda videos; the apparent introduction on the one year anniversary of the October 7 attack of a juice item named for a mastermind of the attack; a video of Harara telling a Jewish customer to leave because he had "a violent hat," referring to the Star of David on the hat; and a repost by Harara to his X account bearing the "Bay Area" screen name of a November 2, 2024 post calling that same Jewish customer "a genocidal, bottom dwelling Zionist scum" who "should be kicked out of every public establishment not just Palestinian owned ones!" There are also text messages that replicate the kind of thing a plaintiff would dream of finding in a defendant's emails—and certainly at trial Radice and the United States will argue these texts are strong evidence of liability.

Radice is certainly of the view that he has uncovered good evidence, even if it was produced later than it should have been, and even though it does not include email. See Motion at 15 ("The 6134 Bates-labeled pages and 2474 native files that Harara produced on or after August 7 include inflammatory documents that Harara willfully withheld until after discovery closed."); id. ("For example, a January 3, 2025 JCH Instagram post shows JCH advertising for sale a t-shirt featuring the Jerusalem Coffee House name ringed by flags with the emblem of Hamas, a designated terrorist organization dedicated to violence against Jews and Israelis."); id. ("His Instagram direct-messages contain both antisemitic tropes and antisemitic slurs.").

With all this evidence, can it really be said that Harara's failings in discovery have prejudiced Plaintiffs to such an extent that a meaningful and fair trial is no longer possible? That adverse inferences are needed because there is not enough evidence for the trier of fact to reliably draw conclusions about what happened?

No. These cases are about whether a coffee shop committed discrimination, and Harara has produced enough documents that Radice and the United States have what they need to go to trial. Even with the nonproduction of email, it is not true that discovery failed or that truth cannot be ascertained. The public policy in favor of deciding cases on the merits applies here.

Accordingly, the Court RECOMMENDS that the district judge DENY the request for terminating sanctions because there's just no need or basis for it. The Court DENIES the request for adverse inferences because it is essentially a request for a directed verdict. Each side should put on their case at trial, and truth should be determined in the normal way. There is no reason for the Court to stack the deck.

But that doesn't mean Harara escapes sanctions. He needs to pay for what he did. His serial violations of Court orders significantly drove up Radice's cost of litigating [the case]. Radice requests $166,500.50 against all Defendants. The entity Defendants have been in default during the period of time when Harara violated the Court orders, so are not the cause of Radice's increased legal expenses, and therefore will not be sanctioned.

Plaintiff's counsel's rates are reasonable. However, both the Benesch and ADL attorneys seek fees for work that preceded the violations of the Court orders, a problem that requires deducting about a third of the Benesch time and about a fifth of the ADL's time. That brings the total down to $118,000. In addition, even though Harara violated multiple discovery orders, it is also true that Plaintiff's counsel litigated [the case] with excessive ferocity. At times it seemed they were not just litigating a discrimination case but were out to destroy Harara. As a result their fees were excessive. The Court estimates that about half of the fees Radice incurred during the time when Harara was violating the discovery orders was due to the violations and the other half was for work that would have needed to be done anyway or that should not have been done at all because it was excessive. Accordingly, the Court SANCTIONS Harara in the amount of $59,000 and ORDERS him to pay that amount to Radice within 30 days.

In his opposition, Harara proposes some remedial measures. However, the Court will not adopt any of them. The proposal to remedy the lack of email production presupposes that Harara will have a lawyer to represent him. Opp. at 16 ("The full inbox Mr. Harara exported on September 3, 2026 will be reviewed by counsel, consistent with the Court's ruling that counsel rather than Mr. Harara conduct that review. That counsel will be either counsel Mr. Harara retains or volunteer limited-scope counsel appointed through the Court's Federal Pro Bono Project under General Order 25, to which Mr. Harara respectfully requests referral. Since his counsel withdrew, Mr. Harara has contacted lawyers and legal organizations and has not found a lawyer who will take his case."). However, Harara's inability to work cooperatively with two sets of counsel means this is an unrealistic proposal. And if no lawyer represents him, Harara's proposal contains no particular deadline by which emails would be produced. Opp. at 16 ("If counsel has not been retained or appointed within 30 days of the Court's order, Mr. Harara will file a status report every 14 days thereafter. In all events, the production under this paragraph will be complete within 90 days of the Court's order; if it is not, Mr. Harara will show cause why not, and the Court may then impose such further measures as it finds appropriate after notice and an opportunity to be heard.").

Harara's proposal to serve further interrogatory responses is highly unlikely to achieve anything. And there is no need for a further deposition of him; Plaintiffs' counsel can cross-examine him at trial….

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. #7953. The Best Creosote Removers of 2026, Picks by Experts

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned & Loved About Them

Published Oct 26, 2026 9:30 AM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

It’s crucial to remove creosote in a chimney with a specially formulated creosote remover before it becomes problematic and, even worse, dangerous. Creosote is a byproduct of burning wood, coal, pellets, or oil, which create gases as they burn. These gases rise through the chimney, coating the inside of the chimney liner as they do. Today’s fireplaces are designed to allow maximum airflow, which reduces creosote buildup, but still, this design doesn’t completely eliminate the issue.

Having a chimney professionally cleaned is one method to remove creosote, but it isn’t the only way. Handy individuals can clean the chimney themselves if they have the right tools, and a variety of creosote-dissolving products are available to help. We spoke to Tim Smith, owner of Actual Chimney Specialists in Averill Park, New York, who says that creosote removers should be a part of anyone’s wood-burning habits: “It is a sure way to manage creosote when you are unaware of what is happening inside of your chimney throughout the season.” He adds that “new wood-burning appliances are much better at burning clean and efficient, which reduces creosote production.” Even so, he recommends having a chimney professional inspect the chimney before the season so you can determine what’s the best option and product for your situation.

The best creosote remover for cleaning a chimney will vary based on the amount of buildup and the cleaning method necessary to remove the accumulation. Our favorite is Meeco’s Red Devil Creosote Destroyer for its ease of use and effectiveness. Ahead, learn why creosote buildup can be detrimental, explore several of the factors to consider when purchasing creosote remover, and discover some more of the best creosote removers on the market to keep your chimney clean and safe.

Bottom line: Regular use of creosote removers and professional inspections are essential for chimney safety and efficiency.

A good creosote remover should be relatively simple to use. The product should treat the appropriate degree of creosote buildup and help the user to maintain a clean chimney. The following products represent some of the best creosote removers on the market, featuring different types designed for the various degrees of creosote buildup. When using any chimney creosote remover that contains chemicals, always carefully follow the manufacturer’s application and safety instructions.

Preventing creosote from building up in a chimney liner and removing existing creosote can be as simple as sprinkling a few teaspoons of Meeco’s Red Devil Creosote Destroyer over firewood or coal every third time a fire is lit in the fireplace. As the fire burns, the remover’s chemicals—which include copper chloride, silicon dioxide, and fixed carbon—coat the chimney liner and keep creosote residue from adhering while also breaking down any existing buildup.

This creosote powder comes in a 2-pound tub, enough for 16 applications. Keep in mind that it is not intended to remove thick, hardened creosote deposits.

Get the Meeco’s Red Devil creosote remover at Amazon, Ace Hardware, or Menards.

No need to climb up onto the roof to remove creosote with the Gardus SootEater Rotary chimney whip brush. Designed to clean wood-burning fireplace chimneys and wood-burning stove flues, this system includes eight 3-foot, flexible quick-connect rods; a whip head; and a drill adapter. The user attaches the whip head to the top of a quick-connect rod and then joins the other end, via the adapter, to a standard drill.

When the drill is turned on, the whip head, which features strong 12 millimeter nylon strings, spins (like a weed eater) and removes creosote buildup from inside the flue or liner. The additional connect rods can be attached as needed to reach higher in the chimney, and since each one is flexible, it’s possible to clean around bends in a flue.

Get the Gardus creosote remover at The Home Depot or Tractor Supply Co.

For an inexpensive way to remove creosote from a chimney or flue, consider Rutland Products’ 2-pound tub of powdered creosote remover. It’s like a smaller version of the Best Overall pick, containing enough remover to treat a wood-burning fireplace or wood-burning stove 16 times; simply sprinkle a 1-ounce scoop to a bed of hot coals one to two times per week.

The heat from a fire releases the active ingredients, which then penetrate first- or second-degree creosote. This remover dissolves the sticky, tarlike residue and turns it into powdery ash that falls harmlessly to the bottom of the firebox.

Get the Rutland Products powder creosote remover at Amazon, Tractor Supply Co., or Rutland.

For hands-off chimney maintenance, the CSL Creosote Sweeping Log is about as simple as it gets. It burns like a standard fire log for roughly 90 minutes, heating the tar along the chimney walls to an ideal treatment temperature while its smoke deposits active minerals onto existing creosote. The treatment keeps working over the next 15 days as the creosote gradually turns brittle and breaks away, and any deposits that remain are rendered less flammable.

The log is accepted by the Chimney Safety Institute of America (CSIA) and is UL-listed, and it’s safe for any type of chimney, including stainless steel liners. It can be used in fireplaces, woodstoves, fireplace inserts, and combination wood/oil furnaces. The manufacturer recommends burning one every 50 fires, or at least once a year. Like other sweeping logs, it’s best suited to routine maintenance rather than heavy, glazed buildup, so it should be paired with an annual professional inspection.

Get the CSL creosote sweeping log at Amazon.

For pellet stove users, Rutland Products liquid creosote remover spray is an optimal treatment that requires spraying the liquid on the pellets before loading them into the stove’s hopper. As the pellets burn, the chemicals release, and the gases penetrate first- and second-degree creosote buildup. The creosote dissolves and dries out, so it falls from the flue and into the bottom of the firebox.

This 32-ounce bottle of spray remover is also suitable for wood stoves and wood fireplaces, where users can spray it directly onto the logs. For the best results, treat pellets or wood once per week to help keep flues and chimney liners clear.

Get the Rutland Products liquid creosote remover at Amazon or Rutland.

Creosote buildup isn’t always limited to the inside of a chimney liner or flue. If a fireplace is not a newer, airtight model, it’s common for fires to emit tiny amounts of soot along the outside of the firebox, leading to dark stains on brick or stone fireplace surrounds and mantels. This sooty creosote residue can be challenging to remove with regular household cleaners, but Quick N Brite fireplace cleaner helps dissolve the residue to make the fireplace look fresh and new.

The 16-ounce bottle of gel concentrate is biodegradable, nontoxic, and environmentally friendly, making it safe for people, pets, and the planet. Apply it to areas with stains and buildup with a wet scrub sponge, then rinse with water and wipe with a cloth. For even heavier residue, the included scrub brush can be used as well.

Get the Quick N Brite creosote remover at Amazon.

Soften glazed creosote and reduce the risk of chimney fires with the Anti-Creo-Soot liquid creosote remover from ACS. This potent anti-creosote spray should be sprayed daily in the firebox, over the wood, and upward in the flue (sprayer not included). It works to break down hardened, glazed creosote deposits in preparation for a professional chimney sweep to clean.

This nontoxic liquid should be applied at least 7 days in a row before scheduling a professional cleaning. Once the creosote is removed, continued use of the liquid will help keep deposits from reforming in the chimney or flue. It is suitable for use in wood- or coal-burning stoves and fireplaces as well as pellet stoves.

Get the ACS creosote remover (various sizes) at Amazon or SaverSystems.

We researched the top creosote removers on the market to compose our list. We looked at different types of products (logs, liquids, powders, brushes) so shoppers could choose what works best for them. Whether you’d prefer a method that you only have to think about once per season or a product you can sprinkle on every couple of fires, we found something that will fit the bill. We also searched for products that were eco-friendly and nontoxic for those who are more environmentally conscious. Even though some products are pricier than others, we were focused on finding good value for the money.

When it comes to how to clean a chimney, the best plan is to take action sooner rather than later. Whether they use chemicals or poles and brushes to eliminate the buildup, creosote removers are most effective when the creosote is at the first- or second-degree stage. After that, it may still be possible for a professional to remove the hardened, glazed buildup, but if the deposits are particularly heavy, the solution may require replacing the chimney liner.

Smith offers some helpful advice about these types of products: “These treatment products will not work very well if the moisture in the firewood is too high.” He says typical firewood should be at 15 to 25 percent moisture content, which will keep the creosote manageable. “If the moisture content is over that, these methods will have a hard time combating the creosote production.” What’s your best move? “Buy your wood the year before so it has a chance to dry a full year. This will ensure you are burning the best way and getting the most heat from your wood. This keeps repairs down and creosote at a minimum.”

The various types of creosote removers all work best before creosote develops into a hardened residue on the inside of a flue or chimney liner. However, while they go a long way toward keeping a chimney free from residue, they are not a substitute for professional chimney service. For the best results, have the chimney professionally inspected and cleaned before the colder season arrives. Then, use the following products to keep it clean while enjoying the fireplace:

Creosote deposits in a chimney can release toxic gases while a fire is lit below. If the gases back up into the home because the fireplace (or stove) isn’t adequately vented, they can cause health problems, such as headaches, burning eyes, skin rashes, and breathing difficulties.

In addition to health concerns, heavy creosote buildup is highly flammable. It may lead to chimney fires that can catch a roof or other parts of a house on fire. In addition to removing the creosote, remember that it’s important to always keep a fire extinguisher near the fireplace or stove. When neglected, creosote buildup is also corrosive and can eat through steel chimney liners and flues.

It’s essential to understand and identify the various degrees of creosote buildup in order to select the most effective product and removal method. Various products remove different creosote stages, indicated by degree as determined by the thickness and physical properties of the deposits.

First degree is the least dangerous level of creosote buildup. It consists of a loose, sooty film that adheres to the chimney liner, much like a layer of dust. At this stage, the creosote is dry and flaky and can be easily brushed away during fireplace cleaning.

As more creosote deposits stick to the chimney’s liner, the heat from subsequent fires transforms them into a thick, sticky substance that adheres to the liner—this is the second degree of creosote buildup. At this point, chemicals are necessary to dissolve the creosote, and scraping or brushing may be required.

If further neglected, the intense heat from fires can turn sticky creosote deposits into a hardened glaze—third-degree creosote buildup—which is difficult to remove and will likely require a professional chimney sweep. At this point, scorching fires in the fireplace can cause the glazed creosote deposits to melt and drip to the bottom of the firebox. This creates an even greater health and fire hazard. Why? Creosote was once used to treat exterior wood timbers, such as those used to construct railroad tracks, to prevent rotting. Studies suggesting that creosote could be carcinogenic (cancer causing) ended the practice.

Creosote is a natural byproduct of a burning fire, but once heavy deposits form, it can be difficult to remove—even for a professional. For those who enjoy wood, coal, or pellet fires, some questions about creosote and creosote remover are common.

It can be. When hot, creosote can release fumes that cause respiratory problems, and contact with bare skin can lead to irritation, redness, or rashes. Some studies also indicate that creosote may be a carcinogen (a cancer-causing agent).

When it comes to what dissolves creosote, yes, creosote removers really do work. However, only use them as recommended and to treat the appropriate degree of creosote buildup.

No, the hotter the fire, the more likely it is to cause creosote.

Burn a creosote log once every 30 to 60 fires, depending on the brand of the log.

Yes, creosote logs will help clean away deposits in a wood-stove flue just as in a wood-burning fireplace.

Smith says that you can’t overuse these treatments; however, he adds that some of the products in the daily treatment types can expose users to cancer-causing chemicals. “Using these chemicals more will put you at health risks, and it may be best to stick to the manufacturer’s recommended application,” he says.

Coal and wood creosote are two different substances. Coal creosote is a thick, oily liquid that is amber to black in color. Wood creosote is a colorless to yellowish greasy liquid. It has a smoky odor.
