#7897. Snow Thrower vs. Snow Blower: What’s the Difference?

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned & Loved About Them

Published Oct 30, 2026 1:53 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

When a winter storm dumps a thick white blanket of the white stuff on your property, a snow blower or snow thrower can be your best friend. But which one do you need? Many often use the two terms interchangeably to describe snow removing power tools, but snow blowers and snow throwers are actually two distinct types of machines. While they serve the same purpose, they differ in size, power, snow removal ability, and price. Understanding the difference between the two is key to choosing a snow thrower vs snow blower to handle your winter snow clearing duties. Here’s what you need to know about.

Snow throwers and snow blowers clear snow in the same way: Both have a spinning auger that lifts the snow and launches it through a chute as you guide the tool along a driveway or walkway. But while snow throwers do this in a single step, or stage, a snow blower uses multiple stages to move the snow. There’s also a size difference: Snow throwers are smaller, more nimble machines that can handle moderate snowfall on smaller driveways, while snow blowers are larger and capable of clearing deeper snow from bigger driveways.

Snow throwers are ideal for removing small amounts of snow that are not extremely deep.They are single-stage machines that scoop up snow with an auger and launch snow out of a chute in a single action. Depending on the size of the snow thrower, they can clear a path that’s 18 to 24 inches wider and between 6 and 12 inches deep. Many can hurl it a distance of 15 to 20 feet, while some can send snow as far as 40 feet.

This Greenworks snow thrower weighs just 32 pounds and, in our tests, was powerful enough to clear snow up to 12 inches deep. Read the review.

Snow blowers are more powerful than snow throwers, making them a good choice for those who need to clear larger driveways or live in areas with harsher winters that receive higher snowfall totals. Like snow throwers, snow blowers have a rotating auger that scoops up snow, but they use two or three stages to clear snow. But instead of launching snow, it sends it to a separate impeller which blows the snow out through a chute and launches it 25 to 40 feet away. Some can even send snow as far as 50 feet away.

A three-stage model is even more powerful. This type of snow blower has an accelerator that breaks up the snow, allowing it to cut through compacted icy snow and large piles of snow more quickly than a two-stage model. Snow blowers can clear a path of snow ranging from 24 to 32 inches wide and 1 to 2 feet deep. With their two stage design in optimal conditions, some are capable of launching snow up to 60 feet.

Ryobi’s two-stage snow blower is easy to maneuver in tight spaces, has a powerful auger, and even works on gravel driveways. Read the review.

Choosing between a snow thrower and snow blower comes down to several factors, including snowfall totals, driveway type and size, ease of use, and price.

The average snowfall totals of the winter storms passing through your area are a big factor in determining whether to go with a snow thrower or snow blower. If snowstorms routinely drop snowfall of more than a foot of snow that’s wetter and more compacted, you’ll need a snow blower’s power and capacity to clear it. If your snowstorms are typically under a foot and consist of fluffy to moderately heavy snow, you can take on winter with a snow blower.

Keep in mind that the depth a snow blower or snow thrower can handle can vary from model to model, so make sure to check the manufacturer’s ratings. Some lighter-duty snow throwers max out at 6 inches, while there are compact snow blowers that might only be able to handle up to a foot of snow.

The type of driveway you’re clearing determines the type of snow removal machine you need. If you’re clearing a gravel driveway, don’t use a snow thrower. Since snow throwers have paddles that scrape across the ground, they can pick up and throw gravel, damage the auger, and send the gravel into your yard.

Snowblowers, in comparison, have skid shoes that prevent the auger housing from coming into contact with the ground, making them capable of clearing gravel driveways. But unlike snow throwers, which clear snow down to the pavement, snow blowers leave a thin layer of snow–about 1/8 of an inch–on smooth pavement.

The size of your driveway largely determines whether a single-stage snow thrower or multi-stage snow blower is the best choice. Snow throwers can cut a swath through snow that’s 18 to 24 inches wide, which makes them best suited for the typical two-car driveway.  Snow blowers have wider clearing widths of up to 32 inches, so they can cover significantly more ground than a snow thrower with each pass. They are a better choice for larger driveways.

Throwing distance is also an important factor when deciding between a snow blower and snow thrower. Most snow throwers can launch snow a distance of 15 to 25 feet away, though there are some single stage models that can throw snow up to 45 feet. A snow blower’s multi-stage design allows them to launch snow further, typically up to 50 feet, which is useful when clearing wider driveways or large patios.

With their ability to remove a wider swath of snow with each pass and launch it further, snow blowers are best suited for handling long winding driveways or larger driveways that hold three or more vehicles. While snow throwers have a narrower clearing width, their small size makes them easier to turn and maneuver, allowing you to clear 4 to 8 inches of snow over a smaller one- to two-car driveways.

However, these are recommendations. You can certainly use a snow thrower to tackle a larger driveway. Just plan on spending more time out in the cold to get the job done. Likewise, you can use a larger snow blower on a small driveway, but it may end up taking you longer. These larger machines require more room to turn and are more difficult to maneuver around smaller driveways.

Snow throwers are smaller and lighter, which generally makes them easier to maneuver, especially in tight areas. The controls on a snow thrower are also relatively simple, so there’s less of a learning curve when operating them.

Snow blowers are much heavier but are usually self-propelled and have power steering, so there’s less physical effort to operate them than a snow thrower. However, they are very difficult to move when the engine is off, which makes it more difficult to get in and out of storage.

A snow blower usually has more controls on the handlebars than a snow thrower, so expect a longer learning curve when learning how to use a snow blower.

Both snow throwers and snow blowers come in battery-powered and gas-powered versions. Cordless electric snow blowers are easier to maintain and start than gas models, operate with less vibration, and don’t produce exhaust. While gas-powered machines were once prevalent, today’s cordless electric models are comparable in clearing width, throwing distance, and snow capacity. That said, gas-powered machines still dominate when it comes to runtime. While it takes minutes to refill a gas tank, it can take hours to recharge a battery.

Snow throwers generally cost less than snow blowers. The transmission, large engines, and self-propelled system on these machines adds to their expense. Single-stage snow throwers are simpler machines, so they cost less. Snow throwers generally cost $500 to $1,000, while snow blowers can range between $800 and $2,000, with battery-powered snow blowers typically costing a couple hundred dollars more.

#7896. 31 Easy, Festive Ways to Dress Up Your Thanksgiving Table

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned & Loved About Them

By Caitlin Castelaz, Updated by Daryna Tobey

Updated Oct 30, 2026 2:47 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

As you plan the tablescape upon which your Thanksgiving dinner will be presented, look to autumn’s stunning natural bounty and colors for inspiration. Earthy green, orange, and red tones can help set the scene, but natural elements like leaves, flowers, pinecones, and foliage, are what will really deliver the “natural abundance” vibe. The best part? Decor that you bring in from outdoors is compostable and inexpensive, if not free.

If you don’t have a ready supply of real leaves, consider creating some of your own, like DIY Candy does. These were made with stencils and thin sheets of cork (both of which you can purchase at craft supply stores). In addition to adding style, these leaves also serve as handy, decorative trivets. You can also purchase premade cork leaf coasters if you don’t want to make them.

Short on time? According to A Beautiful Mess, a beautiful centerpiece can be assembled quickly from items found in the produce department at the grocery store: Group colorful fruits, like oranges, tangerines and pomegranates. Sprinkle green pistachios and sprigs of fresh rosemary along the middle of the table to create the illusion of a decorative runner. When dinner is over, invite your guests to partake of the fruit and nuts as a post-feast treat, or save the tastiest morsels and place them in your kitchen fruit bowl.

The curves of a pumpkin’s stem makes it a natural choice for tabletop decor. Give your simple squash an unexpected twist, as A Night Owl blog does, by attaching a piece of eucalyptus and a nametag to the stem and fashioning a place card. You can purchase faux eucalyptus stems to use for your DIY decor year after year.

Butternut squash is probably in season now at your local farmers market. Bring this culinary hero to the table by featuring it in a Thanksgiving centerpiece, as blog A Piece of Rainbow does here. When placed in a nest of moss and pinecones, it makes a rustic statement.

This simple yet stunning idea from Cherished Bliss isn’t the typical way of serving Thanksgiving cranberries, but it’s certainly stylish. Float a tea light candle atop a handful of fresh cranberries in a water-filled vase. For extra pizzazz, add a sprig of eucalyptus to the water and dip the base of the vase in metallic paint. Or, skip the extras and let the bright berries shine on their own!

The autumn harvest days spent at the local apple orchard might be behind us, but America’s favorite fruit still has a place in your Thanksgiving festivities. Place apples (always in groups of three) of any variety at different places along your table runner, and fill in with pillar candles and faux or real greenery for a rich display.

If you’re burned out on pumpkin-themed decor and pumpkin spice-flavored everything, take a cue from Cupcakes and Cashmere blogger: Swap out the ubiquitous squash for an unexpected edible. Persimmons, for example, are of a similar size, shape, and color but bring a beauty to the table that is distinctly their own.

Cristina Garay at RemodelaCasa uses pears as a beautiful addition to a natural Thanksgiving tabletop display. Add it to an edible centerpiece or place it atop your guest’s place, on its own or with a name card, as an extra touch of hospitality. If, by lucky coincidence, someone has sent you some Harry & David pears for the holiday, why not put them to work before eating them?

Russet, crimson, mustard, and brown: These colors typify the Thanksgiving tablescape, but that doesn’t mean you can’t think outside the box when it comes to your holiday centerpiece. Follow the lead of the blog It All Started with Paint and paint seasonal squash in the color palette of your choice to marry tradition with contemporary style for a look that captures your personality. Or, purchase a set of painted faux pumpkins to use for your holiday table settings every year.

Nature offers an abundance of color this time of year, so use it to your advantage. At the StoneGable blog, napkins are topped with golden-hued leaves, which you can buy online or pluck from your lawn. The centerpiece of tall and short vases and white pumpkins carry through on the theme.

Design Dazzle’s basket of seasonal bounty may look like a headache to assemble, but many of the makings of this Thanksgiving display can be found in your own garden beds. If you do choose to forage in your backyard for your tabletop display, be sure to shake, wash or brush off the greenery, then let it sit for a couple of days before placing it on the table.

Normally hung on a door this time of year, Indian corn can be a beautiful addition to the Thanksgiving Day table. Here, the corn is placed atop plates, along with a seasonal card, to bring color and life to neutral stoneware.

The squirrels in your backyard already know the secret: Acorns are everywhere at this time of year, so there’s no reason not to bring them to the harvest table. Use them as fillers in glass containers or, if you are ready to recreate this DIY craft from Hello Little Home, make acorn napkin ties like those shown here.

Golden-hued wheat is certainly a symbol of the season and the Thanksgiving table. Create miniature sheaves bound with ribbon, as did the blogger at Carolyn’s Homework, or simply use the wheat to create a casual centerpiece of candles, gourds and fruit.

A pie pumpkin, placed atop a dinner plate, makes a wonderful place marker for the Thanksgiving table. Using a paint marker, write your guests’ names on the front of a pumpkin, and set it carefully at each person’s place. It’s a simple gesture but makes for a natural gift they can take with them when they leave and enjoy again, when added to their own homemade centerpieces.

The traditional holiday bird won’t be the only scene stealer this season, when you add feather and cork place cards to your Thanksgiving table. Feathers, corks, and ribbon can be purchased at your local craft store; bind them together to create the look, then watch the expression on everyone’s faces when they marvel at your crafty tablescape.

Bright and cheery, let a sunflower bloom greet each guest when they sit down at the table. Place one inside a folded napkin atop each guest’s plate. For less formal buffet dinners, float a couple flowers in a bowl of water, then place the bowl on a tray filled with rolls of silverware. When your guests go through the line, they’ll see the sunny arrangement and smile.

For a touch of whimsy, sprinkle a handful of fallen leaves over your tablescape. Not for neat freaks, this fanciful display evokes a walk in the woods. However, if you’re playing host to grandma (who never did quite approve of your slapdash cleaning routine), nix this one from your Thanksgiving idea file.

Branches create a natural centerpiece, and a dramatic statement in this country chic home. If you still have trees and shrubs with autumn-colored leaves, consider pruning a selection to decorate your Thanksgiving Day table. Just remember to keep them a reasonable height for dining, or remove them when the meal is served.

Evoke the beauty of nature, without giving the kids ammo with which to torture their cousins: This Thanksgiving printable from Kiki & Company makes an adorable addition to the kids’ table and lends a little fanciness to the little ones’ big meal.

This modern take on a table runner proves that order and symmetry might be overrated. Ruch and wrinkle your runner just so, and nestle vases of bright flowers and little pumpkins among the folds of the fabric for a perfectly imperfect arrangement.

Even after Halloween, pumpkin-carving season persists. Make these clever little votive holders by hollowing out a mini pumpkin and placing a tea light inside. Leave the outside of the pumpkin natural, or gild it with gold-colored paint. The 36th Avenue has the tutorial.

Sometimes simple is best. This understated table setting pairs a single pinecone with dinner plate and charger for an autumnal display that’s perfect for Thanksgiving.

Pumpkins and gourds make great table decorations at a big fall meal. That includes white pumpkins, too!  Here, a grouping of faux white pumpkins and other natural-hued elements set a distinctive Thanksgiving Day table, but it would look just as nice with naturally white (or painted) pumpkins.

Walnuts and pecans are back on the menu at this time of year, so add them to your Thanksgiving table settings for a festive touch. A handful of walnuts gives a name card a boost on this rustic display.

Illumine the simple beauty of natural (or faux) foliage with an arrangement of white pillar candles of varying heights. When the candles start to drip on the kraft paper tablecloth, you’ll know it’s time for pie.

A wooden charger brings a rustic sensibility to a Thanksgiving table of crystal and silver. You can make your own from wood rounds available at most craft stores. Apply wood stain to the rounds or leave them plain for a touch of woodland whimsy.

Another edible arrangement, this one brings together winter seasonal vegetables and fruit (like cabbage and pomegranates) with other colorful picks like bell peppers, globe grapes, and red radishes. Place your produce in a wooden trough or long basket and fill in with parsley and greenery for a unique centerpiece that you can turn into next week’s salad.

Who says evergreens are only for Christmas? Break out the boughs early and fashion them into a delightful place marker. This one from In Honor of Design is made from a couple sprigs of rosemary tied with string.

Nature and artifice combine in this stunning Thanksgiving tablescape. Clear and copper candle holders are complemented with white pumpkins adorned with stripes copper-colored tape, while a patterned table runner continues the theme.

A study in sturdiness, this table runner from Blooming Homestead is nothing more than a pine board stained an elegant dark brown. When laid atop the Thanksgiving table and topped with pinecones, adornments, and a vase full of wheat, it evokes and warmth and cheer.

Mums are the official flower of fall, so give them a spot at the Thanksgiving table. Place small vases of the blooms all along the length of the table for a short centerpiece that’s easy to peer over but still makes a big—and beautiful—statement.

Flowers don’t always have to be arranged in a vase. San Diego-area florist Native Poppy recommends laying a mini-bouquet of dried flowers at every place setting, which guests could then take home as favors. Fresh-flower bouquets are just as pretty, as are single stems in a seasonal color. Placing flowers at each place setting also eliminates the problem of trying to hold a conversation over a tall centerpiece—and probably costs a lot less than that tall centerpiece, too.

#7895. Why Do Construction Barricades Come in Different Colors? The Colors Decoded

Red, yellow, and orange barricades don't always mean the same thing. Learn what common safety colors signal and when to stay clear.

Yellow caution tape is a pretty familiar sight, whether it’s blocking off a wet floor or keeping people out of a construction area. Orange barriers along the highway and red warning signs at job sites are just as common. But barricade colors aren’t random, and they don’t all mean the same thing.

In the U.S., OSHA has rules for certain workplace safety colors, while ANSI provides guidelines for signs and warning tape. Road construction follows a different set of standards. Depending on the location, the same color might serve a different purpose.

Learn what the most common barricade colors mean, where people are likely to see them, and what to watch out for.

There’s a reason red is a common choice for warning signs. OSHA uses it to identify danger, emergency stops, and fire protection equipment. At a construction site, a red “Danger” sign might warn of exposed electrical equipment or another hazard that could cause serious injury. OSHA’s general-industry rules also call for red warning lights at barricades and temporary obstructions.

Of all the safety colors, yellow might be the one people see most often. It shows up on caution tape, warning signs, and around areas where crews are working. OSHA uses yellow to warn of physical hazards, including falls and falling objects. A damaged walkway or an area undergoing maintenance might have yellow tape around it.

There’s no shortage of orange around construction sites. On workplace warning signs, the color often identifies hazards that could cause serious injury, particularly around machinery or equipment undergoing repairs. Orange also makes road construction easier to spot. Crews use orange barriers and signs to warn drivers about upcoming work, lane changes, or other temporary traffic conditions.

Instead of warning people away from something, it usually helps them find safety equipment. A green sign might point toward a first aid station, identify emergency equipment, or provide instructions for workers. It’s especially useful in workplaces where people need to find these resources quickly.

Blue signs typically provide information about workplace equipment or procedures that don’t directly involve a hazard. For example, a blue notice might explain that a machine is temporarily out of service. Unlike red or yellow warnings, blue notices generally provide information rather than warn of immediate danger.

Purple isn’t a color people encounter very often on construction barricades, but it does have a specific safety use. OSHA requires certain radiation warning signs to feature the familiar radiation symbol in purple or magenta against a yellow background. These signs warn people about radiation hazards, including areas where access may be restricted.

Those orange-and-white striped barricades lining roads and highways aren’t quite the same as the warning signs used inside workplaces. The Federal Highway Administration has separate rules for these barriers, which crews use to close lanes, block roads, and direct traffic around construction.

There’s also a purpose behind the diagonal stripes. When a barricade directs drivers around an obstruction, the stripes slope down toward the side where traffic should pass.

OSHA, “29 CFR 1910.144, Safety Color Code for Marking Physical Hazards” OSHA, “29 CFR 1926.200, Accident Prevention Signs and Tags” ANSI, “Z535.1-2022: Standard for Safety Colors” ANSI, “Z535.5-2022: Safety Tags and Barricade Tapes” OSHA, “29 CFR 1910.1096, Ionizing Radiation” FHWA, “Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices, 11th Edition with Revision 1”

#7892. Quartz May Be On Its Way Out—and Here’s How Kitchen Designers Would Replace It

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned & Loved About Them

Published Oct 30, 2026 4:06 PM EDT

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Quartz countertops have long been a favorite choice of homeowners and interior designers alike due to their strength, nonporous nature, modern look, and uniformity. However, recent discoveries and legal challenges regarding the material’s potential health hazards to fabricators have caused quite a stir and are now reshaping the industry.

The main issue is with crystalline silica that’s a natural mineral found in quartz. When particles are inhaled, they can penetrate deep into a person’s lungs, causing damage that can lead to serious respiratory diseases like silicosis, lung cancer, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). And many workers have become ill from breathing in dust containing crystalline silica while fabricating quartz countertops. Australia has already banned many engineered-stone products, while California is pursuing policy rules that would prohibit fabricating engineered stone containing more than 1 percent crystalline silica.

As a result, more and more people are looking for safer countertop options to use in place of quartz. “We have found some homeowners shying away from quartz surfaces,” says Kaycee Conallen, owner of Kaycee Conallen Design Studio in Swarthmore, Pennsylvania. There are many alternatives to quartz countertops, and designers have helped us identify three top options for your new home or next remodel.

Note: There is no evidence indicating a health concern with already installed quartz countertops, so if you already have one, you don’t need to rip it out.

One alternative to quartz countertops is eco-friendly, silica-free alternatives like recycled glass and paper composites. Both eliminate silica risks while providing unique designs ranging from bold, contemporary glass patterns to sleek, solid-color paper finishes.

Recycled glass countertops incorporate post-consumer or post-industrial glass fragments bound in cement or resin, offering distinct visual textures from fine-ground particles to large, jewel-like shards. Notable glass brands include IceStone, Vetrazzo, Curava, GEOS, and Compac Obsidiana Zero. Glass surfaces are effective at resisting cuts, scratches, and heat, though stain-resistance and maintenance depend on whether a resin or cement binder is used.

Paper-based composites work well for those gravitating towards a solid color and solid surface materials, such as PaperStone, Richlite, and Fenix brands. Surprisingly durable, these heavy-duty panels are made from layers of post-consumer recycled paper or paper from FSC-certified forests, which are compressed under heat and pressure with a silica-free and petroleum-free phenolic resin.

While heat resistant to about 350 degrees Fahrenheit, minor scratches and stains may appear, but can be sanded out. “Fenix is a man-made resin and paper combination originally developed in Italy, and we love that it has a beautiful matte finish, feels soft to the touch, and is very durable,” explains Conallen.

“Sintered stone is another strong option for its resistance to heat, scratches, and stains,” notes Blima Ehrentreu, founder and CEO of The Designers Group (TDG) in New York City and other locations. Using a high-tech process, natural minerals like porcelain and glass are combined under immense heat and pressure to replicate metamorphic rock with minimal to zero crystalline silica.

The non-porous nature of sintered stone makes it resistant to staining, scratches, intense heat, and color-fading from UV exposure. Brands that make this type of surface include Lapitec, Dekton, Neolith, Florim, Sapienstone, and Caesarstone, which are actively eliminating or reducing silica content. In addition, many of these surfaces contain recycled content.

Conallen also loves the look of authentic materials like soapstone. “Each slab of stone carries unique characteristics, personality, and porosity,” she explains. Composed mostly of talc, this metamorphic rock is free of crystalline silica and has a distinctive, velvety feel. Soapstone offers design versatility, as it ranges in color from subtle grays and muted greens to charcoal or deep black, sometimes accented by marble-like veining. Not only does it offer a classic, understated elegance to modern spaces, but it is also a sustainable option given its low-energy extraction process, nontoxic nature, and recyclability.

From a functional standpoint, soapstone is very durable. It withstands heat, so you can set hot cookware directly onto the surface without trivets. It’s also nonporous so it doesn’t get damaged by acidic etching, spills, or bacterial growth. The only drawback is that it’s a softer material than most of the other options mentioned, so it can show minor scratches.

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned and Loved About Them

From crown molding and built-ins to creaky floors and drafty windows, old houses are full of charm and challenges. So we’re celebrating all the things that make old homes worth loving, living in, and fixing up. Learn about historic house styles; find practical advice for maintaining your old home; and discover quirky, forgotten features you simply won’t find in new builds.

#7891. Bonfire Season Is Here — Here Are the Dos and Don’ts for Staying Safe

How to not to expose yourself to toxic fumes, burn down the neighborhood and injure the kiddos, plus other tips for enjoying a stress-free bonfire.

Cool fall evenings naturally put our minds on the merits of bones-warming bonfires. And while many create cherished family memories and set the backdrop for festive community events, some end up in tragedy, with emergency room visits and property damage.

“Every season there are always the same preventable mistakes made that lead to injuries,” says attorney Kevin Henrichson. “Falling into the fire, using gasoline, adding fuel when you shouldn’t, failing to supervise children and consuming alcohol all raise the stakes of something bad happening.”

Ahead, experts walk through exactly what to do and not to do to stay safe while enjoying a bonfire.

Notify your local fire department of your plans and ask them for guidance concerning:

“One phone call to the fire marshal’s office takes two minutes,” says fire and home safety expert Eugene Klimaszewski. “Otherwise, the consequence of burning without a permit on a restricted day is a fine, and if it gets away from you, it’s your liability.”

Look for a flat, open spot away from fences, barns, houses, trees and ground vegetation. The National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) recommends keeping bonfires at least 25 feet from the house and other structures.

“That number isn’t arbitrary,” says Klimaszewski. “Radiant heat and drifting embers are what ignite a deck railing, a vinyl fence or the mulch bed against the house. Every ember that lands on a roof or in a gutter full of dry leaves is a coin flip. Most go out. The one that doesn’t becomes a structure fire.”

Build the fire downwind of your home and close all windows and doors on the fire side, to prevent smoke from getting in.

“Even a small amount of smoke reaching an indoor smoke detector is enough to set it off,” says Klimaszewski. If you have a monitoring system, that could trigger a call to the fire department. “At best that’s an embarrassing conversation with the engine company. In towns that charge for repeat false alarms, that’s a bill on top of the embarrassment,” he says.

Pro-tip: If you have an older home, which isn’t airtight, put your alarm system on test mode or notify your monitoring company about your bonfire plans.

Wind can carry embers up to a mile, which means a bonfire on a windy day can easily end with a wildfire or house fire. If your planned bonfire day turns out to be windy, reschedule it. And even if there isn’t a breeze, plan for one by clearing all debris from around the fire pit and building rocks or bricks up higher on the windy side, which protects the fire from the wind plus radiates heat toward you for extra warmth.

Kiln-dried wood is the best. Seasoned hardwoods like oak, cedar and hickory are particularly good because they burn cleaner, longer and hotter than soft woods like pine and aspen (though a little soft wood kindling makes starting a fire a lot easier).

Steer clear of gasoline or other accelerants, as they too often lead to burn injuries, out-of-control fires and noxious fumes. (One year, my neighbor used so much gasoline to start a bonfire that the resulting shock wave from the explosion knocked pictures off of people’s walls three blocks away).

“A lot of people think they can use gas or lighter fluid to get the fire started or revive it, but please never do that because the vapors can flash back and get everyone nearby,” says Henrichson. “Gasoline is particularly dangerous and should never be used to start or revive a fire.”

Pro-tip: If you struggling to start a fire, build up a good kindling base and use a campfire starter or small bit of tightly twisted newspaper. Ample kindling will help you get a hot coal-bed established, which will burn larger logs more effectively plus lessen smoke.

Avoid newspaper, cardboard and other paper products, which tend to break down into large flying embers. Also, never burn anything with adhesives, plastics and other chemicals. The health risks of this are obvious, but plastics and chemicals are hiding in many items you might not realize, including: dryer lint, food packaging with shiny ink, glossy magazines, pressed woods including butcher block, varnished furniture and clothing made with synthetic fibers.

Before lighting the fire, set up a water source in case embers become a problem. That will also make it easier to put it out completely when you’re done. NFPA actually requires a hose, bucket or extinguisher be on hand for all recreational fires, and for fires to be attended at all times.

“A fire that’s left alone for ten minutes while everyone goes inside for more drinks is the one that ends up on the local news,” says Klimaszewski. “And an unattended fire that spreads is the homeowner’s liability, full stop.”

Assign someone to supervise the flames at all times to prevent the fire from getting out of control, and to keep kids and pets from standing too close. Equip the supervisor with proper protective clothing, including a fire-resistant glove, long-handled poker tool, shovel, closed-toe shoes and eye protection.

“The most common injuries I’ve seen are from people falling into the fire, and young children are vulnerable to this because they may want to play in the area where everyone is hanging out by the fire,” says Henrichson. “There should be a no-enter zone that is explained to children every single time, and the person tending the fire should not have any alcohol.”

Watch for loose sleeves, blankets, boots and other combustibles that are too close to the fire. “Those fun marshmallow-roasting memories are great to make, but shaking a burning marshmallow can cause trouble, and if you use metal skewers, they can burn you too,” says Henrichson.

Also, know what to do beforehand if something ends up catching fire. “The old advice that we were told years ago is still true: stop, drop, and roll if your clothes catch fire,” says Henrichson. “Repeat this as necessary every time kids approach, because they don’t always know to stay back.”

Embers can easily reignite hours or even days later, so the best practice for putting out a bonfire is to drown it, stir the ashes, and then drown it again until everything is cold to the touch. Don’t cover embers with dirt, as that actually insulates them, leaving open the possibility for them to reignite if they’re uncovered by a stiff wind.

Pro-tip: Put ashes in a metal container with a lid, on a non-combustible surface, away from the house, garage and deck for several days before they go in the trash, says Klimaszewski. Never put them in a plastic bin or next to the house.

#7889. I Thought I Wanted a Single-Family Home. Turns Out, I Missed the Rental Income

We thought we wanted a single-family home, but adding an ADU made it the perfect place for us.

I’ve always had benchmarks for knowing when I’ve “made it” in life: a car with power windows and locks, a refrigerator with a water dispenser and owning a single-family home. The last one stems from the fact that my wife and I always owned two-family homes. We lived in one unit and rented out the other for over a decade before we finally had the means to move into a single-family home.

But the funny thing was, when we finally got there, something was missing. Our single-family home didn’t feel as rewarding as I thought it would. Ahead, I share why this long-sought-after dream house didn’t quite feel like one and how a new Massachusetts law allowed us to add the missing piece to our family’s forever home.

After 10 years of renting, my wife and I wanted to buy a home. We decided on a two-family property because we were nervous about taking on too much financially. A single-family home seemed like a luxury that was out of reach, but the rental income from a two-family home made homeownership seem feasible and financially safe. Collecting that first rent check was an amazing feeling, and it cut our mortgage payment in half. We were hooked. Being landlords wasn’t always stress-free, but regular rental income gave us so much financial freedom.

Seven years later, we moved into another two-family home that better suited our growing family and kept the first one, too. We continued to work and save for another five years. As we approached 40, buying a single-family home felt like the next logical step. It was the ultimate end goal, right? So we bought a single-family fixer-upper in a nice neighborhood and started making repairs. Our kids settled into a new school district, and we made friends with the neighbors.

At first, it all felt great, but living in a single-family home wasn’t everything we’d hoped it would be. Mostly, we found we really missed the rental income we were used to in our two-family homes. It felt foolish to have a house that only took money out of our bank account without putting any back in. We didn’t want to move, and soaring home prices made buying another property out of the question. To find ways to generate income from our property, I tried renting out our in-ground pool, second garage, and backyard to dog owners. None of those ideas panned out, leaving us without a way to recreate the two-family experience we missed.

Then, in August 2024, Massachusetts enacted a new law to encourage homeowners to build accessory dwelling units (ADUs), or in-law apartments, to ease the state’s housing shortage. These secondary, self-contained living spaces, complete with kitchens and bathrooms, can house extended family members or paying tenants.

My wife and I immediately knew this could be the solution we’d been looking for. Instead of moving to a two-family home, we could add a small apartment to our existing home. We considered our options and decided that converting a portion of our house into a one-bedroom apartment was the most cost-effective.

We researched town and state ordinances and building codes, then applied for a building permit and submitted plans for the proposed project. Because we weren’t changing the footprint of our home, the process went very smoothly. We started the work in August and had everything completed and inspected by December 2024. We received a certificate of occupancy from the town, and our first tenant moved in on January 1, 2025.

Nearly two years later, we have absolutely no regrets about our ADU conversion project. The rental income has been a fantastic addition to our monthly budget, and we’ve had amazing tenants from the start. It has been the missing piece of our dream home and is making a more secure financial future possible for our family.

If you’re considering adding an ADU to your home or property, here are a few things to keep in mind:

While we had been happy in a two-family home, we mistakenly thought we could do better. But after moving into what was supposed to be our perfect, single-family home, we realized we had made a mistake. Our “dream” house began to feel like a financial burden that only sucked up money and never gave anything back. Staying put and adding a small apartment has given us so much more breathing room and transformed our forever home from a burden into a boon.

#7887. We Tested Ryobi’s $129 Pressure Washer — Here’s What It Can (and Can’t) Do

Can this portable power washer possibly compare to the real thing? We put it to the test.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Nothing sets you up for a better spring than taking some time for some seasonal cleaning in the fall, and one of the best tools for autumn home cleanup is a classic pressure washer. If you’ve got a surface or a screen you need sprayed, a pressure washer can deliver enough pressure for all kinds of scrubbing.

But even the most avid pressure washer advocates would tell you they’re also pretty cumbersome tools that require a lot of setup and garage storage space. That’s exactly why I wanted to try out this portable pressurized washer from Ryobi. The concept is intriguing, promising users a fraction of the size, cost and power of a standard pressure washer. I was very curious whether this tool would actually provide more cleaning power than a standard garden hose nozzle.

The first thing I noticed when unboxing the Ryobi One Plus Electric Power Cleaner was how substantial the tool felt. I was expecting it to feel a little flimsy, but the tool felt well-built in my hands. It all assembled easily in just a few clicks, taking only a small fraction of the time it would’ve taken to set up a full-size pressure washer. And if you’re worried about water ruining your battery, don’t be. The entire battery chamber is enclosed by a tightly sealed plastic housing.

For this test, I decided to replicate a classic fall cleanup task: hosing down screens. I wanted a big surface to clean, so I pulled the screen door off the back door and set it up in the backyard. Then, I applied a light coating of flour to the middle of the screen and a light mist of water to lock the flour in place.

From there, I just had to finish setting up the Ryobi pressure washer. It comes with three different nozzles: two flat angled nozzles and one “turbo nozzle” that sprays the water in a speedy spiral. All I had to do was attach the pressure washer to a garden hose, and the tool was ready to go. Then I just set myself up in front of the screen with the pressure washer the recommended distance (1-2 feet) from the screen. ‘

All that was left to do was let it rip. The first thing that stands out when you use this portable pressure washer is that it feels a little underwhelming when you pull the trigger- especially if you’ve ever used a full-sized pressure washer. There’s not much kick, and the water leaves the nozzle at a steady but uninspiring speed. For a few seconds, I was worried the 700psi of pressure wouldn’t be enough to clean up the floury mess I’d created.

But my worries lessened the longer I used the tool. It was gentler than the pressure washers I’d used before, but it provided a consistent stream that quickly started knocking the flour loose from the screen. Things started going even better once I switched to the turbo nozzle. The spin action really helped compensate for the lack of PSI pressure. Within another minute, I had knocked off a ton of the sticky flour from the screen.

A post shared by Family Handyman (@familyhandyman)

So enough waffling… what’s the verdict? It’s pretty clear, as soon as you start using this tool, that the Ryobi tool isn’t going to fully replace a full-sized pressure washer… especially if you need to really blast something. But there are many use cases for a pressure washer where consistency is more important than power. And if you’ve ever accidentally damaged something with a pressure washer, the reduced power of this tool might even be something you consider a pro.

It took a while, but eventually the screen was sparkling clean- so clean, in fact, it was nearly invisible in the doorway. I should also point out that real-world conditions are rarely as messy as the sticky flour mess I created. If you just need to get dust off a screen or mud off a sidewalk, this tool is a significant upgrade over a simple stream from a garden hose. Ultimately, you’re trading power for portability, and whether that works for you will depend on the job you have to tackle. If it’s only needed for routine seasonal cleaning, this pressure washer could be perfect for you.

Just don’t expect it to peel paint off a pole.

#7885. How Old Is Too Old To Use a Chainsaw?

Understand the risks associated with operating a chainsaw as you age with expert-backed advice and safety tips.

While you may take great pride in your ability to take care of things around the house, be careful when it comes to using a chainsaw as you age. Unlike other powered lawn equipment, chainsaws carry a significant risk of personal injury— and can be deadly in the wrong hands.

Ahead, learn how to evaluate when you may be too old to operate a chainsaw and should call in a pro instead, with help from physical therapist Dr. Ron Miller and manual therapist Doug Bertram.

Chainsaw injuries can happen in a fraction of a second and are often due to losing control of the saw during operation. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reports roughly 36,000 chainsaw injuries each year, resulting in serious lacerations, traumatic brain injuries, limb loss or death.

While chainsaws are dangerous to operate at any age, the risks are even higher for older adults. “As we grow older, our ability to control our balance, grip strength, reflex times, eyesight and physical stamina dramatically decreases,” Miller says. “This makes it difficult to operate chainsaws.” It’s crucial that you have the strength and stamina to handle a chainsaw in all conditions to avoid injury.

If you’re not ready to put down the saw yet, consider these tips to do it safely.

Cut smaller logs and branches that are safely on the ground and avoid cutting while on a ladder or felling trees. Hire larger jobs out rather than tackling them yourself.

Consider using a lightweight, electric saw that is easier to control. Regardless of the saw, always make sure the chain is sharp and properly tightened before use.

Wear protective gear: Wearing eye and hearing protection, gloves and sturdy footwear is always sound advice, but don’t overlook chaps too, Miller says. Worn over pants and designed to stop a chainsaw chain, chaps can be the difference between a fatal injury and a superficial wound.

Never cut alone: Always have a cutting partner who remains nearby to help identify dangerous situations and call for help in the event of an accident.

Avoid working to fatigue: “Take breaks to stay awake and alert while operating a chainsaw,” Miller says. Stay well hydrated and fueled to keep your mind sharp during operation and stop when you start to feel tired.

“There’s no age that makes you too old to use a chainsaw,” Bertram says. “[But] you need adequate grip strength, adequate balance and good mental acuity.” It’s less about a specific number and more about your general health and ability. Conduct these physical fitness tests at home to gauge your grip strength, balance, leg and back strength, coordination and endurance. How you perform on these tests will give you a good idea of your functional fitness levels and whether handling a chainsaw is a good idea or not.  When in doubt, hire a pro.

For smaller limbs and logs up to 12-in. in diameter, a bow saw or reciprocating saw with a pruning blade are lower risk options.

Federal law prohibits anyone under the age of 18 from operating a chainsaw in a work setting, but there are no age limits for private chainsaw use on a residential property.

#7884. Trump vs. WSJ Libel Lawsuit over Trump's Alleged Birthday Wishes to Epstein Thrown out

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The court concludes that Trump hadn't adequately alleged facts supporting a showing that the Journal published the article knowing that it was likely false.

From Judge Darrin Gayles (S.D. Fla.) in Trump v. Dow Jones & Co., Inc.:

Those who won our independence believed … that public discussion is a political duty; and that this should be a fundamental principle of the American government. They recognized the risks to which all human institutions are subject. But they knew that order cannot be secured merely through fear of punishment for its infraction; that it is hazardous to discourage thought, hope and imagination; that fear breeds repression; that repression breeds hate; that hate menaces stable government; that the path of safety lies in the opportunity to discuss freely supposed grievances and proposed remedies; and that the fitting remedy for evil counsels is good ones. Believing in the power of reason as applied through public discussion, they eschewed silence coerced by law—the argument of force in its worst form. Recognizing the occasional tyrannies of governing majorities, they amended the Constitution so that free speech and assembly should be guaranteed.

New York Times Co. v. Sullivan (1964) (quoting Whitney v. California (1927) (Brandeis, J., concurring)).

Justice Brandeis's words, as relevant today as they were nearly a century ago, formed the "background" behind the Supreme Court's holding in Sullivan: the First Amendment "prohibits a public [figure] from recovering damages for a defamatory falsehood … unless he proves that the statement was made with actual malice[.]" This constitutional protection is not limited to post-discovery motions and trial. Because "[t]he costs and efforts required to defend a lawsuit through [discovery] could chill free speech nearly as effectively as the absence of the actual malice standard altogether[,]" a public figure plaintiff must plausibly allege actual malice at the outset of the litigation.

This Order addresses President Donald J. Trump's second attempt to plead that Defendants … acted with actual malice when they published an article in the Wall Street Journal … linking him to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein …. As with his first attempt, he has failed. Therefore, for the reasons below, … President Trump's Amended Complaint is dismissed with prejudice….

On July 15, 2025, Palazzolo emailed then White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt ("Leavitt") advising her that Dow Jones intended to publish an article (the "Article") about a birthday letter that President Trump purportedly created for Epstein (the "Letter"). President Trump and his team responded quickly. Leavitt called Palazzolo and told him that the "subject matter" of the proposed Article was false. President Trump, through counsel, denied writing the Letter and warned Dow Jones not to publish the story. {President Trump also denied writing the Letter in an interview before publication.} And President Trump directly told Murdoch that he had not signed or sent the Letter. When Murdoch responded that he would "handle it," President Trump thought the WSJ would not print the Article. Two days later, the WSJ online edition published the Article.

The title of the Article—"Jeffrey Epstein's Friends Sent Him Bawdy Letters for a 50th Birthday Album. One was from Donald Trump"—is in bold print, with a subtitle below reading "[t]he leather-bound book was compiled by Ghislaine Maxwell. The president says the letter 'is a fake thing.'" Leading with a picture of President Trump with Epstein, the Article states the following, in pertinent part:

It was Jeffrey Esptein's 50th birthday, and Ghislaine Maxwell was preparing a special gift to mark the occasion. She turned to Epstein's family and friends. One of them was Donald Trump.

Maxwell collected letters from Trump and dozens of Epstein's other associates for a 2003 birthday album, according to documents reviewed by The Wall Street Journal.

Pages from the leather-bound album—assembled before Epstein was first arrested in 2006—are among the documents examined by Justice Department officials who investigated Epstein and Maxwell years ago, according to people who have reviewed the pages. It's unclear if any of the pages are part of the Trump Administration's recent review….

The letter bearing Trump's name, which was reviewed by the Journal, is bawdy—like others in the album. It contains several lines of typewritten text framed by the outline of a naked woman, which appears to be hand-drawn with a heavy marker. A pair of small arcs denotes the woman's breasts, and the future president's signature is a squiggly "Donald" below her waist, mimicking pubic hair.

The letter concludes: "Happy Birthday—and may every day be another wonderful secret."

In an interview with the Journal on Tuesday evening, Trump denied writing the letter or drawing the picture. "This is not me. This is a fake thing. It's a fake Wall Street Journal story," he said.

"I never wrote a picture in my life. I don't draw pictures of women," he said. "It's not my language. It's not my words."

He told the Journal he was preparing to file a lawsuit if it published an article. "I'm gonna sue The Wall Street Journal just like I sued everyone else," he said….

Justice Department officials didn't respond to requests for comment or address questions about whether the Trump page and other pages of the birthday album were part of the agency's recent documents review. The FBI declined to comment….

Among those who submitted letters were billionaire Leslie Wexner and attorney Alan Dershowitz … Wexner declined to comment through a spokesman … Dershowitz, who represented Epstein after his first arrest, said, "It's been a long time and I don't recall the content of what I may have written….

The book was put together by a New York City bookbinder, Herbert Weitz, according to people who were involved in the process. Weitz, who died in 2020, listed Epstein as a client on his website in 2003.

It isn't clear how the letter with Trump's signature was prepared. Inside the outline of the naked woman was a typewritten note styled as an imaginary conversation between Trump and Epstein, written in the third person.

When he turned 50, Epstein was already wealthy from managing Wexner's fortune and was socializing with Trump, Clinton and other powerful people. He often entertained at this Manhattan townhouse, Palm Beach, Fla., home and private Caribbean island….

Epstein and Trump spent time together in the 1990s and early 2000s and were photographed at social events, including with Maxwell and Melania Trump….

Trump, along with others including Clinton, also appeared several times on flight logs for Epstein's private jet.

A 2002 New York magazine profile of Epstein quoted Trump. "I've known Jeff for 15 years. Terrific guy," Trump said. "He's a lot of fun to be with. It is even said that he likes beautiful women as much as I do, and many of them are on the younger side. No doubt about it—Jeffrey enjoys his social life."

Both men said that they subsequently had a falling-out. Trump has said their friendship ended before Epstein pleaded guilty to procuring a minor for prostitution in 2008, served time in a Florida jail and registered as a sex offender….

Maxwell, a British socialite, was convicted in 2021 of helping Epstein's sex-trafficking and sentenced to 20 years in prison. Maxwell didn't respond to a letter requesting an interview sent to her in prison. Arthur Aidala, an attorney who represented Maxwell, said, "At this point, she is focused on her case before the Supreme Court of the United States." …

Epstein's associations with Trump and many powerful people have been well documented….

On September 8, 2025, the WSJ published an article titled "A Visual Breakdown of the Trump Birthday Letter to Epstein" which compares the signature and typeface, drawing style, third-person point of view, and diction in the Letter with prior communications by President Trump (the "September 8 Article"). The September 8 Article includes President Trump's denial that he wrote the Letter or drew the picture and Leavitt's statement in a social media post that President Trump did not draw the picture in or sign the Letter….

President Trump contends that these statements are false because he (1) did not author, sign, or draw any portion of the Letter or direct anyone else to author it; (2) never made or dictated to anyone any of the statements in the voiceover or had any such conversation with Epstein as portrayed in the Letter; and (3) was not "childhood pals" with Epstein….

The court concluded that Trump hadn't actually alleged "actual malice," which is to say knowing or reckless falsehood:

Here, the Amended Complaint falls short of pleading actual malice. Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false.

As an initial matter, President Trump's conclusory allegations that Defendants acted with malice because they "knew or should have known" the statements in the Article were false, are insufficient to state a claim. See Reed v. Chamblee (11th Cir. 2025) (finding the plaintiff's conclusory assertions that the defendant acted with actual malice insufficient).

Though vague, the Amended Complaint appears to allege that by choosing to publish the Article despite President Trump's and his team's denials, Defendants acted with actual malice. In effect, President Trump argues that once he declared the Letter a "fake," Defendants should have disregarded everything else they learned in their investigation and not published the story.

But that is not what the actual malice standard requires and runs afoul of the First Amendment. Indeed, were that the law, any time a public figure or his team denies an accusation, journalists would be immediately blocked from publishing negative or contradictory press—a result that flies in the face of the "American privilege to speak one's mind, although not always with perfect good taste, on all public institutions[.]" Sullivan.

Moreover, the Article did not ignore or minimize President Trump's denial. Rather, it informed readers that President Trump decried the Letter as a fake and denied writing it. By "allowing readers to decide for themselves what to conclude from the [Article], … any allegation of actual malice [is] less plausible." … "[R]eporting perspectives contrary to the publisher's own should be interpreted as helping to rebut, not establish, the presence of actual malice" ….

President Trump's argument that the WSJ Defendants' investigation was inadequate, and therefore an indication of malice, fares no better. As detailed above, a failure to investigate, without more, does not establish actual malice. Rather, "a plaintiff must show the defendant deliberately avoided investigating the veracity of the statement in order to evade learning the truth."

The Amended Complaint comes nowhere close to this standard. Indeed, the Article details a thoughtful and detailed investigation. Before running the story, Defendants contacted President Trump and his team, Justice Department officials, and the FBI for comment.

President Trump and his team responded with his denial, the Justice Department did not respond at all, and the FBI declined to comment. Defendants also attempted to speak with Maxwell; she did not respond to their request and her attorney stated that she was focused on her case before the Supreme Court. In addition, Defendants reached out to other individuals named in the Birthday Book, including Leslie Wexner and Alan Dershowitz, and to individuals involved in binding the Birthday Book, who confirmed that Weitz put the book together. In short, President Trump's allegation that Defendants failed to conduct an adequate investigation is rebutted by the Article and is insufficient to establish actual malice.

{President Trump argues that Harte-Hanks Communications, Inc. v. Connaughton (1989), supports his position that Defendants' purported failure to investigate is enough to support an inference of actual malice. However, in Harte-Hanks, the Supreme Court expressly stated that "[a]lthough failure to investigate will not alone support a finding of actual malice, the purposeful avoidance of the truth is in a different category. Here, President Trump has not alleged any facts, beyond conclusory allegations, that support an inference that Defendants purposefully avoided the truth.}

Grasping at straws, the Amended Complaint attempts to manufacture flaws with the investigation. First, it alleges that the investigation was lacking because Defendants only reviewed the Letter but did not have a copy in their possession. The Court cannot discern any substantive difference—and certainly not one that would establish actual malice—between Defendants reviewing the Letter before publication and obtaining a copy of the Letter. Defendants reviewed the Letter and later reported on its contents. Nothing in the law suggests that Defendants needed to obtain, retain, or publish a copy.

In addition, President Trump's focus on Maxwell is entirely misplaced. The Eleventh Circuit has found "allegations that the Defendants failed to fully investigate their statements by intentionally choosing not to speak with any witnesses who could have refuted the allegedly defamatory statements" insufficient to plead actual malice. And any argument that Defendants "purposely avoided" the truth by either not disclosing what Maxwell told them or by refusing to speak with her is difficult to reconcile with President Trump's own allegations.

The Amended Complaint alleges that "Maxwell has stated, subject to penalty of perjury for lying to a federal officer, that she did not remember President Trump submitting a letter for Epstein's 50th birthday." Based on this allegation, Maxwell had little to offer to Defendants' investigation. In short, references to Maxwell are a red herring and simply do not establish that Defendants "actually entertained serious doubts as to the veracity of the published account[] or was highly aware that the account was probably false."

President Trump's argument that the Article omits certain facts does not save his claims. First, how or why the voiceover in the Letter was typewritten or how the voiceover was confirmed to be in the third person are inconsequential details that have no bearing on whether Defendants published the Article knowing its contents were false or with reckless disregard as to its falsity. Moreover, Defendants' decisions about how to investigate and what to include in the Article do not establish malice. "Obviously the author of an article will have to choose which facts to include and which to omit. It is impossible to print all of the facts on which an opinion or belief is based …. Were the courts or criticized [parties] to be allowed to dictate the contents of such articles, censorship would have won out over free speech and the right to dissent."

Finally, the allegation that Defendants intentionally omitted President Trump's denial that he signed the Letter or a discussion on whether the signature on the Letter is authentic, is belied by the Article. It states, multiple times, that President Trump denies writing the Letter and that "[i]t isn't clear how the letter with Trump's signature was prepared." . This is more than sufficient to encompass any denial that he "signed" the Letter or that the signature on the Letter is authentic.

The Amended Complaint's reliance on the September 8 Article to establish malice is equally unavailing. Nothing in the law suggests that a journalist must report on every piece of evidence they uncover before going to print. Moreover, it is unclear why President Trump argues the September 8 Article shows that his signature "could not be more different" than the one in the Letter, when it contains several examples where President Trump's actual signature and sketches are similar to those in the Letter. At bottom, the September 8 Article does not support a finding that Defendants knew or should have known that President Trump did not sign the Letter….

NEXT: American Cities, Population >50K, Named After Foreign (Excluding British) Political Figures

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

Without using them, drip lines and low spots can turn into serious home safety hazards.

We researched and tested 10 different ice melt products to see which delivered the best results. Nearly every brand improved walking conditions and had a positive impact on overall traction and safety. Some were more capable of handling the heavy-duty demands of high-traffic residential and commercial areas. Others were safer for pets and the environment, making them great for home use. Based on our expert’s feedback and our hands-on test results, we chose the Natural Rapport The Only Pet-Safe Ice Melt You Need as our top pick. While they may not be quite as diverse as snowflakes, ice melts do come in a variety of forms, each with its own distinct features. We tested each product in the following list ourselves to help you choose the best ice melts for your needs.

This Natural Rapport ice melt is one of the safest ice melts for pets, plants, and the environment. It’s less corrosive on metal, wood, and concrete than conventional rock salt, and it is also safer on carpet and other flooring materials, should your furry friends or kids track it into the house.

Many environmentally friendly products melt slowly because they use mild formulas. But we were pleasantly surprised by how fast-acting and long-lasting this ice melt was. Its time-released formula not only started working right away but also kept melting, preventing our sidewalks and driveway from refreezing. The crystals are green, so it was easy to see where we’d applied them, helping to prevent waste. Also, our dogs repeatedly walked over the colorful ice melt with no adverse reactions.

Ultimately, this ice melt took the top award because it offers a combination of performance and environmental friendliness. It has organic compounds to help it break down quickly, and thanks to the inclusion of soil-supporting compounds, it may even enrich the soil to a small degree. We spread some over a patch of grass during testing, so we’re interested to see what happens over time.

Snow Joe is a leader in snow removal products, and it has formulated a fantastic ice melt product with the Premium Enviro Blend Ice Melter. It’s made for extreme cold and has a chemical composition designed with the environment, pets, and people in mind.

This blend has an anti-corrosion agent that helps it break down easily while minimizing damage to concrete, asphalt, and yards. It also has a green dye that makes monitoring its performance and presence on the ground easy. When the green coloring fades, it’s time to add more. This formulation did an excellent job melting ice and maintaining clear walkways. We also had a property management company test it, and they were impressed.

Though some may prefer ice melt that comes in a bucket or ice melt shaker, we found the durable bag-style packaging of this Snow Joe eco-friendly ice melt easy to reach into and move around. Be aware, however, that if the open bag gets wet, the contents will bind together and consolidate into a giant rock. We kept ours in the garage, and it was fine.

Get the Snow Joe Enviro Blend ice melt (various sizes) at Amazon, The Home Depot, Walmart, Best Buy, or Snow Joe.

Since almost all ice melt formulations contain salt or chlorides, this salt-free option from Safe Paw is quite unique. It’s a great choice if your household is sensitive to salts or if using anything corrosive is not viable (such as around a classic car, near expensive equipment, or on a newly paved surface). It’s also nonconductive, making it safe around electrical components.

This product comes in a granular form and doesn’t have sharp edges like rock salt. Thanks to its nonabrasive texture, our dogs had zero issues walking through it. They even played right where we tested this product and showed no adverse effects. That’s also likely partly due to the blend’s chemical composition, which isn’t as aggressive as other formulas. While that means it doesn’t melt ice as quickly as some of the heavier hitters we tested, it’s still effective.

In addition to melting a bit more slowly, it also doesn’t work at quite as low temperatures. In our tests, it melted ice in as low as 15 degrees Fahrenheit but struggled if it was colder. Though the label claims it works at -2 degrees Fahrenheit, the manufacturer only guarantees it down to 10 degrees Fahrenheit. We think 10 degrees is accurate—any lower than that, and we’d say all bets are off. Don’t let this ice melt’s small bag fool you: This Redmond’s Nature’s Blend is packed with concentrated dye-free, urea-free, and polymer-free nontoxic ice melt chemicals that effectively bust ice and slush over an up to 400-square-foot area. Get the Redmond ice melt at Amazon or Ice Slicer.

When people think about removing snow from roofs, they often imagine doing so manually. That’s because few ice melt products are made to address ice buildup on roofs—which is what makes this ice melt such a unique product. The tablets are composed of calcium chloride and designed to be thrown onto roofs to prevent snow and ice buildup from wreaking havoc on gutters and adding weight to vulnerable areas. For those living in areas with heavy snowfall where ice dams often form, they are a worthy investment.

During testing, we aimed for problem spots and tossed the tablets up. While snow began to slough off the roof relatively quickly, we struggled to verify the exact rate at which the tablets melted the ice since we couldn’t see it happening from the ground. Still, for their intended purpose, they worked well.

The Roof Melt tablets aren’t granular or spreadable, so they aren’t compatible with larger surface areas like driveways. You could probably use them on the ground where drainage is constricted and problematic, but other options will be more economical for that purpose. If you deal with dangerous ice dams on your roof, however, these tablets are worth having around to quickly and easily resolve the issue.

The best way to determine how effectively various ice melts perform is to fully test each product. As residents of Montana, we began our testing in the aftermath of a winter snowstorm that turned bitter cold. We applied the products to gravel, pavement, and grass in temperatures as low as -6 degrees Fahrenheit.

As the snow went through several melt/freeze cycles over the coming days, it formed icy spots under our rooflines and in several low spots. We tested the ice melts in freezing temperatures on water drips and overnight freezes that created walking hazards each morning. We analyzed how long it took to apply each product, how quickly they melted ice and snow, their degree of pet friendliness when used around our dogs, and a number of other hands-on factors. Lastly, we compared pricing, packaging, and ease of application.

Ice melt products are designed for use either before or after snow or ice has fallen. Their application prevents ice from forming or melts it into a slush that’s easier to clear with a standard snow shovel. Each type of ice melt will perform differently depending on its form and chemical composition. Other variables, such as temperature, ground type, melting time, and environmental impact are essential to consider before purchasing an ice melt product.

Ice melt is available in solid and liquid formulations, each with pros and cons. Solid ice melt typically comes in pellets and granules. It works well for many applications and is typically the go-to solution for road crews dealing with icy and snowy weather. Pellets and granules are generally less expensive and easier to store than liquid formulas, and they add a “crunchy” texture on surfaces that adds grip for walking and driving. Their main downsides are that they scatter more easily across icy surfaces, making them harder to apply with precision, and that they tend to be slower acting and more likely to clump together, which sometimes makes them less effective.

Liquid ice melt is a wise choice for lower-temperature situations and times when faster results are necessary. That said, some products must be applied before ice forms rather than after. When applied, liquid is less likely to scatter, staying in place for longer-lasting results. Liquid de-icers, which tend to cost more, can be more challenging to transport and store because of their weight. Plus, if heavy rain ensues, the product can get washed away.

Self-heating ice melt, which comes in pellet and granular form, generates its own heat when in contact with ice and snow—a process known as an exothermic reaction. Unlike other products that must absorb moisture to create a brine to melt the ice, self-heating ice melt can get right to work.

Ice melts work by absorbing the moisture on the top of the ice, creating what’s called brine, and working its way down to break the bond between the ice and the surface. This creates cracks and flakes that are safer to walk on and easier to remove. All of these products have a temperature limit. If temperatures plummet beyond a product’s ice melting point, the chemicals will no longer be effective. Here’s what to expect from the various ice melt types available:

Many of the chemicals in ice melts can potentially damage surfaces, so it’s important to consider where the product will be used. The most common areas—driveways, sidewalks, decks, and porches—can be composed of different materials, such as concrete, asphalt, wood, and metal. Packaging and product descriptions of the best ice melts will reveal what materials they can be used on safely, so be sure to read this information prior to purchase. It would be unwise to apply a product that could corrode concrete, rust metal, or damage wood on those surfaces around the home.

The quest for comfort and convenience in frigid weather has led to the invention of such products as heated jackets, heated gloves, and electric snow shovels. Similarly, certain ice melts have been developed to work in colder climates. Some products won’t work in temperatures lower than 20 degrees Fahrenheit. This is acceptable if the temperature in an area seldom gets that low, but these products won’t get the job done if you live in a colder spot. For locations where temperatures can reach less than 20 degrees Fahrenheit, you’ll want to purchase a product specifically made for lower temperatures.

The time it takes a product to melt ice and snow depends on several factors. Liquid ice melters and self-heating ice melters act fairly quickly. Unlike solid melters that take time to absorb moisture and create the brine, liquid products are already a brine. Self-heating ice melters have a similar advantage: Instead of absorbing moisture, the pellets will heat up more quickly and melt the ice and snow faster than other ice melters. Regardless of which form you choose, there will still be some downtime while you wait for it to work, which you put to good use cleaning your windows with an ice scraper.

Longevity refers to an ice melt’s ability to keep working beyond the initial application period. A long-lasting ice melter is especially helpful when snowstorms or icy rain continue throughout the day. Although long-lasting ice melt tends to be more expensive, the cost can even out since smaller amounts of product tend to get the job done.

The chemicals in some ice melters can be hazardous to pets and plants. According to Alex Blutinger, Medical Director of Veterinary Emergency Group in Greenwich, Connecticut, “Melting ice can be very dangerous to animals, specifically because of the harsh ingredients in ice melt products. Ingestion of these chemicals can cause stomach upset, vomiting, and diarrhea. It may also irritate the paw pads and exposed areas of the limbs.” Dr. Blutinger says that, if you suspect your pet has been exposed to unsafe deicing chemicals, you should wipe your pet’s paws with a damp cloth or baby wipe to minimize ingestion through liking and reduce the risk of skin irritation. While using a pet-safe ice melt is smart, you can also reduce exposure using paw was or booties.

Certain elements in ice melters can also do environmental damage, such as killing wildlife that may ingest the pellets or aquatic life if the chemicals reach waterways. Many people are concerned about the impact of using large amounts of these products outdoors, so it’s important to read product information carefully to understand the dos and don’ts of using ice melt.

To ensure you get the best performance out of your purchase (or even a homemade ice melt), try the following de-icing tips and tricks.

If you’re not keen to try to melt ice without salt and want more information about ice melts, here are answers to some commonly asked questions.

Generally speaking, calcium chloride is better for ice melt. It’s effective at low temperatures, is a good choice for concrete, and comes in pellet, granule, and liquid forms. #7882. 4 Common Tools With a Hidden Second Function Most People Never Use

Some everyday tools hide useful features in plain sight. These four have built-in cutters, openers, and other functions worth knowing about.

A pair of pliers can sit in the same toolbox for years without its owner ever noticing the cutting edge near the hinge. The same goes for measuring tools, utility knives, and even gadgets in a kitchen drawer.

Some everyday tools have other tools built in, but those extra features are easy to overlook. Anyone who has spent time on home improvement projects knows how frustrating it can be to search for a tool, especially when the one already in hand could do the job.

Of course, features vary by model, but these four familiar tools have some useful extras worth knowing about.

Some pliers have built-in wire cutters near the hinge, just behind the gripping jaws. These can trim soft wire without needing a separate pair of cutters. Not every pair has this feature, though. It’s also worth checking whether the tool has wire strippers, which remove insulation without cutting through the wire itself.

Some wire strippers have small, threaded holes near the handles that allow users to shorten machine screws. The screw goes into the appropriately sized hole, and squeezing the handles cuts it to length. This feature can come in handy when installing electrical fixtures or other hardware that requires shorter screws.

Some manual can openers have a bottle opener built into the handle or near the cutting mechanism. Depending on the design, it may look like a small notch or hook in the metal. Other models have magnets that help lift cut lids from cans without touching the sharp edges.

Many nail clippers have a small metal file that folds out from beneath the lever or sits along the body. It helps smooth rough edges after trimming. Some models also have a pointed tip for cleaning beneath nails, although the design and placement of these extra features vary.
