#7863. How to Test Your Home’s Water Quality

Old Houses AREN’T Scary: What We’ve Learned & Loved About Them

Published Nov 3, 2026 12:05 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

We use water every day for drinking, cooking, cleaning, and bathing, but how often do we stop to think about what’s actually in it? Water that looks clean can contain potentially harmful contaminants, including lead, bacteria, and chemicals. The good news is, learning how to test water quality at home is pretty straightforward, whether you’re using an inexpensive DIY test kit, or you mail a sample to a certified laboratory. We’ll walk you through the testing process, explain what your results mean, and help you figure out what to do if you find a problem.

Even if your water looks clean doesn’t always mean it’s safe to drink. Contaminants and certain bacteria can be in there without changing the water’s appearance, taste, or smell. Testing your water helps identify potential health risks and gives you a clearer picture of what’s coming out of your faucets.

“A common misconception is that water is safe if it looks, smells and tastes fine,” says Dr. Eric Roy, Chief of Science at Culligan International. “But the reality is that contaminants such as lead, arsenic, and ‘forever chemicals’ (PFAS) cannot be detected by our senses.”

Water testing can also reveal less serious issues, such as high mineral content. Hard water, which contains elevated levels of calcium and magnesium, can cause scale buildup in pipes and appliances, leave spots on dishes, and make soap less effective. Testing can also help you get to the bottom of unpleasant tastes, unusual odors, or discoloration.

Knowing what’s in your water helps you decide whether you need a filtration system, a water softener, or another treatment method. And even if your water is perfectly safe to drink, you might still want to improve its taste or overall quality.

Bobvila.com may earn a commission from purchases made through these links.

Testing your water quality is a simple process that takes just a few minutes of hands-on work, depending on the type of test you choose. At-home water test kits give you quick results for common water-quality indicators, while mail-in laboratory tests offer more detailed information about potentially harmful contaminants.

Before getting started, read the instructions included with your test kit carefully. Different tests have different sampling requirements, and even small mistakes, such as touching the inside of a collection bottle or flushing the faucet when you shouldn’t, can affect the accuracy of your results.

The best testing method depends on what you’re looking for. Inexpensive, at-home test kits typically use strips or color-changing solutions to check for pH, chlorine, and hardness. They’re useful for identifying common water-quality issues, but generally lack the precision to detect harmful contaminants at very low concentrations.

For health-related concerns, such as lead, arsenic, bacteria, or PFAS, choose a mail-in kit analyzed by a certified laboratory. As Dr. Jess Goddard, chief science officer at SimpleLab Inc. explains, “If you’re making a health decision or about to spend money on treatment, you definitely want lab results behind it.”

Safe Home’s mail-in water test kit checks 200 qparameters, including 7 inorganics, 31 metals, and 20 pesticides and herbicides. Read the review.

Before collecting your water sample, wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water and clear the area around the faucet. Wipe away any visible dirt or debris, and remove the faucet aerator if your testing instructions require it. Some tests, particularly those for bacteria, may also require disinfecting the faucet opening before sampling.

Be careful not to introduce contaminants during preparation. Avoid touching the inside of collection bottles or their caps, and wear disposable gloves if recommended by your test kit. Always follow the manufacturer’s instructions, as preparation requirements can vary depending on the contaminants being tested.

For many water tests, you’ll need to run cold water through the faucet for a couple of minutes before collecting your sample. This flushes out stagnant water that’s been sitting in your plumbing, helping you collect a sample representative of your incoming water supply. However, always check your kit’s instructions first, as some tests require a different approach.

“For example, some lead-testing protocols require collecting the first water from a cold tap after several hours without use,” explains Rich Razgaitis, co-founder and CEO of FloWater. “If you flush the pipes beforehand, you may wash away the very evidence you’re looking for.”

Once the faucet is prepared, collect your sample according to your test kit’s instructions. The process differs slightly depending on your testing method:

Keep your fingers away from bottle openings and inside surfaces to prevent contamination. Seal samples immediately and follow any storage or shipping instructions.

Now it’s time to test your sample. The process will depend on whether you’re using an at-home kit or sending your water to a laboratory.

Note: At-home kits aren’t always dip strips. Some use reagents, test vials, or incubation procedures for bacteria. Always follow the instructions for the specific kit you have.

Once you’ve tested your water, the next step is figuring out what the results mean. Most at-home testing kits use color-coded charts to indicate the concentration of different substances in your water, while laboratory reports provide more precise measurements, often in parts per million (ppm), parts per billion (ppb), or milligrams per liter (mg/L).

Compare your results with the reference ranges provided by the kit or laboratory, paying particular attention to any contaminants that exceed health-based guidelines. Keep in mind that detecting a substance doesn’t automatically mean your water is unsafe.

“When interpreting results, a common mistake is assuming that a detection automatically means you have a health risk,” explains Goddard. “You need to put the result in context, first, and compare the detected concentration to a health guideline to determine if there’s a problem.”

Here’s what some common water-quality findings mean and how to address them.

Water hardness measures the concentration of dissolved minerals, primarily calcium and magnesium. According to the U.S. Geological Survey, water containing 121 to 180 ppm of hardness (measured as calcium carbonate) is considered hard, while anything above 180 ppm is very hard.

Hard water is generally safe to drink, but it can cause mineral buildup in pipes, faucets, and appliances. If your results indicate hard or very hard water and you’re experiencing these problems, consider installing a water softener. These systems reduce calcium and magnesium levels to help prevent scale buildup.

iSpring’s water softener is an electronic magnetic softener that treats mineral buildup but doesn’t remove heavy metals from water. Read the review.

Lead can enter drinking water through old pipes, solder, and plumbing fixtures, particularly in older homes. There is no known safe level of lead exposure, so any detected lead deserves attention, especially in households with children.

If a lab test detects lead, use a verified safe drinking-water source while investigating the problem. Contact your water utility or local health department for guidance, and consider having your plumbing inspected. A water filter independently certified for lead reduction can help reduce exposure, but replacing lead-containing plumbing may be necessary to address the source.

Finding E. coli in drinking water is a serious concern because it indicates fecal contamination. If your test detects E. coli, stop drinking the untreated water and contact your local health department or water utility.

For private wells, a professional may recommend inspecting and disinfecting the well, followed by additional testing to confirm the water is safe. UV treatment or other disinfection systems may also be appropriate for certain ongoing bacterial problems.

Boiling water can kill many disease-causing microorganisms, but it won’t remove chemical contaminants such as lead or nitrates. Follow the specific guidance provided by your health department rather than assuming boiling will solve every water-quality problem.

Nitrates can enter groundwater through fertilizers, septic systems, and agricultural runoff. Elevated levels are particularly dangerous for infants because they can interfere with the blood’s ability to carry oxygen.

The EPA’s drinking-water limit for nitrate is 10 mg/L measured as nitrogen (NO3-N). If your results exceed this level, switch to a verified safe water source for drinking, cooking, and preparing baby formula, and consult your local health department.

A reverse osmosis system certified for nitrate reduction may be an appropriate long-term solution. Do not boil nitrate-contaminated water, as evaporation can increase the nitrate concentration.

Arsenic and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) can be present in drinking water without any noticeable change in taste, smell, or appearance. Both can pose health risks, depending on the substance and concentration.

If lab testing identifies levels above applicable health-based guidelines, use a verified safe drinking-water source while seeking advice from your health department or a qualified water-treatment professional.

Depending on the contaminant, an appropriately certified reverse osmosis or activated carbon filtration system may help. Check that the specific system has been tested and certified to reduce the substance identified in your results.

The Waterdrop G3P600 installs under the sink and has a digital display that monitors the presence of TDS in the water. Read the review.

Not every unusual result indicates a health risk. Elevated iron can cause reddish-brown staining, while chlorine may give treated municipal water an unpleasant taste or odor. High mineral concentrations can also affect how water tastes.

If testing confirms that the issue is aesthetic rather than a health concern, you may be able to address it with a relatively simple treatment system. Activated carbon filters can improve chlorine taste and odor, while specialized iron filters can help reduce staining caused by elevated iron levels.

“A filter that improves taste isn’t necessarily removing lead,” says Razgaitis. “A water softener addresses hardness, not every health concern. UV treatment targets microorganisms but doesn’t remove dissolved chemicals.”

Whatever your results show, choose a treatment system that is independently certified to address the specific contaminants in your water, rather than assuming any filter will do the job.

Testing your home’s water quality is a simple but important step toward making sure the water you use every day is safe. Whether you use an at-home testing kit or send a sample to a certified laboratory, following the proper collection instructions will help you get reliable results.

Remember: Not every unusual reading indicates a health risk, but potentially harmful contaminants should always be taken seriously. Once you understand what’s in your water, you can make informed decisions about whether filtration, water softening, or other treatment is necessary.

Yes, you can test your home’s water quality using an at-home testing kit. Most kits use test strips or chemical reagents to check for common water-quality indicators such as pH, chlorine, and hardness. However, DIY kits have limitations, particularly when detecting potentially harmful contaminants at very low concentrations. For more comprehensive testing, the EPA recommends using a state-certified drinking water laboratory.

Common signs of poor water quality include unusual tastes or odors, cloudy or discolored water, and staining around sinks and faucets. White, chalky residue on fixtures can also indicate hard water. However, these symptoms don’t necessarily mean your water is unsafe. According to the CDC, harmful germs and chemicals may be present without affecting how water looks, tastes, or smells.

At-home water tests are a convenient, inexpensive way to screen for basic water-quality issues, such as hardness, pH, and chlorine levels. However, laboratory testing is generally the better option if you’re concerned about contaminants such as lead, arsenic, PFAS, or bacteria. These tests require greater accuracy and sensitivity than most DIY kits can provide. For example, the CDC recommends using a state-certified laboratory to test private well water.

There’s no single list of five indicators that covers every drinking-water concern, but homeowners should pay particular attention to total coliform bacteria, nitrates, pH, total dissolved solids (TDS), and lead.

#7862. Is a Reverse Osmosis Filter System Actually Worth It? We Break Down Every Cost

What’s lurking in your water? RO filters get rid of everything from microplastics to heavy metals, but are they overkill?

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

In this installment of Home 2.0, we dive into reverse osmosis filtration for the kitchen, its benefits and hidden costs — plus which households should invest in the technology, and who can skip it.

I’ve lived in some places with questionable drinking water. One town issued a notice that the municipal water supply had experienced a sewage incident. Another had an arsenic problem. I’ve also lived on well water, with concerns of contamination from nearby agricultural fields.

My solution used to be buying five-gallon jugs of spring water. But that was costly and a hassle, so six years ago, I switched to an under-sink reverse osmosis (RO) filter for my drinking and cooking water.

Under-sink RO filters work like this: water passes through a series of filters, including an RO membrane, which removes dissolved substances — including lead, arsenic, nitrates, forever chemicals, chlorine, fluoride and sediment — down to 0.0001 microns. The cleaned water then comes out through a faucet, installed near the sink.

“Reverse osmosis provides the safest level of drinking water possible,” says international water filtration specialist Andrew D. Daily. “It strips out 100% of bacteria, cysts, dissolved solids, chlorine, rust, viruses and microplastics.”

But RO systems are also a considerable investment. So, we asked a range of health and plumbing experts for their thoughts on who should get an RO system, plus how to pick the right one. Ahead is what they said, how much RO systems cost up front and over time, and whether it’s worth the upgrade.

RO water systems range from a few hundred dollars to over $1,000. The good news is that if you have basic plumbing knowledge and are comfortable drilling a hole in your countertop, installing one can be a DIY task. Otherwise, pro installation usually runs upwards of $300, not including add-ons like a refrigerator/ice-maker connection, leak protection, an additional electric outlet and other plumbing modifications.

The biggest downside to RO systems is that they waste water. For every gallon that comes out of the faucet, somewhere between one-half and four gallons get flushed down the drain through the filtration process. That means if you use 5 gallons of water a day for cooking and drinking, the RO system wastes between 2.5 and 20 gallons.

Over a year, that adds up to between 500 and 8,500 gallons, depending on your RO system. On the low end, that’s only a few pennies more on your yearly water utility bill, but on the high end, it could be close to $100.

Some RO water systems also require electricity. The amount of power they consume varies by model, but usually falls between 20 and 40 watts per hour. Since RO systems typically run for less than an hour a day, even if you live in a place with high electricity rates, they should add only a few dollars a year to your electricity bill.

Maintaining RO systems is an easy DIY task, though some people choose to pay a pro to keep track of it for them. Expect to spend roughly the following for DIY maintenance:

Daily recommends buying only name-brand filters, even though they’re more expensive. “Name brands follow strict regulations,” he says. ”Generic China-based deals often do not provide the same protection.”

A quality RO system can last 10 years or longer with proper maintenance. “Many parts, including filters, membranes, faucets and tanks can be replaced individually,” says plumbing expert Danielle Smith. “Once a system gets older, though, replacement may make more sense than repeated repairs.”

“The biggest thing for me is convenience,” says environmental and wellness expert Helen Christoni, who has an AquaTru system. “We use water all day long, drinking it, cooking with it and filling water bottles. Once installed, it just became part of my kitchen and my family’s daily health.”

Herman Hartanto, founder of Tampa Fast Home Buyer, has a Waterdrop G3P600 in his kitchen ($429 retail). It’s a tankless model, a feature he appreciates since it takes up minimal cabinet space. He also likes the display with real-time reports on total dissolved solids (TDS) and filter health. His only complaint is the occasional noise it generates. “The pump that draws the water on demand makes quite loud noise, which I can feel clearly at night when everything is silent,” he says.

Personally, I’ve used two RO filter systems. My first one was an iSpring, which I chose because of its affordability. It worked well, but like Hartanto, I found the pump noisy (even though mine had a water-holding tank). My second one, which I’ve only recently installed, is a Waterdrop X12 Pro, which I chose to upgrade to because of its water-saving efficiency, ability to add calcium and magnesium back into the water, clear display and range of other premium features. So far, I’ve found it to be quiet, efficient, and free of quirks (though at $1,400 off-sale, the price is a bit of a shocker).

Depending on what type of contaminants you have in your water, there are several alternatives to an under-sink RO water filter:

“Find out what’s in your water before buying anything,” says Smith. “Don’t choose a system based only on how many stages it has or how many contaminants the box says it removes. Instead, start with your water and choose the system around what you actually need.”

If you’re worried about contaminants like microplastics, arsenic, lead, forever chemicals, pesticides and pharmaceuticals, then an RO filter is a good choice.

“Water quality can vary tremendously depending on where you live, and even your home’s plumbing can affect what ultimately comes out of your faucet,” says Christoni. “Reverse osmosis addresses such a broad range of contaminants, and with an under-sink system, that purified water is available all day long without having to think about it.”

For Daily, the biggest reason to invest in a RO system is microplastics. “The amount of microplastics found in human brains, blood and organs have been increasing yearly,” he says. “Although there is not enough information to prove a detrimental effect on our health, many of my clients choose a cautious approach to water treatment.”

Otherwise, Daily says that RO filters are overkill in most U.S. cities, where tap water is generally considered safe. Even in Mexico, where water is often contaminated, he usually recommends sticking with under-sink ultrafiltration systems, since they’re a fraction of the cost, don’t waste water and don’t require power or space for a reservoir.

If you’re currently buying bottled water, then yes, an RO system will soon pay for itself. But, otherwise, it really just depends on what you want to remove from your water. If you have arsenic, nitrates, salts, microplastics, fluoride, sulfates and other dissolved solids (TDS), RO systems are a great solution.

Otherwise, a less-expensive ultrafiltration system might be a better choice. Either way, having an under-sink filtration system is a good way to ensure your family has access to clean water, both on a daily basis and after flooding events and other natural disasters that contaminate city and well water.

#7860. Step Up Your Game With a DIY Folding Step Stool

This weekend project walks you through every cut and joint to make a foldable step stool you’ll actually use every day.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Turn leftover hardwood scraps into a rock-solid folding step stool that puts wobbly plastic versions to shame.

At some point in our lives we will need a folding step stool. You know, the one that stays out of the way but, gives you that little extra boost when you don’t need a full step ladder. In my case, I find myself reaching for a step stool more often than I’d like to admit especially when trying to reach into a work truck. When I need something, I prefer to make it and am happy to share the steps with you. Just because it is small doesn’t mean it isn’t as satisfying to make – enjoy!

On the miter saw and/or table saw, cut the top step (A), all four legs (B), the guides (C), ad the bottom crossbrace (E). Set aside everything but the legs (B) until later.

Using a compass with a pencil, draw 1-1/2-inch diameter half-circles at the bottom of each leg (B) to match the 1/2-inch width of the leg.

Use a disc or belt sander with a coarse-grit sandpaper (80 or 100-grit) to shape the ends of the legs by sanding up to the marked pencil lines for your arch. Once you have sanded to the line, work your way up to 220-grit sandpaper for a smoother finish.

Using a router table or a router equipped with a 1/4-inch round-over bit, round over all the edges of the step (A) and all four legs (B). Be sure to use clamps to hold the pieces while making your passes with the router.

With all the parts machined, sand all the components to 220 grit and apply a couple of coats of a wood finish of your choice. Allow the finish to dry before moving on to assembly.

Spread wood glue in hole 3 at the top of each inside leg (B). Insert the ends of the 3/4-in. dowel cross brace (D) and tap the legs on with a rubber mallet until D is fully seated.

Set the 1-1/4-in.-square cross brace (E) between the bottoms of the legs, with its bottom edge 2-1/8 in. up from the bottom of the legs. To keep the legs parallel while you drill, clamp a scrap the same length as the cross brace (E) between them at mid-height. Check for square.

Using hole 4 in each leg as a guide, drill a 1/2-in. hole about 1 in. deep into the center of each end of the cross brace (E). Glue 1/2-in. dowels, cut longer than the holes are deep, and drive them through the legs with a mallet until they bottom out in the cross brace (E).

Lock each of the four joints with a single brad nail through the leg into the dowel. Trim the protruding ends of all the dowels flush with a pull saw.

Flip the top step (A) upside down. Position the guide rails (C) 1/2-in. in from each side and centered front to back, leaving 1-1/2-in. at the front and back. Trace around each rail.

Drill two 1/4-in. holes, 3/4-in. deep, centered on each outline. Keep the bit plumb when drilling (or drill at the drill press).

Insert dowel centers in the holes. Align each rail with its outline and press down to mark the hole locations. Drill matching 1/4-in. holes in the rails, about 7/8-in. deep. That’s slightly deeper than the dowel needs, which leaves room for glue.

Glue and insert 1/4-in x 1-1/2-in. dowels and secure the guide rails (C) to the step (A).

Thread 1/4-inch x 3-1/2-inch carriage bolts through hole 1 in the center of the legs to connect an outside leg to the outside of each of the connected inside legs. Put a washer between each pair of legs and secure with a nylon lock nut on the inside of the inside legs.

Connect the two outside legs (B) to the sides of the guide rails (C) by threading 1/4-inch x 2-1/2-inch pan head screws through hole 5 in the guide rails and through hole 2 on the outside legs. Use a washer on the outside of the guide rails and pliers to hold the nylon lock nuts while you tighten them into the 5/8-inch countersunk holes.

The strap acts as a stop, limiting how far the legs can open. Wrap one end of an upholstery strap around the middle of the top cross brace (D) and staple it in place with a narrow-crown stapler. Open the stool until the seat sits level, then pull the strap snug and staple the other end centered on the underside of the top step (A). Use several 1/2-in. staples at each end so the strap holds securely.

A step stool should be about 11 to 16-in. wide to fit both feet comfortably side by side. For a portable or compact version, stay toward the narrow end of that range.

A single-step stool should be 6 to 9-in. tall. That’s a good height for reaching into a truck bed, helping kids reach a tall bathroom sink, or getting to the top pantry shelves.

#7857. 12 Defendants Indicted for Threats Aimed at Causing University of Michigan and Others to Sever Ties with Israel

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Some excerpts from the long First Superseding Indictment in U.S. v. Hakim (E.D. Mich.), filed Oct. 21, alleging conspiracy to transmit threats in interstate commerce as well as, for two defendants, witness intimidation and destruction of property to prevent seizure (8 of the 12 defendants had originally been indicted in May); the targets included UM officials and businesses connected with them, as well as the Jewish Federation of Metropolitan Detroit:

The defendants are a group of individuals associated with the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor. After the October 7, 2023, Hamas terrorist attacks on Israel, the defendants and unindicted conspirators orchestrated detailed plans to threaten University of Michigan leaders, law enforcement, and businesses with coordinated criminal acts. Their goal included forcing the University of Michigan and other businesses to sever all perceived ties with the State of Israel.

To accomplish this goal, the defendants and their unindicted conspirators, in the Eastern District of Michigan and elsewhere, used encrypted messages, social media, and overseas collaboration platforms to research, target, and attack their victims. Then, they posted pictures of their attacks on social media, along with additional threats and warnings. Their criminal activity included spray painting threats, breaking windows, and throwing glass jars filled with noxious chemicals into family homes. They marked their victims with threatening symbols used by Hamas, including red inverted triangles and red handprints. They used the internet and social media to broadcast their message to ensure their threats and commitment to continuing criminal activity were heard by their victims and others who support Israel….

The defendants and unindicted conspirators coordinated and planned their criminal activity, targeting selected victims using encrypted online group chats, websites, "teach ins" (seminars designed to encourage action), and other meetings. They also initiated an online campaign against their targets by using social media platforms (Twitter/X and lnstagram) that were, at times, connected to student groups at the University of Michigan, including the former Students Allied for Freedom and Equality (SAFE) (University of Michigan's chapter of "Justice in Palestine") and the TAHRIR Coalition.

On or about October 20, 2023, the defendants and unindicted conspirators publicly posted a list of demands on social media directed at University of Michigan leadership. Among other demands, they required the University to make a "full and complete divestment" from the State of Israel and any business supporting the State of Israel. Unsatisfied by the University's response, the defendants and unindicted conspirators "prepared to take action" against the leadership by what they called "autonomous actions." Some of those "autonomous actions" included, but were not limited to, forcibly entering and occupying University of Michigan buildings, defacing buildings, and blocking and disrupting events on campus. The defendants and their unindicted conspirators also posted threats on the internet that included photos of their "autonomous actions." …

On or about May 2024, the defendants and unindicted conspirators participated in a "Gaza Solidarity Encampment" at the University of Michigan. Local police documented twenty-six criminal incidents directly related to the encampment. During the encampment, the defendants and unindicted conspirators used the internet to warn their opposition that "we look to our martyrs and freedom fighters for guidance … the student intifada will never be silenced." The defendants aspired to achieve the acclaim of the 1960s domestic terrorist organization "Weather Underground."

When the University shut down the encampment, the defendants and unindicted conspirators turned to individual targets for their criminal "autonomous actions." The defendants and unindicted conspirators held meetings where they collaborated to identify various specific targets of their "autonomous actions." The targets included University of Michigan leadership, businesses, and anyone they believed supported—directly or indirectly—the State of Israel.

The defendants and unindicted conspirators used the internet to research personal addresses, photographs, political and social connections, business ownership, and other personal details. They performed surveillance on their targets and counter-surveillance on law enforcement. They discussed methods by which to harm their targets and their families, including poison, bombs, and psychological torture. For example, on or about May 21, 2024, D-3 PAIGE ELIZABETH FEYOCK and D-4 AHMET KEREM KORKAYA (a medical student at the time) exchanged the following messages in which they agreed to "kill," "torment," and "terrorize" their targets:

KORKAYA: we are finding [V-4]'s address if we don't have it already [so I can] drive my car into it.

KORKAYA: [V-4]'s entire family is now on my hit list.

FEYOCK: Let's get [V-4's] kids bruh / and [V-2's] too.

KORKAYA: wallah [by God] paige i wanna do something/ the only way to clear my conscious [sic].

KORKAYA: wallah [by God] I'm gonna be the dirtiest fucking doctor ever/ I'm gonna be [V-l]'s doctor /poison her ass slowly.

FEYOCK: (agreeing) We need people following [V-1]/ get into that house then bum it down.

From approximately October 2023 through and including April 2025, the defendants and unindicted conspirators targeted individuals and businesses in the Eastern District of Michigan and elsewhere, including: The University of Michigan's President, Chief lnvestment Officer, Provost, and members of the Board of Regents and their businesses; a University of Michigan police officer; Rolls Royce Solutions America, Inc.; Maersk, Inc.; and the Jewish Federation of Metropolitan Detroit.

The defendants and unindicted conspirators recruited participants to engage with them in their "autonomous actions." Their planning efforts included purchasing supplies, meeting to coordinate and distribute supplies, mapping routes, performing surveillance, and using internet-based collaboration tools to draft threats to their targets.

As part of the conspiracy, the defendants and unindicted conspirators traveled at night to the targeted homes and businesses. They damaged and defaced homes and businesses with spray painted messages, threats, and symbols, including inverted triangles, red handprints, and phrases such as "INTIFADA" and "DIVEST NOW." The defendants and unindicted conspirators also left demand notes containing additional threats, caulked doors shut, bike-locked entryways, broke windows, and threw glass jars filled with butyric acid and dye into the targeted homes.

The defendants and unindicted conspirators took photographs of the destruction and posted the photos online with "official statements" and additional warnings and threats such as "you cannot hide" and "we only come back stronger." …

On or about April 7, 2024, through on or about April 18, 2024, D-2 AMATULLAH ALIASGAR HAKIM, D-3 PAIGE ELIZABETH FEYOCK, Unindicted Co-conspirator One (UCC-1 ), and others used CryptPad.fr to create a meeting agenda that included "targeting the Board of Regents." The plan called for "[m]ore deep-diving on all of regents." Under "House visits," the notes warned: "Be cautious about timing - middle of the night might appear more threatening."

On or about May 15, 2024, at approximately 5:53 a.m., conspirators and others trespassed on [V-1 's] house in the Western District of Michigan. They littered the yard and porch with small tents, sheets wrapped to look like dead bodies, dismembered and bloody baby dolls, and a broken crib. They taped a demand note to the front door ordering, among other things, that the University of Michigan divest from Israel….

On or about June 3, 2024, at approximately 1:38 a.m., D-1 ZAINAB ALIASGAR HAKlM, D-2 AMATULLAH ALIASGAR HAKlM, and other conspirators vandalized V-2's law firm in the Eastern District of Michigan by throwing red paint balloons at the building and leaving imprinted red painted handprints on the windows. They spraypainted messages on the building and sidewalk:

DIVEST OR FUCK OFF FREE PALESTINE UM KILLS FUCK YOU [V-2's last name] DIVEST NOW

On or about October 7, 2024, at approximately 4:20 a.m., D-1 ZAINAB ALIASGAR HAKIM, D-2 AMATULLAH ALIASGAR HAKIM, D-4 AHMET KEREM KORKAYA, D-5 JONATHAN HONGRU ZOU, and other conspirators vandalized the Jewish Federation of Metropolitan Detroit in the Eastern District of Michigan by spray painting inverted red triangles on the sidewalk and building and painting over surveillance cameras. They spraypainted messages on the building and sidewalk:

On or about March 15, 2025, Unindicted Co-conspirator Seven (UCC-7) provided D-5 JONATHAN HONGRU ZOU and D-6 ALEXANDER MATTHEW SEPULVEDA with a vehicle to drive to V-7's [the University of Michigan Provost's] house in the Eastern District of Michigan, where they, along with conspirators, smashed a large window by throwing two glass jars containing an unknown blue substance and food compost at it, one of which landed in a bedroom of V-7's house. They also spraypainted V-7's house with inverted red triangles and the words:

DIVEST FREE PALESTINE NO HONOR IN GENOCIDE

#7856. What Is “Heart Attack Snow,” and Why Is It So Dangerous?

Heavy, wet snow can turn an ordinary winter chore into a health risk. Learn why people call it heart attack snow and how to shovel safely.

Shoveling snow can be a dangerous winter chore. Icy walkways can cause serious falls, and prolonged exposure to the cold can lead to hypothermia or frostbite. Another safety concern is something called “heart attack snow.”

The name sounds dramatic, but it points to a real concern for people clearing sidewalks and driveways in winter. For those in snowy climates, understanding the risks of heart attack snow is important before picking up a shovel.

Understanding the risks can help prevent a routine chore from becoming a medical emergency.

Heart attack snow is a nickname for heavy, wet snow that’s harder to shovel than dry, powdery snow. The name comes from the strain that lifting this type of snow can place on the heart. According to the National Weather Service, snow with a higher water content weighs more, making each shovelful harder to lift.

The added effort can quickly raise heart rate and blood pressure. Cold temperatures also cause blood vessels to narrow, making the heart work harder. The American Heart Association warns that this combination can trigger a heart attack or sudden cardiac arrest.

The association says the risks are especially concerning for “people who already have cardiovascular risks like a sedentary lifestyle or obesity,” including those with a history of smoking, diabetes, high cholesterol, or high blood pressure. People who have previously suffered a heart attack or stroke also face greater risks.

Even lighter, powdery snow can be dangerous, especially when large amounts require repeated lifting or hours of clearing.

Before heading outside, people should warm up indoors and stretch gently. Dressing in layers helps protect against the cold, while staying hydrated is important even when someone doesn’t feel thirsty.

The American Heart Association recommends pushing snow rather than lifting it whenever possible. When lifting is necessary, smaller loads and frequent breaks can help limit physical strain. A snow blower can also reduce the amount of lifting, although operating one still requires effort.

Slippery surfaces are another concern. “Walking on ice is extremely dangerous,” according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The agency recommends using rock salt or another de-icing product to keep walkways clear of ice. Sand can also help prevent slipping.

People with heart disease or significant cardiovascular risk factors should have someone else handle snow removal, according to the American Heart Association.

Recognizing the warning signs of a heart attack is equally important. Chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath, dizziness, nausea, cold sweats, or discomfort in the arms, back, or jaw can all signal a serious problem. Symptoms aren’t always severe and can vary from person to person.

Anyone experiencing possible heart attack symptoms should stop shoveling immediately and call 911. The American Heart Association advises against waiting to see whether symptoms go away.

American Heart Association, “Snow Shoveling, Cold Temperatures Combine for Perfect Storm of Heart Health Hazards” American Heart Association, “Warning Signs of a Heart Attack” National Weather Service, “Winter Weather Preparedness” Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, “Safety Guidelines: During & After a Winter Storm”

#7855. We Are Underlings

In line with my belief that it’s important to always keep the resumé fresh, I signed up for first aid training six months ago and the first class is today. The Nine Circles exalts dying and death, but not for guests. Plus, most of us sit for nine hours a day and eat greasy meals at lunch, putting us at risk for croaking in our cubicles. A knowledge of first aid does not help me do my back-of-house job better, though if a colleague has a heart attack at work, I’ll be able to perform cpr while waiting for the paramedics to arrive. Even though we’ll be taking an exam during the final class, I’m treating these training sessions as a vacation from my desk. The best part is that Charles and Charlotte are also taking the course; he’s doing it because he cares about the welfare of other employees and she’s doing it because she’ll be on park grounds from time to time working on the new attractions.

Three months ago, Human Resources sorted everyone with a Chinese surname into the Cantonese training sessions without first checking whether we could read or write the language. HR’s mandate seems to be cart before horse. Although it was embarrassing to admit that I was illiterate except for menus and select street signs, I reported that my understanding of body part names and medical terminology was limited to English. (What’s the word for spleen in Cantonese? I still don’t know.) Human Resources Associate Gallant Sum instructed me to take the course on evenings and weekends at a community centre with our expat colleagues—the Nine Circles would still pay the fees, he assured me, but the company would not consider these thirty hours as overtime. But then it turned out that the executive team wanted some of the bilingual Hong Kong staff members to take the course in English to better serve international guests and vips, so Human Resources had to scramble to implement these classes on top of the final push to hire an additional hundred people to round out the team.

Charles and Charlotte are already in the meeting room when I arrive at 9:12 a.m., the official start time at the Nine Circles.

“Is this an actual first aid training session or a mass firing?” Charlotte asks, as she scans the room to see which colleagues are present.

“My tour with Pamela Poon, Raymond Shek, and Jade Chen Church went pretty poorly yesterday, so I can imagine why I’d be fired,” I say.

“I’m sure it wasn’t as bad as you think,” Charlotte says.

“Well, I didn’t make any serial killer jokes this time,” I say. Then I’m relieved to spot the Secretary to the Head of Project Delivery. “Helen Chan’s here, and I don’t think they would fire any of the secretaries. Everything would come to a stop if even one was terminated.”

“She’s pretty essential to the park opening on time,” Charles says. “Remember when she went on vacation?” When Helen took her annual leave to get married and go on her honeymoon, the paperwork for the air filtration system for the Afterlife lab went missing and Project Delivery started construction without understanding that the omission of this system violated building code. Charlotte spotted the error and reported it to the executive team and managerial staff. She noted that without air filtration it would be unsafe to display some of our most famous corpses. No one listened to her because she’s not head of her department. The Chaplins and I discovered, during an investigation that we conducted on our own time, that a Project Delivery manager had buried the paperwork to save money, but his gamble resulted in a million-dollar mistake. For reasons unknown, that manager still has a job at the Nine Circles, and somehow Helen got written up for this incident despite eight underlings reporting to the executive team that it was not her fault.

I have one of the jobs that is considered nonessential. I don’t fetch coffee or set up conference calls or schedule important meetings or handle corpses.

What I don’t say is that out of everyone in the training room, most of whom are junior staff from Administration, I have one of the jobs that is considered nonessential. I don’t fetch coffee or set up conference calls or schedule important meetings or handle corpses. No one up on aside from the Executive Director seems to understand that marketing is necessary to get paying guests through the turnstiles. Mirabella Lam, Educational Programmes Manager, believes that the high quality of her programming is enough to draw a crowd and insists that trying to attract attention is crass.

“But how will the public know about your projects if we don’t spread the word?” I once asked Mirabella during an all-team meeting. “We do good work,” she said, directing her comment toward the Executive Director. The ceo, Dalton Northcott, was not in attendance that day, or Mirabella would have addressed him instead. One can sum up Mirabella’s work philosophy as “managing up.” I later discovered I’d made a sworn enemy with my well-meaning query. Mirabella is employee ten, so even though she doesn’t outrank most of us in terms of the org chart, she wields her seniority as a sort of authority.

Many underlings have never met the ceo. With his travel schedule, he’s rarely at the Hong Kong offices. Early on, when the team was smaller, I met Dalton at the groundbreaking ceremony and asked him how to keep my houseplants alive—I’d read that he had a PhD in botany and an impressive orchid collection. His response was warm and engaging, yet I could sense he had boundaries in place that prevented the interaction from becoming overfamiliar. This gave me a false sense of safety—I believed the ceo was a leader I could trust.

The first aid teacher arrives and does not introduce himself. Instead, he says, “Where are we going to eat lunch?” Then he wipes his sweaty forehead with a faded pink towel.

There’s a ten-second silence that feels like an eternity. Many of the participants in this training session are under twenty-five and are too shy to make eye contact when they do their rounds with the mail or set up a projector for meetings. There is no way any of us are going to give up our lunch hour of rest (or work catch-up) to entertain our first aid teacher, but we have to figure out a diplomatic way to communicate this information.

“Most of us brought our lunches,” says Charlotte.

“There’s a food court downstairs in the mall, as well as a supermarket,” I say. We were supposed to have moved into the offices built on park grounds six months ago, but the sprinkler system keeps going off and no one can figure out how to fix it, so now they’re pulling out the entire thing and reinstalling it and most of us are still in our rented office space in the mall. On the way in every morning, I pass Celine, Chanel, and Louis Vuitton and see the salespeople lovingly dusting handbags that cost more than my monthly salary.

The teacher looks disappointed. Did he imagine we’d want to discuss the finer points of guts and gore while eating dumplings? When it’s clear no one is going to invite him to lunch, he opens his PowerPoint presentation. The first slide features a grainy black-and-white scan from a newspaper.

“What’s happening here?” he shouts. None of us can figure out what’s depicted in the image.

The blobs could be a cat playing the piano. “Come on!” he says. “What would you do if you came across this accident?”

“The photo is a bit on the blurry side,” says Charles, ever polite.

“Common sense! First thing at a scene, no illegal touch!” says the teacher.

I wonder if he’s had complaints against him while administering cpr. I don’t remember any instruction about illegal touch from my previous first aid training sessions in Canada. Icarus Sun from Administration, whose clothes always look shrunken in a cool streetwear way, is taking notes. I wonder if he’s writing Do not molest the injured person.

The room is airless, making me sluggish. I yawn and unzip my jacket. “Wah,” says the teacher, switching to Cantonese. His eyes are on my tits. “I thought you were going to take it all off.”

I zip my jacket back up. Charlotte and I look at each other. “What a perv,” she whispers. No one else in the room seems to have noticed what has happened, not even the Human Resources Associate who is observing the session to ensure everything goes smoothly, so I let it pass. “In a few weeks, I will introduce you to a beautiful lady for cpr,” the teacher says. “Her name is Annie.” Icarus is still taking notes. CPR on beautiful lady! “But what’s going on in the slide?” asks Charlotte.

“You will understand when you meet the beautiful lady!” the first aid teacher says with a wide smile on his face. As the minutes pass like snails trying to cross a freeway during rush hour, I think about all the unanswered emails in my inbox and slip into a dissociative state.

#7854. U.S. Government Contractor Arrested for Allegedly Leaking National Defense Information

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

A U.S. government contractor was arrested by the FBI this morning for allegedly leaking national defense information to another individual who repeatedly posted classified information to an online publication.

“National defense information is classified to protect the American people from bad actors around the world who wish to do us harm,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “The details alleged in this affidavit reflect the behavior of a government contractor who exempted himself from a federal law governing the protection of classified information. The Department of Justice will continue prosecuting individuals who leak classified information and put our national security at risk.”

“The FBI arrested the subject after he was caught allegedly betraying his oath and leaking classified defense information,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “Protecting America’s secrets is a top counterintelligence priority of this FBI - and anyone caught abusing their position of trust within the government by jeopardizing national security and putting our brave warriors at risk will be met with the full weight of justice.”

“Following a referral from the Agency, on Friday, October 23rd, the FBI arrested a contractor who provided services to CIA for alleged unauthorized disclosures of classified information,” said CIA Director John Ratcliffe. “The unauthorized release of classified material poses grave risks to our national security, intelligence sources, ongoing operations, and our officers. There is absolutely zero tolerance for leaking, and anyone who violates their oath will be held accountable and prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”

“As alleged, Brinksman reached far outside his own duties to obtain some of our Nation’s most closely held secrets and handed them to a romantic partner he knew intended to publish them,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “That is not carelessness. It is a betrayal of his oath and the American people who entrusted him to fulfill his duties honorably. Those cleared to hold our Nation's secrets undertake a solemn obligation to protect that information. If proven at trial, this conduct is a grave violation of the Espionage Act, and the National Security Division will prosecute it as such.”

Ian A. Brinksman, 42, of the District of Columbia was arrested following a search of his residence and charged by criminal complaint with unlawfully transmitting national defense information.

According to the criminal complaint, beginning in 2020, the defendant worked as an employee of a U.S. government agency based in the Eastern District of Virginia and later in 2022 began working as a developer for systems integration for “Company 1,” a contractor to the same U.S. government agency. During all times relevant to the complaint, Brinksman held a Top Secret security clearance with Sensitive Compartmented Information (SCI) access.

As further detailed in the complaint, Brinksman had an ongoing personal relationship with an individual who maintains an online publication on Substack (Individual 1). A fundraising article reportedly published by Individual 1 in September 2026 claimed Individual 1 had “published reporting based on classified [relevant U.S. government agency] assessments.” Individual 1 posted on her social media profile, “I also accept leaks.”

The FBI Chicago Field Office is investigating the case with substantial assistance from the Washington Field Office.

Trial Attorneys Eli Ross and Kathryn DeMarco of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Vito Iaia for the Eastern District of Virginia are prosecuting the case, with valuable assistance from Assistant U.S. Attorneys Tejpal Chawla and Stuart Allen for the District of Columbia.

Charges in a complaint are merely allegations, and every defendant is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

#7853. Federal Court Rejects Trump Lawsuit Seeking to Block Certification of Alaska Senate Election Results

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The court found the administration lacked standing to bring the suit. But there are also major substantive problems with Trump's position.

Today, in United States v. Alaska, federal district Judge Sharon Gleason ruled against the Trump administration's lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska Senate election results on the grounds that doing so might be necessary to prevent "voter confusion" caused by the presence of two candidates with very similar names on the ballot. As I have explained previously, Dan J. Sullivan can potentially be confused with Dan S. Sullivan (the incumbent GOP senator). Evidence gathered by the New York Times suggests Democrats may have deliberately recruited Dan J. to run, in hopes of siphoning off votes from Dan S. on this topic.

Today's ruling dismisses the Trump lawsuit on the grounds that the United States lacked standing to bring the suit. Most notably, it failed the standing requirement of "redressability." The remedy requested by the administration - blocking certification until the federal government could further "investigate" the issue, would not actually redress the harm of voter confusion, and certainly could not do so while maintaining legally required secrecy of the ballots. In addition, Judge Gleason emphasizes that the federal government's proposed remedy would likely intrude on the powers of the state government,  create more voter "confusion" than it forestalls:

The Supreme Court "has repeatedly emphasized that lower federal courts should ordinarily not alter the election rules on the eve of an election…" "Such late-breaking, court-ordered rule changes can 'result in voter confusion and consequent incentive to remain away from the polls,' and thus undermine the '[c]onfidence in the integrity of our electoral processes . . . essential to the functioning of our participatory democracy.'"

The United States maintains that it is "not seeking to alter the time, place, or manner of Alaska's election" [which the Constitution generally leaves under state control]. And yet it seeks a court order preventing the State from certifying the election if certain circumstances occur; a court order requiring the State to segregate and preserve certain ballots; and a court order permitting the United States to conduct an investigation into the intent of those voters who cast ballots for Daniel J. Sullivan. These requests certainly involve the time, place, and manner of Alaska's election, which are the responsibilities of the State, not the executive branch of the federal government. Clearly, if this Court were to order that certain ballots will be segregated and subject to a future and as yet unspecified investigation by law enforcement, it would likely result in voter "confusion and consequent incentive to remain away from the polls."Such late-breaking changes to the election rules are strongly disfavored.

In addition to these procedural problems with the Trump lawsuit, it also deserves to be rejected on the substantive merits. I covered some of the reasons why here and here. See also the excellent amicus brief filed by prominent election law scholar Rick Hasen, which goes into these issues in greater detail. Quite simply, there is no federal law giving the administration the power to block certification of election results based on "voter confusion."

As explained in one of my earlier posts about this case, Democrats deserve blame for seeking to deceive voters in this way, even though it is highly unlikely it would cause enough confusion to change the outcome of the election (various aspects of the Alaska ballot and election system reduce the already low odds of that happening). But for reasons summarized in the same post, this kind of thing is far from the worst example of exploitation of voter ignorance. Lies and deceptions about public policy issues are far more significant.

Today's decision may be appealed. But I think it highly unlikely that the appellate court (or the US Supreme Court) will reverse it.

NEXT: 12 Defendants Indicted for Threats Aimed at Causing University of Michigan and Others to Sever Ties with Israel

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.

#7852. Debra Webb and Allison Brennan on villains, suspense, and writing standalone thrillers

USA Today Bestselling author Debra Webb began her career writing romantic suspense but by the early 2000s had started to lean into darker suspense. A few years later she was fully immersed in the world of thrillers. It was at the very first International Thriller Writers conference in Phoenix, Arizona where she met Allison Brennan.

Flash forward twenty years and Debra’s first standalone thriller, The Woman I’ve Become, is slated for October of this year. Longtime friend and fellow author Allison Brennan was one of the first to read the upcoming release and called it a “page-turning thriller!”

New York Times Bestselling author Allison Brennan also began her career writing romantic suspense for Ballantine Books, but in 2011 launched the Lucy Kincaid FBI thriller series. Now she has two series—the Quinn & Costa FBI thrillers, and the Angelhart Investigations PI series—and writes the occasional stand alone. Whisper Creek is her third standalone thriller, out in June. Allison is thrilled that the amazing Debra Webb is stepping into the standalone world.

Allison Brennan: I can’t believe it’s been twenty years. Twenty! Talk about feeling my age.

Debra Webb: No kidding! But I have to say it has been an amazing ride! The best part is we’re both still doing what we love–writing books!

AB: I absolutely loved The Woman I’ve Become. I honestly didn’t realize it was your first standalone! You’ve written a gazillion books. Haha. Why this one? What gave you that itch to write this book with this heroine?

DW: Thank you so much. It was time to do something different. I’ve always written stories with an eye toward what comes next for these characters. I love working with a large cast of characters, providing lots of options for moving forward with the next chapter in one or the other’s life.

DW: But when this story idea first sprouted, it was all about this one woman and the secrets she used like stones to build a life. As the story developed it became about how the story would end. How you battle your demons when they find you and they always do. Really, at its core this one is about survival and how this story would end. In fact, that was the working title, How This Ends.

I’m of the opinion that characters are the heart of our stories, yours and mine. Your newest release, Whisper Creek, is a perfect example of characters being the heart of a very twisted drama! What creative spark brought these characters into such a twisted and dangerous situation. I love, by the way, how you developed two distinct threats!

AB: Story is ultimately about character. Without character, it’s just a cool plot. The people make it a story worth reading.

AB: I’m sure you know this better than most writers, but writing isn’t easy. No book is “easy” to write. But some books are easier than others, where the story flows chapter by chapter and you, as the author, are whisked away while you write. For me, that book is Whisper Creek. While I had to do a lot of research about farming, northeast Texas, and storms, the story itself practically wrote itself. As for the creative spark, it was basically just “what if”—what if the bad guys are caught in a storm and can’t get away? And while that is an important part of the plot, the story is really about the McKenna family trying to save the farm against both man and Mother Nature.

DW: Your readers are going to love it! Research is so important in what we do. Although we write fiction, it’s crucial that we get things right–or at least believable.

AB: Agreed! Though research is also my favorite form of procrastination, haha.

DW: The storm in your story is such a unique element. It’s difficult to fight Mother Nature lol. Perhaps even harder to outsmart her. Do you have a favorite element you’ve used to thrust your characters into the middle of danger?

AB: Whatever works for the story. In Whisper Creek, I needed a storm in an area that was prone to flooding. I needed my characters to be cut off from the outside world in a realistic way. The last “wilderness thriller” (that’s what my editor calls these books, where setting and weather are an integral part of the story) was set during a snow storm. The next (I’m writing now!) is set in the Bob Marshall Wilderness in Montana. Not during a storm, but it’s a rugged and unforgiving landscape. But I love any type of story where the danger is organic to the plot!

DW: Your “wilderness” thrillers do sound awesome! And yes, it’s always better if the danger is organic. In The Woman I’ve Become, I ushered the characters from the city, Manhattan, to the place where the trouble started so many years before—Westport, Connecticut. It was a homecoming of sorts. Going back to where it all began. Sometimes it’s the going back to that place where the damage was done that builds the tension and fear best. But it also increases the danger in this story because there is the element of isolation at the family lake house.

Primarily it felt right for the characters to face-off in the place where it all started. When a story “feels right” the flow is smoother. As you say no story is “easy” to write but it sure helps when it flows the way you had hoped!

AB: I don’t think “normal” people (i.e. – not writers!) understand when we say it “feels” right, LOL. But that’s exactly how I think as well! We know intuitively when the story is working and when it’s not. Here’s a question I get a lot and I never have a good answer. How do you know when a story will make a good series and when it is really a stand alone? How did you know with The Woman I’ve Become? I usually say, “It’s about the characters” but that doesn’t feel complete enough.

DW: Wow! What a great question and also a difficult one to answer. Again, I believe it’s in part the “feeling” of wanting or needing to continue with the element that makes the series whether it’s the setting or the characters (really, usually the characters). I’ve written lots of series.

One of my favorites is the Faces of Evil series. That one I knew right from the moment the spark came that it would be a series. When Julia and Wendy from The Woman I’ve Become started to speak to me, I knew their story would be a stand alone. I understood that whatever happened, I needed to finish this thing that began between them decades before. It felt, as we’ve discussed, right.

AB: We have to trust our guts. Most of my series I create as a series. Either a police procedural where readers often expect characters to grow over time. For the Quinn & Costa series, I wanted to take my core group but move them around the country so they didn’t investigate in one place. For my Angelhart series, I wanted to focus more on family (a family of P.I.s) so set the book in Phoenix. Again, it just felt right!

Plus, I think with standalones, the characters aren’t usually in a position to have multiple crimes or mysteries in their life. This one “thing” that is happening IS their mystery, if that makes sense.

DW: You are spot ont! Which leads to another point that folks who aren’t writers sometimes don’t understand. When we’re developing a story idea (whether born of a plot element or a character), the synopsis or plan for the story ALWAYS changes because, believe it or not, the characters take the lead.

With every story I’ve written, it starts out as the story I want to tell but about a hundred pages in it becomes the story the characters need to tell. There’s this connection to the characters you’ve created that takes over, don’t you think?

AB: Hundred percent. I have never stuck to a synopsis; I don’t plot. People often don’t believe me, but it’s true. Usually my synopsis is all backstory. I know where the characters are when the story starts and why, but everything after the inciting incident changes as I write. The story feels more organic and natural that way.

But mostly, it’s the only way I can write. After fifty-two books, I don’t really want to mess with that (mostly) works! And yes, I know you have twice as many books as me!

DW: Yes! We are alike in that! My synopsis is basically back story as well. I often wonder if the editor thinks “I don’t remember that from the synopsis.” The characters lead and that’s the best way to tell a story. Once you know those characters you can trust them completely. They know where they need to go!

AB: Yes, exactly! And I find that I have to edit the first hundred pages a lot more than the last three hundred when I’m done with my first draft.

DW: Same here! Getting back to the research, I sometimes wonder if you and I were perhaps cops or PIs in another life. We so love the police procedural aspect of our stories. I catch myself when watching television (series and the news) anticipating what the cops will do next.

AB: I have loved mysteries and cop shows from early childhood. I grew up on Trixie Belden and Nancy Drew and my mom and I would watch Hill Street Blues, she let me stay up late to watch it! I’ve done several ride alongs with local police, participated in the FBI citizens academy, toured Quantico, viewed an autopsy, and more.

Now I have people I can call when I need information (including my daughter, who is a Phoenix PD officer!) I’ve found when I’m writing my standalones, where there is no law enforcement or it’s on the edge of the story, that I have to really think more about what an average person without training would do in these situations.

DW: Those are amazing resources and certainly adds to the realistic feel of writing from the perspective of the police or a private investigator. We share the love of those childhood stories and some of the best cop shows ever! But we’re both also very good at creating villains. Those shoes are a little tougher to step into when writing depraved killers. How do you do your research for those characters?

AB: I have a workshop called “The Villain’s Journey” taken in part from Christopher Vogler’s “The Writer’s Journey.” Basically, the villain is the hero of his own journey. That means he has clear (even if he’s crazy) motivations, goals, and conflicts. Why is he the way he is?

And not all villains are depraved. Some just do bad things. I need to know WHY. Once I know that, I can write them. Also, I remember that (usually) not all villains are a hundred percent evil. There needs to be at least one redeeming characteristic, something that makes them more human to readers. But sometimes the evil villains are the most fun to write! LOL.

DW: Every writer should go to your workshop on Villains. It is so true that we have to remember that the villains are people too. And, as you say, not all are depraved. There are levels of evil and each villain must have a reason they are the way they are… one that made them who they are. That background and motivation is as important for the villain as it is for any other character.

And the redeeming characteristic is absolutely essential. The human side of a villain is what draws the reader to him or her even when they don’t want to be drawn. I love how perfectly you defined exactly how to create the perfect villain!

Which brings me to the “bad thing.” The incident, the reason the characters must do what they do. Where does your inspiration for that important story element come from?

AB: I have no idea. I’m not being flip! Usually there are several little ideas that come together that give me that AHA! moment. For the Quinn & Costa series, I wanted a mobile FBI unit loosely based on the real-life Evidence Response Team. I only knew one of the characters when I started, and Kara Quinn wasn’t supposed to be a series character, but took over book one. (Then I had to figure out how to have an LAPD detective on the team permanently!)

For Whisper Creek I knew there was going to be a storm, and I knew that there were bad guys trapped in the storm. I knew the mother of the ranch (a widow), but the four kids all sort of developed as I wrote them. And there was no grandma in the synopsis that I pitched my editor, but she really makes the book.

And I didn’t know that the cat who escaped the barn in the prologue would become such an important part of the story! Have you ever had characters who you didn’t think would be important become pivotal to one of your books?

DW: Like you, I can seldom explain where the trouble comes from in a story as I’m beginning. More often than not I have a character who is in a situation and I build from there: what happened before and what happens after. Occasionally I know, as I did, in part, with my Vera Boyett series. I knew there were human remains in the cave and that the two older sisters had put them there. All the rest came as I wrote the story.

And, yes, those characters, human or animal, who turn into stars are so fun. In The Woman I’ve Become it’s the lakehouse caretaker. She’s so feisty! She evolved into such a great character.

AB: She was absolutely one of my favorites! I’m so glad I got to read an early copy of The Woman I’ve Become.

DW: It really has been such a pleasure talking about writing with you, Allison. Before we go, I’d love to give readers a glimpse into our everyday lives. What’s an average day for you?

AB: My writing life has changed over the years. When my kids were little, I was actually far more productive. I knew I HAD to write when they were in school because once they got home we had sports, homework, theater, and all the stuff that comes with raising a big family. Now, my youngest is twenty-one and I have all the time in the world…so I tend to procrastinate, haha.

But, generally, I wake up around 5 in the morning, go for my morning walk, have coffee and play word games, then sit at my computer from about 7-8 to respond to email, post on social media, etc. Then I have breakfast, and by 9, I start writing. I try to get up to walk and stretch a couple of times, but often forget. By 4 I’m brain dead and call it quits, whether I’ve written 500 words or 5,000 words. I used to write at night, but I don’t have the bandwidth anymore. (Unless I am near the end of a book and am super excited…even now, I’ve been known to write into the wee hours of the morning once or twice a month!)

I also now have a grandson! I babysit him once a week, so that’s my “day off.”

What about you? How do you write and what has changed over the years?

DW: You are amazing! Had to say that! My writing life is similar to yours! And I agree that it was far more structured back when I had school age kiddos. These days I’m up between five and six (sometimes earlier if I’m excited to get started).

I don’t do anything except make coffee before writing. It’s easier for me if I don’t let the world in first. I just dive in and do all the other stuff, social media, emails, etc., later. I write until I reach the point I wanted to reach that day (sometimes a few pages, sometimes a whole chapter). Then I do all the other stuff that life requires.

I also do the fun stuff. You know how I love renovating houses and treasure hunting at junk stores. Nowadays I’m pretty big into gardening, flower and vegetable, and there are the goats and chickens. DW: I am sure your beautiful children will be giving you lots of grandbabies in the future! Ah, what’s next? First, I will write as they say until they pry my cold, dead fingers from the keyboard! I’m working on a new cop series, Flynn & Beckett, for Thomas & Mercer and then comes my next standalone. Before we go, please tell us what’s coming next for you!

AB: I’m with you—I’ll always write. I can’t imagine retiring. I’m definitely looking forward to your new series! DW: You are amazing, Allison. Be sure and drop by Allison’s website (allisonbrennan.com) for more about her books. I’d love you to drop by mine (debrawebb.com) and check out what’s new and coming soon. Thank you all so much for listening in to our conversation! Cheers!

#7851. Yes, Different Curb Colors Have a Meaning — A Guide to Decoding Them

A painted curb can tell drivers where to park, stop, or unload. Here's what red, yellow, green, blue, and white curbs usually mean.

Finding a parking spot isn’t always as simple as pulling up to an empty space. Sometimes different curb colors come with their own parking rules, and drivers might not know what those colors mean. The different curb colors help drivers know where they can park, stop, or drop someone off.

The California Driver’s Handbook lists five common colors: red, white, yellow, green, and blue. But those colors don’t mean exactly the same thing everywhere. Cities have their own parking rules, and some areas have restrictions that only apply during certain hours. Los Angeles, for example, has different rules for loading zones, while Seattle uses yellow paint to mark some areas near driveways that drivers need to keep clear.

Learn what the five colors generally mean and what drivers should know before parking.

Red curbs generally mean drivers can’t stop or park there, even for a few minutes. That includes waiting in the car while someone runs into a store. They’re common near fire hydrants, intersections, and bus stops, where parked cars could block traffic or get in the way. Some red zones still allow buses to stop to pick up or drop off passengers.

White curbs usually allow drivers to stop long enough to pick up or drop off passengers. They’re often found outside hotels, schools, and hospitals.

But they aren’t regular parking spaces. Drivers generally need to stay with their vehicles and leave once their passengers get in or out. Some cities have different rules, though. San Francisco, for example, also allows certain white curbs to be used for quickly loading or unloading goods.

Yellow curbs usually mark loading zones. They’re often found near businesses where delivery drivers need somewhere to stop while dropping off packages or other goods. Commercial vehicles can typically use these areas for a short time, although some cities allow passenger vehicles to stop there, too. These aren’t regular parking spaces, and nearby signs usually explain how long drivers can stop.

Green curbs generally mean drivers can park, but only for a short time. They’re common near businesses where customers might need to stop for a few minutes. The time limit isn’t always the same, so drivers should check the curb or nearby signs before leaving their cars. Some spaces also have parking meters or restrictions during certain hours.

Blue curbs mark parking spaces for people with disabilities. Cities often place these spaces near building entrances to make them easier to access. Drivers need a valid disability parking placard or qualifying license plate to park in these spaces. Without one, they can’t use the spot, even for a quick stop.

The striped areas next to accessible parking spaces also need to stay clear so people have enough room to get in and out of their vehicles.

#7849. How To Spot a Flood-Damaged Car Before You Buy It

Learn the subtle signs to look for to avoid buying a flooded car.

With the average cost of a new car approaching $50,000, it can make more financial sense to buy used. But, while the lower price point is appealing, mechanic David Martin says to shop carefully and to check any used car for signs of flooding. “Engine computers, sensors, electrical connectors and wiring are vulnerable to corrosion, expensive to fix and could endanger lives,” he says. Not all cars that have been in a flood will be given a flood title, and unscrupulous sellers will mask this fact from would-be buyers. Ahead, learn how to tell if you’re buying a flood-damaged car, with expert-backed advice from Martin.

Use your nose to detect water damage inside the vehicle. “If the car smells musty or moldy, watch out,” Martin says. “Also, pay attention to cars that have strong air freshener or detergent scents. They could be used to mask flood-related mildew.” Additionally, look for silt or mud in glove compartments or under seats where it may have been overlooked during cleaning. Finding it is a tell-tale sign the car has been flooded. Also look carefully for condensation behind instrument panels and interior and exterior lights.

Check for any rust or flaking metal on the car’s underside, especially on brake lines and around the fuel tank, Martin says. Lift the hood and look for corrosion on the battery terminals and engine components, then open the car doors and inspect the door hinges for signs of rust.

Vehicle upholstery and carpeting can reveal signs of flooding. Feel for dampness and look for stains, as well as loose, wrinkled or buckled carpeting. Additionally, pull seat belts all the way out to check for stains, mildew or mud and look for mismatched or recently replaced carpeting and upholstery.

Turn on the car and do a thorough test of the car’s electrical components. Check the power windows, door locks, seat controls, and backup camera. “Make sure all lights, the air conditioner, heater, wipers, turn signals, stereo and navigation systems work,” Martin says. “And test them more than once.” Even if an electrical component is working, check to make sure it’s working properly. Flickering lights and intermittent functioning can also be signs of water damage.

Flood-damaged cars may be moved across state lines and retitled, so always get a Carfax report, which tracks a vehicle’s complete history regardless of location. Additionally, run the vehicle’s VIN number through the National Insurance Crime Bureau. “The service can identify whether a car has been reported stolen or labeled as salvage by insurance companies due to flooding,” Martin says. “But, while these reports can be helpful, they don’t cover everything.That’s why having a certified mechanic inspect a used car before you buy is a smart investment.”

Even if you don’t suspect a car has been flooded after looking it over yourself, a professional mechanic could catch subtle signs you missed, as well as any other mechanical issues with the vehicle. Ask them to specifically check for signs of flooding.

Yes, a flood-damaged car can still have a clean title and show no record of flooding in its history.

No, not if you intend to drive it. Issues can continue to arise years after a flooding event that can impact the vehicle’s functioning. However, you could buy a flooded car with the intention of using it for parts.
